title: Value of Things: In the rearview mirror
summary: Some of you are undoubtedly confused at the title. The Texans are coming off of a bye week, so what exactly are we looking at in the rearview mirror? Well, this is what we would lovingly call self-scouting. We are looking at the Texans season rankings in the various categories to see if we can […]
full_text: Feb 2, 2023; Houston, TX, USA; Houston Texans head coach Demeco Ryans speaks to the media during his introductory press conference at NRG Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Erik Williams-USA TODAY Sports Some of you are undoubtedly confused at the title. The Texans are coming off of a bye week, so what exactly are we looking at in the rearview mirror? Well, this is what we would lovingly call self-scouting. We are looking at the Texans season rankings in the various categories to see if we can identify key points that they will need to improve on for the rest of the season, Obviously, if you are 2-5 on the season then there are definitely some things to improve on. However, not all 2-5 football teams are created equal. Teams like the Dolphins and Titans repeatedly (although not the last two weeks) get their doors blown off. The Chargers have been an absolute mess and I am watching two dreadful teams on Sunday night football as I type this. The Texans are minus seven points in point differential which would seem to predict a 3-4 or even 4-3 record in some instances. So, clearly it is not completely awful. So, the numbers we look at could be the beginning of figuring out a way around this. The team is 1-4 in one score games. Maybe some better luck is coming their way in the second half. Maybe there is one key adjustment they can make on either side of the ball to turn their fortunes around. The main thing is that the record really doesn’t accurately tell us what is going on with this football team. Key Numbers Total Yards: Offense 2367/13, Defense 2394/22 Rushing Yards: Offense 593/29, Defense 686/16 Passing Yards: Offense 1774/6, Defense 1708/29 Penalties: 58/508 (30th) Sacks: Offense 15 (17th). Defense 21 (2nd) Turnovers: Offense 3 (2nd), Defense 6 (26th) Points per game: Offense 23.6 (15th), Defense 24.3 (19th) Obviously, many of these numbers cut both ways, but there are a few that stand out when we get to the good, bad, and ugly on the season. We usually do great, good, and bad in victory, but with the team 2-5 victory doesn’t feel like the way to go. I should point out that they are mostly even in total yards and passing yards. They are in the positive on the plus/minus. It almost seems like they are finding creative ways to lose football games. This feels like a .500 team and that is where you would think they would end up. The Good We will actually get to C.J. Stroud later in the week, so we will not say too much on him in this space. However, there has been growth in the passing game in general. The team had some finds in the draft and free agency in terms of skill position players. Jaylin Noel looked a lot better before he went down with a season ending injury. Foster Moreau was a really good addition as a secondary tight end. We should remember this when we are levying our complaints about free agent signings and draft picks gone wrong. Not everything is negative and not everything is positive. Most seasons have both in somewhat equal measure. The difference would be the sheer number of injuries the Texans have sustained on both sides of the ball and there is little that can be done about that. The Bad A very significant part of me feels sorry for Nick Caley. For the last year and a half he has been the most convenient whipping boy for the fanbase and those of us at BRB have certainly participated in that whipping and I might be the most guilty party. This is where we point out that they have surrendered the second fewest turnovers in the NFL and are in the middle of the pack in points per game and total yards. So, whether or not you torch Caley depends largely on whether you are looking at it from 10,000 feet or five feet. The closer you look the more cracks you see in the veneer. You begin to notice one of the worst rushing attacks in the NFL. You notice an offense that looks dead at key points in games after the opposing polo has managed to scheme up something to stop the offense. Caley is just not good at adjusting on the fly. He can’t draw up a third and one play to save his life. These are things you can’t necessarily see when you look at just the aggregate data. Maybe even more importantly, we notice that key changes to personnel seem to come too late or not at all. David Montgomery was clearly inferior to Woody Marks, but stayed in the starting lineup until he was hurt. Xavier Hutchinso is still getting snaps over Marvin Harrison Jr. and was getting them over Jaylin Noel for much of the season. Maybe even more glaring, Keelan Rutledge is one of the lowest rated guards in the NFL according to PFF, but a superior Wyatt Teller is waiting on the bench. Evan Brown is one of the bottom five centers in the NFL and only a couple that could be called starters are listed below him. Part of this is on Nick Caserio for the players he gives to Caley. However, the other part is on Caley for not recognizing that certain guys needed to be replaced in the lineup. I know you don’t want to kill Rutledge’s confidence, but there comes a point when the best five guys need to be out there. More than anything, this probably goes to DeMeco Ryans more than anything. This isn’t a smash mouth running football team. It hasn’t been that at any time during Ryans’ tenure. I get that this is what he wants and that makes perfect sense, but at some point you need to go with what you are. You are a spread em’ out passing football team. You might as well lean into that. The Ugly The words we just said about the offense could be echoed about the defense. The main difference is that the defense was supposed to be a top five unit in the NFL. They certainly have not been that with the exception of the Tennessee Titans game. I could certainly write off the Jacksonville game to the field conditions or the Buffalo and Cincinnati game to playing top five quarterbacks in the league. There comes a certain point when you run out of excuses. There are three problems that we can isolate with the defense. The first is a lack of turnovers. Six turnovers through seven games is simply not good enough. That could be a function of performance, but it is probably more a factor of luck. Sometimes the bounces just don’t go your way. Still, there were a couple of prominent opportunities for picks that would have turned two losses into wins. A 4-3 start certainly looks a lot better than 2-5. The second problem is the same as above. Reed Blankenship is dead ass last in safeties according to PFF. I would say that we would be surprised, but PFF also rated him as one of the worst safeties last year. Somehow Caserio thought he was a good guy to sign anyway. Add in the fact that some other players (almost all in the secondary) have not played good football this year and you have the makings of a disappointing defense regardless of scheme. That brings us to scheme. The Texans have played more lax and more bend but don’t break defense. The obvious reason was to avoid big plays, but they still have given up a ton of big plays. They rely on the front four to get home and they do more often than most teams, but they need to have more consistent pressure. More importantly, they used to make life miserable for quarterbacks. Things have been way too easy for them this season. Ryans may not want to consider personnel changes or scheme changes, but after seven weeks the “it’s early” mantra just isn’t going to fly.
author: Scott Barzilla

title: At 2-6, why is Shane Steichen sticking with Daniel Jones?
summary: It’s time to investigate for malpractice, no? Shane Steichen is deciding to stick with Daniel Jones as the Indianapolis Colts’ starting quarterback, he told reporters Monday. Apparently, getting whooped 42-7 in Jacksonville after 21 games with Jones was not enough to convince Indy’s fourth-year coach to make the same change he made after 10 starts […]
full_text: Indianapolis Colts quarterback Daniel Jones throws a pass during a training camp practice at Gand Park Sports Campus in Westfield, Ind. — August 10, 2025 | Thomas Butler-Guerrero It’s time to investigate for malpractice, no? Shane Steichen is deciding to stick with Daniel Jones as the Indianapolis Colts’ starting quarterback, he told reporters Monday. Apparently, getting whooped 42-7 in Jacksonville after 21 games with Jones was not enough to convince Indy’s fourth-year coach to make the same change he made after 10 starts with his first draft selection. I’m not here to say Jones is the whole problem in Indianapolis, but you’re wrong, Shane. Jones is halfway through the least-efficient season of his eight-year NFL career. In eight games, the veteran quarterback has career-lows in completion rate (60%) and passer rating (68.7), with just five passing touchdowns against nine interceptions and 12 total turnovers. Since signing with Indy, Jones has scored 30 total touchdowns against 17 interceptions. Steichen explained his decision by mentioning “it goes back to the preparation and the command he has of the offense”, doubling down saying that he believes Jones gives the Colts the best chance to win right now. #Colts HC Shane Steichen, asked if Daniel Jones is held to a softer standard: “It goes back to the preparation and the command he has of the offense. …” “You want to have accountability, but like I said, I feel in this situation that he gives us the best chance to win.” pic.twitter.com/2jsFHaf1Jk — James Boyd (@RomeovilleKid) November 2, 2026 Somebody slam the buzzer, because once again, you’re wrong. Indianapolis sits at 2-6 after four consecutive defeats, coming off their worst performance in Duval County. The Colts have lost 13 of their last 15 games dating back to the 2025 collapse, while Jones has lost nine of his last 11 starts. Reminder that Richardson is 8-7 in 15 career starts. The Colts have already begun the fire sale, trading cornerstone All-Pros Quenton Nelson (2027 third, 2028 fifth) to Seattle and DeForest Buckner (2027 fourth) to San Francisco for future draft compensation. Whatever playoff aspirations that remained by Halloween have effectively disappeared overnight. The Colts have waved the white flag in 2026, so there is a legitimate argument to start Anthony Richardson in the final year of his rookie contract. I was in attendance for every training camp practice at Grand Park Sports Campus in Westfield, and will start off by saying the continued concerns were obvious. Richardson struggled with handling snaps, pre-snap reads and the finer details of operating an NFL offense. Jones was absolutely running Steichen’s run-pass-option offensive scheme better, with the starters of course. Richardson was stuck competing for the backup job while playing with the second unit, and sometimes with the third unit. Indy’s lack of development with Richardson will at some point be a talking point on what exactly not to do with a first-round QB. Those concerns haven’t magically disappeared, but at some point, the young quarterback has to get out of timeout and learn on the fly. Remember how rusty Richardson looked after essentially losing his rookie season? That’s how rusty Jones looks now and it’s midway through the season. Development demands playing time, and Indianapolis has done very little to give its former fourth overall pick a legitimate opportunity to get out of the dog house. Richardson offers a different look that Jones simply does not have off a torn Achilles. Richardson’s athleticism, mobility, arm strength and capability to threaten defenses with his legs and his arms is something that opponents “foam at the mouth at” when facing the Colts today. Those are the words from star running back Jonathan Taylor after the punishing loss on Sunday. Sure, Jones is more comfortable running play-action and run-pass-option concepts that have become Steichen’s bread and butter, but this scheme is not producing results. The Colts allowed six touchdowns on Sunday, while their offense has scored just five touchdowns combined over the last four games. Jones is getting pulverized, struggling to push the football downfield and repeatedly putting the defense in short fields with too many turnovers. There’s Indy’s $100 million financial commitment to Jones from 2025 through 2027, but at this point, that investment can’t continue to dictate who plays quarterback. Ed Dodds needs to pull a Moneyball style trade to send either Jones or Richardson to Baltimore, so at least he will do what’s best for the organization moving forward. The Colts have four games before their bye week, with the struggling Dallas defense coming into town. Steichen might believe Jones gives Indianapolis the best chance to win right now, but the better question is why is Jones given a different leash than Richardson, who was benched after 10 NFL starts.
author: Thomas Butler-Guerrero

title: Horsepower or Horseplay? Individual highlights from Week 8’s blowout loss at Jacksonville
summary: That was easily one to forget, as the Indianapolis Colts got blown out, 42-7, on the road against the Jacksonville Jaguars—keeping their sorry winless streak alive in Duval County, where the Horseshoe hasn’t won since 2014. I’d rather not relive one of the worst performances of the past decade by Indianapolis collectively, but we’ll keep […]
full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FL - NOVEMBER 01: CJ Allen #53 of the Indianapolis Colts reacts after a play during the game between the Jacksonville Jaguars and the Indianapolis Colts on November 1, 2026 at EverBank Stadium in Jacksonville, Fl. (Photo by David Rosenblum/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images That was easily one to forget, as the Indianapolis Colts got blown out, 42-7, on the road against the Jacksonville Jaguars—keeping their sorry winless streak alive in Duval County, where the Horseshoe hasn’t won since 2014. I’d rather not relive one of the worst performances of the past decade by Indianapolis collectively, but we’ll keep this weekly piece alive and not beat an already dead horse that is this 2026 Colts team too much for brevity’s sake: Horsepower LB CJ Allen: During his first career start, the Colts rookie 2nd round pick, who’s been slowed by injuries and arguably an initial first-year learning curve, delivered—with a team-high 10 tackles, a sack , a tackle for loss, and QB hit. With the Colts jumpstarting their rebuild earlier last week, this is clearly a ‘play the kids movement,’ which means Allen should continue to see continued starts and playing time to grow, develop, and for the Colts own internal evaluation going forward. After not playing at times to begin this season (*non-injury related), this first start was really encouraging by Allen nevertheless. Horseplay WR Josh Downs: To his credit, Downs had the only Colts’ touchdown on the afternoon, near midway through the 3rd quarter, down 35-0, on a 6-yard catch from Jones, but after requesting a trade earlier in the week from Indianapolis, was largely quiet and had an arguably poor effort recovering a fumble on a trick play . Downs did not make himself available to the media post-game . It’s a little surprising to me that Downs has shown such recent indifferent to the franchise that took a shot on him in the 3rd round of the 2023 NFL Draft and even initially started him 9 games as a rookie. Typically, public “trade requests” are reserved for proven veterans, who’ve earned the opportunity to continue their playing career elsewhere. Whether it’s for a 3rd or 4th round pick as Indy’s trade compensation return, count me as one who’s ready to move on without Downs this week. TE Tyler Warren: Better days are ahead for the Colts’ 2025 first round pick, who had just 18 total receiving yards on 4 receptions and a whopping 10 receiving targets after being blanketed by the Jacksonville defense collectively. However, perhaps most egregious on the afternoon, was a Colts quarterback Daniel Jones’ interception that went right through Warren’s hands and led to a 92-yard pick six return by Jaguars safety Rayuan Lane III with 10 seconds left in the first half. It was already well over, down 21-0 for Indianapolis, but that was clearly added salt on the Colts wound Sunday. Veteran DB Effort: Colts starting safety Cam Bynum shockingly finished with 0 tackles in this one , while their starting outside veteran cornerbacks showed very little extra effort and arguably made their own “business decisions” when attempting to tackle the Jaguars respective ball carriers. Even during an ongoing initial rebuild, you still have to have veterans leading by example out there and playing the right way, and right now, it looks like the remaining Colts defensive veterans still here have mailed it in already.
author: Luke Schultheis

title: Which Colts players should still matter by 2029?
summary: The Indianapolis Colts are in a difficult position, and after Sunday’s humiliating 42-7 loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars, it’s becoming increasingly clear that the franchise is much further away from contention than many originally believed. At 2-6, with Chris Ballard having already been fired and two of the organization’s most accomplished players traded away, Indianapolis […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MO - SEPTEMBER 20: Tyler Warren #84 of the Indianapolis Colts celebrates a touchdown with Matt Goncalves #71 in the first quarter of an NFL game between the Indianapolis Colts and Kansas City Chiefs on Sep 20, 2026 at Arrowhead Stadium in Kansas City, MO. (Photo by Scott Winters/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Indianapolis Colts are in a difficult position, and after Sunday’s humiliating 42-7 loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars, it’s becoming increasingly clear that the franchise is much further away from contention than many originally believed. At 2-6, with Chris Ballard having already been fired and two of the organization’s most accomplished players traded away, Indianapolis appears headed toward another significant rebuilding period. Unfortunately, this may not be a particularly quick turnaround. The Colts have already surrendered their 2027 first-round pick in the Sauce Gardner trade, and with several established veterans approaching free agency or the later stages of their careers, there is a legitimate argument that Indianapolis will struggle to compete next season as well. Even if the organization manages to find its next franchise quarterback in 2028, expecting that player to immediately transform the team into a contender would be unrealistic. With that in mind, I’m looking at 2029 as the first reasonable target for Indianapolis to become a legitimately competitive team again. That doesn’t mean the Colts cannot improve before then, but building a roster capable of consistently competing with the NFL’s best will require several successful drafts, meaningful player development and a much clearer long-term plan from whoever takes over as general manager. So rather than evaluating who deserves to start for the Colts today, I wanted to examine which players currently on the roster could realistically contribute to a winning team in 2029. Just as importantly, what roles should those players occupy? Someone might be a starter in Indianapolis right now but only qualify as a rotational player on a Super Bowl contender. Others could become genuine building blocks who remain with the franchise for the next several years. Age, contracts, performance and potential development all factor into these evaluations. I’ve separated 50 players into five categories, ranging from established players worth building around to those who likely won’t be part of the organization’s next competitive window. The projected ages refer approximately to the 2029 season, while several players would need extensions or new contracts to remain with Indianapolis by then. 1. Build around them These are the players I believe could hold legitimate starting roles on a competitive Colts team in 2029. Some are already among the best at their positions, while others are young enough to develop into important long-term contributors. Sauce Gardner — CB1 | Age 29 in 2029 Gardner is arguably the easiest player to include in this category. The Colts invested two first-round selections to acquire him from the New York Jets, and his four-year, $120.4 million extension runs through the 2030 season. While injuries have limited him at times, he remains one of the NFL’s premier cover corners and should still be performing at a high level in 2029. Indianapolis has already committed significant resources to making him a cornerstone of its defense, and barring a dramatic decline, Gardner should remain the team’s No. 1 cornerback throughout its next competitive window. Tyler Warren — TE1 | Age 27 Warren is another relatively straightforward selection. The former first-round pick has already demonstrated the versatility and receiving ability necessary to become one of the league’s better tight ends, and he should be entering his physical prime by 2029. His rookie contract runs through 2028, with Indianapolis holding a fifth-year option for 2029. Given his potential, I would expect the Colts to exercise that option if he continues developing as anticipated. Warren could become a foundational piece of the next offense, particularly if Indianapolis finally finds a long-term answer at quarterback. Bernhard Raimann — LT1 | Age 32 Raimann has experienced a somewhat disappointing 2026 season by the standards he established over the previous few years, but that shouldn’t erase the fact that he remains a quality starting left tackle. Indianapolis signed him to a four-year, $100 million extension running through 2029, providing valuable stability at one of the NFL’s most important positions. Although Raimann will be entering his early 30s by then, offensive tackles can remain effective well beyond that age, and there is little reason to believe the Colts should be looking for his replacement anytime soon. He might not be among the five best tackles in football, but he’s more than capable of protecting the blind side of a quarterback on a winning team. Alec Pierce — WR2 | Age 29 Pierce received a substantial four-year, $114 million extension during the 2026 offseason, meaning Indianapolis has already committed to keeping him around through 2029. His combination of size, speed and downfield ability makes him a valuable offensive weapon, although I believe his ideal role on a genuinely competitive team is as a complementary No. 2 receiver rather than the primary receiving option. Pierce can stretch defenses vertically and create explosive plays, but the Colts would benefit from eventually finding a more complete WR1 who can consistently win in multiple areas of the field. That would allow Pierce to focus on the strengths that make him such a dangerous player. Adetomiwa Adebawore — DT1 (3-technique) | Age 28 Adebawore might be the most exciting developmental piece on the Colts’ defensive line. His athleticism and ability to generate interior pressure have become increasingly apparent, particularly following his recent two-sack performance against Minnesota. With DeForest Buckner now in San Francisco, Adebawore has an opportunity to establish himself as the organization’s long-term starter at the three-technique position. However, his rookie contract expires after this season, making an extension an immediate priority. If Indianapolis can retain him and his development continues, he has the potential to become one of the defense’s most disruptive players by 2029. CJ Allen — MLB1 | Age 24 Allen is one of the few players on the roster who could still be several years away from reaching his prime when the Colts are ready to compete again. The 2026 second-round pick has started showing encouraging signs in recent weeks, demonstrating the instincts, physicality and range necessary to eventually become a reliable starting middle linebacker. His rookie contract runs through 2029, providing Indianapolis with a young defensive player who should still be relatively inexpensive during the proposed competitive window. While it’s far too early to call him a star, Allen has shown enough to make me comfortable projecting him as the long-term MIKE linebacker, assuming his development continues. Matt Goncalves — RG1 | Age 28 Goncalves has quietly developed into one of the more dependable young players on the offensive line and looks capable of holding down the starting right guard position for years to come. His rookie contract expires after the 2027 season, meaning Indianapolis would need to negotiate a second deal to retain him through 2029. Given his age, versatility and improvement since arriving in the league, that should be a priority if his performance remains consistent. The Colts have already lost Quenton Nelson and cannot afford to keep replacing quality offensive linemen. Goncalves may never reach Nelson’s level, but he has the potential to become a long-term starter on a competitive offensive line. Cam Bynum — FS1 | Age 31 Bynum is somewhat different from the younger players in this category because he will be entering his 30s by the time Indianapolis is ready to…

title: That performance from the Colts was as bad as it gets
summary: Ugly. That is the best and most PG word I can think of to describe what we witnessed on Sunday in Jacksonville. That is if “we” even watched that game. Maybe you tuned in out of curiosity in the first quarter, but if you stuck around from beginning to end, you are stronger than I […]
full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FLORIDA - NOVEMBER 1: Wide receiver Parker Washington #11 of the Jacksonville Jaguars runs for a first down in the second quarter against the Indianapolis Colts at EverBank Stadium on November 1, 2026 in Jacksonville, Florida. (Photo by Parker S. Freedman/Getty Images) | Getty Images Ugly. That is the best and most PG word I can think of to describe what we witnessed on Sunday in Jacksonville. That is if “we” even watched that game. Maybe you tuned in out of curiosity in the first quarter, but if you stuck around from beginning to end, you are stronger than I am. That was rough. A shattered franchise must now pick up the pieces and figure out what to do. The Indianapolis Colts weren’t just bad on Sunday; they were horrific. It definitely fit the vibe of Halloween weekend because it was downright terrifying. 28-0 was the score at halftime as a fumble and an interception returned for a touchdown led the way. Tyler Warren had four receptions on ten targets for 18 yards. Ouch . One of them bounced off him and into the arms of a Jags defender who took it to the house. That was the last moment, if there were any before, that one might have thought this team had any fight left. Daniel Jones is barely throwing the ball downfield. His 144 yards isn’t going to cut it. Actually, it didn’t, as Anthony Richardson came into the game late. Was it because of the blowout, or is there something more? Rumors are starting to swirl that the Colts might make a change. Swapping quarterbacks won’t fix this defense, though. The tackling and coverage were atrocious. This is Chris Ballard’s roster, ladies and gentlemen. The roster is being picked over like a carcass on the side of the road. The effort is seemingly gone, and other teams are set to feast. As bad as it is, it might get worse. The Colts are back to no viable quarterback, a place where Chris Ballard has had this team for years. They don’t have a first-round pick either. I’m not sure if the Colts have hit rock bottom yet, but it sure is dark. I don’t want to see where they go from here.
author: Jon Spradley

title: Jaguars Winners and Losers From Week 8: Jags Dominate Lifeless Colts
summary: As we have said in this column all year: sometimes you just need to beat the brakes off a bad team. The Jacksonville Jaguars did just that on Sunday, winning 42-7 over the hapless and directionless Indianapolis Colts.  Sunday’s box score was just about as good as it could possibly get with Trevor Lawrence throwing […]
full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FLORIDA - NOVEMBER 1: Defensive end Travon Walker #44 of the Jacksonville Jaguars celebrates sacking quarterback Daniel Jones #17 of the Indianapolis Colts in the first quarter at EverBank Stadium on November 1, 2026 in Jacksonville, Florida. (Photo by Parker S. Freedman/Getty Images) | Getty Images As we have said in this column all year: sometimes you just need to beat the brakes off a bad team. The Jacksonville Jaguars did just that on Sunday, winning 42-7 over the hapless and directionless Indianapolis Colts. Sunday’s box score was just about as good as it could possibly get with Trevor Lawrence throwing effectively and with command. Bhayshul Tuten played incredibly well and even Brian Thomas Jr. caught a ball. Defensively, the Jags had four sacks with one even coming from Travon Walker. The Colts suck but it still was a needed divisional win to keep the Jaguars atop the AFC South and in the hunt for a top overall AFC seed. Jacksonville even got better news later in the day when Baltimore Ravens’ quarterback Lamar Jackson hit injured reserve before Thursday night’s game in Baltimore. Unfortunately for Jacksonville, the injury bug bit the team hard Sunday with DaVon Hamilton being the big name hurt. Hamilton was carted off the field and it has been reported he tore his quad and is done for the year. But such is life in the National Football League. For now, it’s time for a Victory Monday celebration. WINNERS Bhayshul Tuten The Jags made an incredible decision when they decided to give the running back room keys to Tuten. It has paid off in a huge way with almost inarguably Tuten’s best game coming Sunday against the Colts. The second-year running back led the team in both receiving (two catches for 55 yards and one score) and rushing (16 carries for 104 yards and one score). He scored twice in one game for the second time in two consecutive tries. His 159 total yards were the most by a Jag since 2023. Tuten’s hard, downhill running style gives the Jags an extremely helpful punisher on offense that most teams simply are not prepared for. When Tuten is tooting along, the Jags are a nasty offense that can score with the best of them. Every touch by Bhayshul Tuten against the Colts. Contact balance, elusiveness, leg drive, and speed is all there. Total package pic.twitter.com/eJsIXL4SvK — Billy M (@BillyM_91) November 2, 2026 Nate Boerkircher The conversation on Nate Boerkircher has been very fun. No, he does not get 20 targets a game but he certainly makes the most of them when he does. The rookie second-rounder caught just one pass on Sunday, but he took it for 31 yards and a score. Like Tuten, he has touchdowns now in back-to-back games after going scoreless for the first five games of his career. Boerkircher caught his pass for Lawrence – who did an incredible job to evade pressure – and found himself wide open. It wasn’t a one-handed leap like last week, but the rook has caught all five of his targets in his last three games. Trevor Lawrence finds a wide open Nate Boerkircher for his 2nd TD pass of the first half! INDvsJAX on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/H3ubmhXBZo — NFL (@NFL) November 1, 2026 The Defensive Line For weeks, or even years at this point, we have all been calling for sacks from this defensive line. That all fixed itself on Sunday. Jacksonville left its game against the Colts with four sacks. Foye Oluokun, Travon Walker and randomly rookie safety Jalen Huskey all had full sacks. Josh Hines-Allen and Arik Armstead were both credited with .5 each. You would have to go all the way back to the opener when the Jags had that many sacks in a game when they had five against the Browns. In terms of PFF grades, three Jags defensive linemen were among the top-five graded players. It got so bad for the Colts that even Rayuan Lane (who had a nice game by the way) was getting pressures. Finally, a full-circle game from that defensive line unit. top five Jaguars in Week 8 PFF grading RB Bhayshul Tuten (90.8) EDGE Josh Hines-Allen (89.7) EDGE Dennis Gardeck (83.7) EDGE Travon Walker (82.6) LT Walker Little (77.6) https://t.co/QU2db5rSUT — Gus Logue (@gus_logue) November 1, 2026 As an aside, with Hamilton’s injury, this probably forces the hand of the Jags to make a play for a run-stopping defensive lineman. That trade could very even include sending Brian Thomas Jr. somewhere else. Maybe this is all addition by subtraction in the end. Travis Hunter Sunday was not a “Travis Hunter game” but he just simply rocks as a Jaguar. He looks cool in the rivalries and is an asset on both sides of the ball. He truly is a force multiplier because offenses have to be worried about throwing near him and defenses have to worry about his quick shift speed as a receiver. Yeah, it took a little for it all to shake out in terms of usage, but it is all working well now. Look at all of the eyes on Travis Hunter on the Tuten TD after setting this play up in the first quarter pic.twitter.com/JbniHAFZ8L — John Shipley (@_John_Shipley) November 2, 2026 Al’s Pizza Courtesy of two Daniel Jones picks to Lane and Branson Combs (never thought I’d type those names together) Jaguars fans can get 50% Al’s Pizza with the code PIZZAPICKOFF. What’s better than some pizza and the knowledge that at least two AFC South teams are utterly horrible? LOSERS Injuries That Hamilton injury is going to be an issue. No telling how big or when, but it’s going to change some things. And he was not alone. Walker got banged up and so did guard Ezra Cleveland. No injury is worse than seeing Hamilton carted off the field Sunday morning after how well he has been playing, though. Christian Barmore is a name that comes to mind to replace Hamilton, but we will have to see. That victory on Sunday could have been that much better if the Jags were to come out of it healthy. The Rest of the NFL There are some real bad teams in the NFL. The Jacksonville Jaguars aren’t one of them. Across the league, the Bucs won a game without completing a pass. The Titans took the Bengals to overtime. The Cowboys lost again. The Chargers lost AGAIN. The Vikings still can’t score on offense and the Eagles might just quit playing football altogether. A decent bit has been said about how cupcake the schedule ahead is for Jacksonville, but so what? We can’t help that we are good when everyone else outside of like three seems seemingly suck. What a great time to be a fan of the Jaguars. Give us your thoughts on Sunday’s game and some names of who you might want to see the Jags acquire to replace Hamilton. And we will see you right back here on a short week as the Jags look to keep the good vibes going against Baltimore on Thursday.
author: Henry Zimmer

title: Jacksonville Jaguar News: Jags earn ‘A’ in blowout win over Colts
summary: The Jaguars took advantage of a Colts teams on that Sunday that just finished sending two of their cornerstone players elsewhere. Jacksonville won 42-7 and may have just forced the Colts to continue selling off their best remaining pieces on the roster to fully embrace the upcoming rebuild. For their efforts, CBS Sports’ John Breech […]
full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FL - NOVEMBER 01: Runningback Bhayshul Tuten #33 of the Jacksonville Jaguars runs in for a touchdown during the first half of the game against the Indianapolis Colts at EverBank Stadium on November 1, 2026 in Jacksonville, Florida. (Photo by Don Juan Moore/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Jaguars took advantage of a Colts teams on that Sunday that just finished sending two of their cornerstone players elsewhere. Jacksonville won 42-7 and may have just forced the Colts to continue selling off their best remaining pieces on the roster to fully embrace the upcoming rebuild. For their efforts, CBS Sports’ John Breech gave them a shining “A” grade in his weekly report card series. ‘‘It took eight weeks, but Bayshul Tuten finally had his breakout game, and it was impressive: The Jaguars running back topped 100 yards on the ground with a TD, and he added another 55 receiving yards with another TD. This was exactly what the Jags were hoping to see from Tuten when they let Travis Etienne leave in free agency. Tuten has been good this year and it looks like he might be ready to make the jump to great. Defensively, the Jags came out of their bye on fire: They harassed Daniel Jones to the tune of three sacks and Rayuan Lane III added a 92-yard pick-six that essentially iced the game in the second quarter (Yes, this game was over in the second quarter). The blowout win meant the Jags could bench several starters in the fourth quarter, a huge perk for a Jacksonville team that has to turn around and play on Thursday night.” Do you think this was the correct grade? full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FLORIDA - NOVEMBER 1: Defensive tackle Davon Hamilton #52 of the Jacksonville Jaguars leaves the game in the second quarter against the Indianapolis Colts at EverBank Stadium on November 1, 2026 in Jacksonville, Florida. (Photo by Parker S. Freedman/Getty Images) | Getty Images The worst came true for Jacksonville after seeing defensive tackle DaVon Hamilton carted off the field Sunday. During Jacksonville’s lopsided 42-7 win over the Indianapolis Colts, Hamilton was carted off the field with a leg injury. That injury is now being reported as a torn quad which should keep Hamilton sidelined for the rest of the season. Sources: #Jaguars standout DT DaVon Hamilton suffered a torn quad in Sunday’s win over the #Colts , and he’s expected to be out for the season. Hamilton will undergo more tests today, but a massive hole for Jacksonville. pic.twitter.com/suJ2Hvp1av — Ian Rapoport (@RapSheet) November 2, 2026 It goes without saying how big, both physically and figuratively, Hamilton has been for Jacksonville along the defensive line. He’s the anchor for Jacksonville’s league best rush defense, which allows the fewest yards per carry in the league at 3.4 per. The Jags have allowed just one rush of over 20 yards, and are tied for the league lead in rushing first downs at just 30 all with Hamilton in the middle. Prior to his injury, Hamilton had a half sack and one forced fumble on the year as well as pitching in as the team’s emergency long snapper out in London. The former Ohio State product is also in a contract year, with the Jags able to get out of his three-year contract starting at the end of the season if the injury potentially presents itself as something far worse. Hamilton’s injury could now force the Jaguars now to make a move for a defensive tackle. Washington’s Daron Payne is off the board as he too is injured, but someone like New England’s Christian Barmore could be someone Jacksonville could pair alongside Arik Armstead during the team’s run at a Super Bowl. Jacksonville did pick up Ruke Orhorhoro as insurance along the interior and he has played in all seven games. The team could also choose to slot Travon Walker more in the middle. The Jags did draft Albert Regis in the third round of this year’s draft, but he has been mostly inactive this year. Jags fans, let us know your thoughts in the comments below.

title: 3 Numbers to Know From the Jaguars’ Win Over the Colts
summary: The Jacksonville Jaguars mollywhopped the Indianapolis Colts in Week 8, moving to 5-2 on the season. Heck yes. Here are a few stats that stand out from the win. 1 That’s the number of players in Jaguars history to record a game with 100-plus rushing yards, 1 rushing touchdown, 50-plus receiving yards, and 1 receiving […]
full_text: Jacksonville Jaguars running back Bhayshul Tuten (33) smiles as he crosses the goal line during the second quarter of an an NFL football matchup at EverBank Stadium on Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026, in Jacksonville, Fla. [Corey Perrine/Florida Times-Union] | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Jacksonville Jaguars mollywhopped the Indianapolis Colts in Week 8, moving to 5-2 on the season. Heck yes. Here are a few stats that stand out from the win. 1 That’s the number of players in Jaguars history to record a game with 100-plus rushing yards, 1 rushing touchdown, 50-plus receiving yards, and 1 receiving touchdown. We just witnessed The Bhayshul Tuten Breakout Game. And it was glorious. Every touch by Bhayshul Tuten against the Colts. Contact balance, elusiveness, leg drive, and speed is all there. Total package pic.twitter.com/eJsIXL4SvK — Billy M (@BillyM_91) November 2, 2026 Tuten became just the sixth Jaguar to score multiple touchdowns of 25-plus yards in the same game. The only other Jaguar with one rushing touchdown of 25-plus yards and one receiving touchdown of 25-plus yards in the same game is Fred Taylor, who did it in Jacksonville’s divisional round blowout against the Miami Dolphins in January 2000. The only other NFL player to do that so far this season is Jaylen Warren, who also tortured the Colts back in Week 5. Tuten finished with 106 rushing yards to notch his first 100-yard rushing game at the pro level. By the looks of it, I’d guess it will be the first of many. “I think with the run game, it started with my reads,” Tuten detailed postgame. “I was much cleaner on it and just harping on my details with my landmarks and that kind of stuff. Just playing fast and physical, not having to worry about anything. Then in the pass game, for me just being where I’m supposed to be. Trev did a great job dumping it down to me. It’s all she wrote from there when the ball’s in my hands. So, I think it was both running and receiving was great for me.” 1.1 That’s how much Expected Points Added (EPA) the Jaguars averaged on pass plays out of 12 personnel (two tight ends), according to SumerSports. It’s the best such figure by any offense in Week 8 entering Monday Night Football, and the ninth-best such figure by any offense in any game so far this season. For context, the Los Angeles Rams averaged 0.21 EPA per pass play when Matthew Stafford won MVP last season. When Jacksonville passed with two tight ends on Sunday, their offense was four times as efficient as the 2025 Rams. Brenton Strange recorded his longest career catch on a 46-yard pickup with a second tight end (Nate Boerkircher) and an extra offensive lineman (Wyatt Milum) on the field. Later, Boerkircher hauled in his longest career touchdown on a 31-yard bomb with three tight ends. “He wants to see me succeed just as bad as I want to see him succeed,” Boerkircher said of Strange postgame. “Like I said, I am very blessed to be in this situation.” Trevor Lawrence posted a career-high 153.3 passer rating — despite no Jaguars wide receivers finishing with 25 yards. Tuten and Strange (55 yards apiece) were his top weapons. Liam Coen is like that. 7 That’s how many consecutive wins of 17-plus points the Jaguars have at EverBank Stadium. It’s the third-longest such streak of games at a team’s home stadium in NFL history, trailing only the 1999 Super Bowl Champion Rams and the 1948-49 NFL Champion Eagles. Jacksonville has also scored 34-plus points at EverBank Stadium the same seven-game stretch. That’s tied for the longest such streak in league history, joining Peyton Manning’s 2012-13 Broncos and Sid Gillman’s 1960-61 Chargers. The Jaguars’ stadium renovations will prevent them from maximizing their home-field advantage until 2028. In fact, Sunday’s game against Indianapolis was the only game Jacksonville will play at EverBank Stadium over an eight-week stretch this season. Shoutout to the team for showing out for the city with the few opportunities they have. “We haven’t been at home much,” Coen said postgame. “Wanted to be able to put on a show for our home fan base and give the people some excitement.” “We’ve typically played well at home and I think that that’s something these guys take a lot of pride in. They understand and feel the limited opps that we do have in this stadium, that we want to take advantage of those opportunities and jump out. And we played complementary football. Typically when we do that and we’re getting turnovers and we’re able to get some points off of turnovers, that’s usually a recipe for success and our guys kind of sense that. They feel that. They do a nice job of capitalizing on that.” DUUUVAL! Join the game-day conversation on the SB Nation app! Kansas City Chiefs’ late collapse vs. Denver Broncos opens up AFC West race | ESPN Reid did have another option, especially with Butker’s struggles this season when kicking long field goals. full_text: (Photo by Justin Edmonds/Getty Images) | Getty Images Disappointing. Discouraging. Disheartening. Many adjectives could describe the feelings after the (5-2) Kansas City Chiefs ’ fourth-quarter collapse against the (6-2) Denver Broncos in Week 8, but Chiefs Kingdom isn’t alone in suffering a crushing defeat this weekend. Before the Chiefs kicked off later in the afternoon, the Dallas Cowboys blew a 24-10 lead in the fourth quarter against the Arizona Cardinals in front of the home fans at AT&T Stadium. Former Chiefs backup quarterback Gardner Minshew turned back the clock and delivered a vintage gunslinger performance to lead Arizona back and win 33-30 in overtime. It kept Dallas from improving to 4-4 and closing in on the (4-2-1) New York Giants in a division that feels completely up for grabs, with the shortcomings of the (2-4-1) Washington Commanders and (2-6) Philadelphia Eagles this season. According to the national fans in SB Nation’s ‘Reacts’ poll from Sunday, the Cowboys’ collapse was the only loss that was more “crushing” than the Chiefs losing their grip on the game and the division race in Denver. The (4-4) Baltimore Ravens were in a close third place after a blowout loss to the Buffalo Bills on the road; the crushing part of the defeat was the news that quarterback Lamar Jackson (thumb) may be out for the rest of the season. Do you think the Chiefs were the most crushing defeat of Week 8? Or does Dallas take the cake? Let us know in the comments.

title: Andy Reid talks about Chiefs’ self-inflicted issues in loss to Broncos
summary: On Monday afternoon, Kansas City Chiefs head coach Andy Reid took questions from reporters after the 28-24 loss to the Denver Broncos on Sunday in Week 8. The game featured a fourth-quarter lead blown and an AFC West lead relinquished, everything coming down to a final fourth-and-goal stop by Denver’s defense. Reid opened the video […]
full_text: (Photo by AAron Ontiveroz/The Denver Post) | Denver Post via Getty Images On Monday afternoon, Kansas City Chiefs head coach Andy Reid took questions from reporters after the 28-24 loss to the Denver Broncos on Sunday in Week 8. The game featured a fourth-quarter lead blown and an AFC West lead relinquished, everything coming down to a final fourth-and-goal stop by Denver’s defense. Reid opened the video call by acknowledging how often the Chiefs shot themselves in the foot. “When we stalled, we normally had something that was self-inflicted that stalled us,” Reid reflected during his opening statement. “Not necessarily what [Denver] did. Then, defensively, we really did a nice job up through the three quarters, then the fourth quarter, had some missed tackles, we slipped in one case in a spot, and thus, couldn’t make the tackle and put us in a bind there with them driving the long field.” This lack of a play by linebacker Nick Bolton came to mind when Reid mentioned a defensive player slipping over the middle. However, this game had more follies. Reid explained what went wrong on the 54-yard field goal that was pushed to the right and missed with roughly two-and-a-half minutes to go. “I could kind of see what he saw on that as far as he went up going too far right, but I see why he went right, too,” Reid said. “We never talk about the protection on that and the overloads, but when you have a heavy overload on the left side and penetration there, that’s going to alter a kicker; that’s just what you do as a kicker. “It’s no different than what quarterbacks do when they’re throwing the football, so sometimes, you have to alter the alignment there, so I get it, he just went a little bit too wide on it, but we have to do a better job of the protection for him there.” When asked a follow-up question clarifying that Reid was implying Butker would have seen his kick blocked if not adjusted to the right, the head coach confirmed that was his belief. It wasn’t Butker’s struggles nor the decision to kick that doomed the chance to go up six points late in the game, it was the blown protection! However, there may be no more frustrating play on second look than the team’s third-and-goal run from the one-yard line that was stuffed. Running back Kenneth Walker received the handoff and was immediately met by defenders. “That was one of our self-inflicted wounds there,” Reid remembered. “We didn’t block it right on the right side there; we have to make sure we get our assignment right.” The biggest point of contention for reporters like Sam McDowell of The Kansas City Star is the lack of a threat the Chiefs pose to run a quarterback sneak. He asked Reid about that, because as you can see from the replay, Denver had no bodies in the strong-side A-gap and was vulnerable to a sneak. Still, Reid doesn’t see the problem in the Broncos’ lack of respect for the sneak call. “Other than that, we’ve been pretty successful without sneaking it over time here,” Reid added. Nothing feels as self-inflicted with the Chiefs’ offense as letting a freak play from seven years ago dictate play-calling in short yardage. In an era of the “Tush Push,” the Chiefs have dwindled away from even lining up a tight end under center and sneaking it that way. We've seen the Chiefs experiment with guys like Jet, Mecole, and Travis on read-option looks for short-yardage or red-zone packages Having an actual QB run those looks makes those plays less risky, and Fields may even raise the upside of those play calls pic.twitter.com/EXXYkCOzV2 — Ron Kopp Jr (@RonOnChiefs) March 19, 2026 Backup quarterback Justin Fields is a run threat and has not seen the field once this season. The wrinkle could still be coming, but there was no wrinkle on third-and-goal in Denver. After a series of fourth-quarter errors, Kansas City beat itself as much as the Broncos did on Sunday, and it remains to be seen how much the team will adjust its strategies based on what Denver and the Seattle Seahawks exposed over the last two weeks.

AFC Standings Going into Week 9 1. Buffalo Bills (6-1) — AFC East leader 2. Denver Broncos (6-2) — AFC West leader 3. Pittsburgh Steelers (6-2) — AFC North leader 4. Jacksonville Jaguars (5-2) — AFC South leader As of now, the Bills are in the driver’s seat to earning a postseason bye and making the conference’s road to Super Bowl LXI go through New Highmark Stadium. The Chiefs’ matchup with Buffalo on Thanksgiving night could be Kansas City’s final chance to stay alive for the No.1 seed. Jacksonville currently sits as the lowest seed among the division leaders because of an early bye week, but the Jaguars lead the NFL in point differential (+85) and look like the most complete team in the conference right now. Denver’s 3-1 record in the AFC so far gives them a current leg up over Pittsburgh (3-2). 5. Kansas City Chiefs (5-2) 6. Cincinnati Bengals (5-2) 7. New England Patriots (5-3) The Patriots currently hold the tiebreaker over another 5-3 AFC playoff contender — the Cleveland Browns — due to a 5-1 record against conference opponents compared to Cleveland’s 3-3 mark. The Chiefs are also 5-1 against AFC teams so far, giving them a leg up on the Bengals, who are 4-2 in-conference. Cincinnati lost its first head-to-head matchup with division-leading Pittsburgh, but the rematch is in a couple of weeks and could vault the Bengals into the top-4 seeds. 8. Cleveland Browns (5-3) 9. Las Vegas Raiders (4-4) 10. Baltimore Ravens (4-4) The remaining AFC teams with records at or above .500 could make things interesting any given Sunday, but don’t feel as threatening as the seven teams currently in the playoff picture. The Chiefs will still play the Bills, the Bengals, and the Patriots this season.

There was no reason to have Butker try a kick in those conditions. That should have been a punt. Let's hear your biggest takeaways from the Chiefs' 28-24 loss to the Broncos — Arrowhead Pride (@ArrowheadPride) November 2, 2026 Chiefs fans on X were also asked for their biggest takeaways from the loss. Here were some of the top comments: Dustin @wtxjayhawk They could hold tryouts in the KC Metro and find a dude off the street that’s a better field goal kicker than Butker. The dude is so washed it’s unbelievable. 9WPND5 @9WPND5 That one is on Andy Carson Wendt @Carsonwendt2 This all started when Andy refused to go for it on 4th and inches. Milsurp Mike Andy must give up the play calling sheet. He is getting away from under center far too often. Also, punting on 4th and inches was cowardly and calling a pass play on 3rd and 2 when Walker was running it down their throats where Mahomes took the sack is unforgivable. Also… Fire Toub. Jon @j_coleman71 That loss is squarely on Andy. Horrible coaching in the fourth quarter. Brad Hughes @solocoach13 Andy Reid lost this game on quite a few occasions. There’s a common theme in the most liked and rec’d comments from Chiefs fans last night: head coach Andy Reid and the coaching staff as a whole mismanaged the late lead on the road. The collapse matters more because of the stakes in the AFC West race. The question from here: will that be a recurring theme against contenders, or a blip on the radar against a Broncos team that seems to magically pull these fourth-quarter comebacks out constantly, especially in Denver?
author: Ron Kopp Jr.

title: Chiefs Week 8 snap count analysis: Cyrus Allen sees season-high workload
summary: Welcome to Arrowhead Pride’s weekly snap-count analysis! Let’s take a closer look at the Kansas City Chiefs’ snap counts in the 28-24 loss to the Denver Broncos in Week 8. The starting lineups are courtesy of NFL Game Stats and Information, and the snap-count data comes from Pro Football Focus’ premium stats. Starters (offensive): LT Kahlil Benson, […]
full_text: (Photo by Alika Jenner/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome to Arrowhead Pride’s weekly snap-count analysis! Let’s take a closer look at the Kansas City Chiefs ’ snap counts in the 28-24 loss to the Denver Broncos in Week 8. The starting lineups are courtesy of NFL Game Stats and Information, and the snap-count data comes from Pro Football Focus’ premium stats. Starters (offensive): LT Kahlil Benson, LG Mike Caliendo, C Creed Humphrey, RG Trey Smith, RT Jaylon Moore, QB Patrick Mahomes, WR Rashee Rice, WR Xavier Worthy, RB Kenneth Walker, TE Travis Kelce and TE Noah Gray Starters (defensive): DE George Karlaftis, DT Chris Jones, DT Khyiris Tonga, DE Felix Anudike-Uzomah, LB Nick Bolton, LB Drue Tranquill, LB Jack Cochrane, CB Kristian Fulton, CB Nohl Williams, S Alohi Gilman and S Chamarri Conner Did not play: QB Justin Fields, OT Joshua Ezeudu Inactive: QB Garrett Nussmeier (Emergency third QB), CB Mansoor Delane (Shoulder), FB Ben VanSumeren, DE Jack Pyburn, DE Tyreke Smith and OT Diego Pounds The big takeaway: Cyrus Allen is moving up the depth chart In Denver, wide receiver Xavier Worthy led all skill-position players in snaps (64) by playing 94% of the time the unit was on the field. It felt like wideout Rashee Rice (38 snaps, 56% of the offensive snaps), in his return from the hamstring tweak, was playing on a pitch count due to the soft-tissue injury Rookie wide receiver Cyrus Allens stepped up to play 30 snaps, including 22 reps on pass plays. He out-snapped second-year wideouts Jalen Royals and Andrew Armstrong by 8 snaps, although those two saw more action in run-blocking situations. Allen caught two passes on three targets, but the miss was nearly a huge play downfield; it appeared Allen wasn’t anticipating the ball in tight coverage, so he slowed down on his route. He may not have been as open as it appeared due to that hesitation, but he still could’ve had a chance at a tight-window completion, a similar play as the ones he made in training camp to originally start the hype train. Allen’s 20 yards over the two catches were more than Worthy (13 yards) produced in less than half the playing time. The Offensive takeaway: Emmett Johnson is earning more and more touches Lead back Ken Walker played 55 snaps and dominated the run share, but rookie Emmett Johnson had his breakout game despite just 13 offensive snaps. He saw just one handoff, but gained 15 yards on the tackle-breaking, highlight-reel play. Johnson saw 12 snaps on pass plays and ran routes on 11 of those snaps (staying in for pass protection just once). He caught all five of the passes thrown his way and totaled 128 yards, including the 73-yard touchdown catch-and-run in the first half. With 143 yards from scrimmage, Johnson out-produced Walker (84 yards) in 1/4 of the playing time. He also played nine snaps on special teams and gained 44 yards on his only kickoff return of the afternoon. With return specialist Nikko Remigio struggling, Johnson should be strongly considered as the primary returner moving forward. The Defensive takeaway: Jadon Canady emerges as L’Jarius Sneed replacement The primary slot defender moving forward is Chris Roland-Wallace, and that seemed to be the case even before L’Jarius Sneed was placed on the Reserve/Injured list on Saturday. Roland-Wallace played 49 snaps in Denver and dominated the slot snaps. However, rookie cornerback Jadon Canady was active for the second time this season and made an impact for the first time on defense. As the sixth defensive back in the Chiefs’ Dime defense, a pass-down package predicated on coverage, Canady took seven snaps and made two tackles on third downs that were short of the sticks. He only defended pass plays; he may not be ready to man the slot on neutral downs and defend the run, but he looks like an asset for the Chiefs’ coverage moving forward. title: 5 things we learned from the Chiefs’ heartbreaking collapse in Denver
summary: Last week’s loss sucked. The Kansas City Chiefs were dominated and outplayed in every phase of the game. This one hurt more. Not just because the Chiefs should have beaten the Denver Broncos, but because of how they lost and what was at stake in the AFC West. It felt like the defense played well […]
full_text: (Photo by Matthew Stockman/Getty Images) | Getty Images Last week’s loss sucked. The Kansas City Chiefs were dominated and outplayed in every phase of the game. This one hurt more. Not just because the Chiefs should have beaten the Denver Broncos , but because of how they lost and what was at stake in the AFC West. It felt like the defense played well enough to win. It also felt like the offense moved the ball well enough to win. It wasn’t the 90% of the plays that cost the Chiefs; it was the minutiae . The little things that all add up to a team coming up one play short when they needed it the most. Here are five things we learned from the Chiefs losing to Denver 28-24 in Week 8. 1. Sack Nation is dead The Chiefs’ pass rush isn’t bad. It’s non-existent. \We’re almost halfway through the season, and the Chiefs have recorded a total of eight sacks. It’s tough to come to grips with the fact that Chris Jones is no longer the game wrecker he once was. Peter Woods left early with a neck stinger , but he hasn’t been a difference-maker in his short time in the NFL. And that’s about it for interior pass rushers who still have a shot at getting to the quarterback. The edge rushers are faring a little bit better, getting the occasional pressure, but close only counts in horseshoes and hand grenades. “George Karlaftis got close there” – feels like a perpetual theme. Always so close — Sterling Holmes (@HomestretchKC) October 26, 2026 It’s embarrassing to still refer to the Chiefs’ pass rush as “Sack Nation.” Especially when one of the few things they do well is knock down passes. So I’m proposing we retire the moniker Sack Nation and come up with a more fitting one. I propose: The Batting Cage. 2. The coaching staff needs to make better choices The choice to trot Harrison Butker out to attempt a 58-yard field goal in the rain when he has failed to convert anything over 50 yards, when you’re up three with two and a half minutes left to play, is a wild decision to make. I get trying to show faith in your guy who has shown up for you in the past. But part of being a head coach is having the huevos rancheros to know when a guy is cooked or in a slump, and make the tough/sometimes unpopular choice to adjust accordingly. The same goes for defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo’s refusal to adjust his scheme and game plan to attempt to generate more pass rush. Or the unforgivable crime of slipping into prevent defense when Kansas City was up by two scores late in the fourth quarter. I won’t get into special teams coordinator Dave Toub here, because those huevos went bad two seasons ago; now they’re just stinking up the chicken coop. There was a lot of pressure on Chiefs kicker Harrison Butker coming into this game after Justin Tucker was signed after what I’m told was an outstanding tryout. Butker went 1/2 and missed a crucial kick late. pic.twitter.com/sbuTghT6HM — James Palmer (@JamesPalmerTV) November 2, 2026 We’ll see if the Chiefs make the move to call up Justin Tucker this week. Speaking of huevos. I hope the organization finds the internal fortitude to skip plan B (Tucker) and find a less slimy solution to their kicking woes than a sleazeball who is no better than Deshaun Watson. Perhaps a guy like free agent Tanner Brown, who was the UFL’s Special Teams Player of the Year in 2026 , making three field goals from 60+ yards this past season. 3. Emmett Johnson deserves a bigger role There were a few bright spots in this game. But for my money, the brightest was rookie running back Emmett Johnson, who at times seemed to be single-handedly trying to will this team to victory. Johnson finished the day with 128 yards receiving and a touchdown. He also had a clutch kick return late in the fourth quarter that set up the Chiefs with a short field and a chance to win. Going back to making questionable decisions — you have to wonder, on their final drive, if Andy Reid and offensive coordinator Eric Bieniemy should have ridden the hot hand a little bit more and fed Johnson. Maybe it wouldn’t have mattered. Maybe they would have gotten in the endzone; we’ll never know. Regardless, Johnson needs to be an explicit part of this team’s game plan moving forward. 4. Situational football matters Offensive coordinator Eric Bieniemy was brought in to enforce discipline and improve the Chiefs’ situational football. So, seeing a game-winning touchdown wiped off the board by a false start on what should have been the final play is disheartening. Jaylon Moore on the False Start Penalty and more from Travis Kelce on how the team just has to be better and some honest words on how he's been the past couple weeks. pic.twitter.com/mh6oXIaU5Z — Harold R. Kuntz (@HaroldRKuntz3) November 2, 2026 These are the things Bieniemy was brought back to clean up. We’ll see if he’s up to the task. 5. If Brett Veach doesn’t make a move, it’s on him I like Brett Veach as a general manager, but let’s be real for a second. If he doesn’t make at least one, maybe even two, significant moves between now and the trade deadline, he is letting this team down. I’m not usually one for going all in for a championship run. But this is probably tight end Travis Kelce’s last season. This might be the last time to get Chris Jones another ring if his decline continues. The Chiefs need help at wide receiver. Rashee Rice is really good at doing one thing, but it’s still just one thing. Why waste this season by waiting for rookie Cyrus Allen to develop? Allen’s ceiling is that he evolves into a player like Josh Downs. You have the chance to go get Josh Downs, so go get him. The same goes for a pass rusher. Some really bad teams have really good pass rushers. After finishing with six wins last season and losing back-to-back games, it’s clear that this team needs a player or two to get them over the hump. With where things stand, Veach’s actions are the only ones that may put them over the top.
author: Rocky Magaña

title: Chiefs News: Brett Veach is looking for receivers before trade deadline
summary: The Kansas City Chiefs wouldn’t be fixing everything by adding a wide receiver, but regardless, general manager Brett Veach is actively looking for one with just over a week before the NFL trade deadline. Just before Kansas City blew the 11-point lead in the fourth quarter, CBS sideline reporter Tracy Wolfson made sure to share […]
full_text: Credit: Denny Medley-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Kansas City Chiefs wouldn’t be fixing everything by adding a wide receiver, but regardless, general manager Brett Veach is actively looking for one with just over a week before the NFL trade deadline. Just before Kansas City blew the 11-point lead in the fourth quarter, CBS sideline reporter Tracy Wolfson made sure to share a report with the nearly-national audience about her conversation with Veach. “I had a chance to speak with GM Brett Veach, who told me that, with Tyquan Thornton being out for the season and Rashee Rice having a history with soft tissue injuries, they will explore what’s available at the wide receiver position.” “You’ve heard Josh Downs or Brian Thomas Jr. being mentioned, but over the next week, they will make calls and see where everything stands and who is available.” Wolfson’s report was accompanied by a graphic labeled “Wideout Woes” that showed the Chiefs’ rankings among NFL teams’ wide receiver rooms: 27th in receptions (59) 30th in yards (735) 31st in percentage of team receiving yards (49.9%) Chiefs Kingdom, bring the noise to the SB Nation app! Join fellow Chiefs fans to react to every explosive play and game-changing moment in real time. Chat live throughout the game Browse with fewer ads Easily jump between communities Enjoy faster commenting and posting Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android . Download the SB Nation app on your mobile device! For Apple devices, click here . For Android devices, click here . The latest Kansas City Chiefs news Chiefs, Steelers, Commanders have interest in Brian Thomas Jr. | Pro Football Talk 2024 first-rounder Brian Thomas Jr. has interest in a fresh start. And multiple teams are believed to be interested in acquiring him. Currently, the Chiefs, Steelers, and Commanders have interest. The Steelers, we’re told, have greater interest in Colts receiver Josh Downs. Downs, however, is Kansas City’s Plan B, if they can’t get Thomas away from the Jaguars. Five things that stood out about the Chiefs’ loss to the Broncos in Denver | The Kansas City Star The Chiefs’ initial third down never stood a chance. Because the center, of all players, never gave it one. Creed Humphrey has something of the yips with his shotgun snaps. They’re significant plays. The eventual incomplete pass was worth minus-1.5 points, per the RBSDM model. And an incomplete pass was best-case scenario after Patrick Mahomes scrambled just to collect the ball and alertly fire it out of bounds. Broncos score 15 unanswered to win as Chiefs stopped at goal line | The Athletic “The reality of things is we got to fix a lot,” tight end Travis Kelce said after the game. “The little things, mistakes — and it starts with the person you’re looking at. I’m one of them. I’ve been frustrated with myself on how long I’ve been in the league, and the procedural stuff that’s happened for the past three games, really — since the bye. It’s frustrating. You just can’t f—ing do it, excuse my language. I’ve got to be better for my teammates, and that sets the tone for a lot of people in this room.” It looked like more Mahomes magic. Then the Broncos won a nail-biter — again. | NBC News When Denver’s goal-line stand held firm after it sacked Mahomes on the final play, the game became the 35th of this season with a game-winning score in the final four minutes of the fourth quarter or in overtime. (The NFL record through eight weeks is 36.) Perhaps the ending, as wild as it was, should have been expected. Over the past two seasons, Denver’s 16-2 record in one-score games is the league’s best. “It has to come from we’ve done it before,” Broncos coach Sean Payton said. Andy Reid defends Harrison Butker, but the numbers don’t | CBS Sports Here’s the thing, though: 54 yards isn’t really within Butker’s range anymore. It may have been during his prime, but these days, he is not nearly consistent enough from that distance to justify trying that kick. Here’s what we wrote just last week, for example, when Butker missed a pair of field goal attempts in the Chiefs’ loss to the Seattle Seahawks: Through 2023, he made 89.1% of his total field goals, and 28 of 40 (70%) from beyond 50 yards. Since then, though, Butker has made just 82.2% of his kicks, and only 8-of-18 (44.4%) from beyond 50 yards. He missed one of those 50-plus-yard kicks short by several yards in this game, making him just 1-of-5 from 50-plus this year, and he missed another from 45 yards out, pushing it wide to the right. ‘Dogfight for division’: Chiefs face key stretch against trio of sub-.500 teams | KSHB 41 Aside from games on Nov. 27 at Pittsburgh (6-2), Dec. 25 against Buffalo (6-1) and Week 17 at New England, every other team on the Broncos’ schedule has a losing record except Las Vegas (4-4), which might be feisty enough to take a game off their longtime rivals. Meanwhile, Kansas City faces a stretch beginning on Thanksgiving with five straight games against teams at .500 or better before wrapping up the season at the Los Angeles Chargers and against the Raiders at Arrowhead. Around the NF L Ravens’ Lamar Jackson needs thumb surgery, will be placed on IR | ESPN “Obviously, it sucks the way this game is kind of cruel like that,” Ravens safety Kyle Hamilton said. The Ravens are dealing with a run of injuries at quarterback and are unsure who will start Thursday night’s game against the Jacksonville Jaguars. Backup quarterback Tyler “Snoop” Huntley left the game in the second quarter and didn’t return because of a right toe injury. Minter said he’s not sure of Huntley’s status. Buccaneers’ Todd Bowles on zero-completion win over Falcons: There’s a ‘first time for everything’ | NFL.com Tampa Bay instead outlasted the Falcons, 16-0, in a rain-soaked affair at Raymond James Stadium despite Mayfield attempting only three passes and converting on none of them, as the Bucs became the second team (1974 Bills) in the Super Bowl era to win a game without a single completion. “I have not,” head coach Todd Bowles said when asked if he’s ever won without a completion, per the team’s transcript, “but there is a first time for everything.” Lions All-Pro linebacker to remain in hospital after scary neck injury | USA Today Campbell went down after making a tackle against Vikings tight end T.J. Hockenson in the fourth quarter. He remained down on the field as the training staff and medical personnel surrounded him and the cart arrived. Campbell was loaded onto a backboard before the cart took him off the field. Lions teammates took a knee and looked concerned as staff attended to him. Defensive end Aidan Hutchinson was in tears while the game was paused. In case you missed it on Arrowhead Pride Chiefs-Broncos: The Big takeaway from a Big loss in Denver A false start by right tackle Jaylon Moore negated a potential game-winning touchdown by Rashee Rice, which was a theme of this game. According to Josh Dubow of the Associated Press , the Chiefs committed eight penalties for 75 yards in the first half — the fourth time a Chiefs team has done that with Andy Reid as head coach. Overall, the team finished with 11 penalties and 105 penalty yards going against them, but there was still a chance on fourth-and-6. With nowhere to go with the ball, Mahomes succumbed to a sack, and the game was over. title: Chargers Week 8 PFF Grades: Herbert struggles despite great protection up front vs. Rams
summary: Justin Herbert turned the ball over in the seventh consecutive game to begin the 2026 season. He ended with a pair of interceptions thrown and another fumble that luckily was knocked out of bounds before the Rams could secure it. Most days, it’s easy to turn around and blame the offensive line who normally puts […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CA - NOVEMBER 01: Joe Alt #76 of the Los Angeles Chargers guards Kam Curl #3 of the Los Angeles Rams during an NFL game between the Los Angeles Chargers and the Los Angeles Rams on November 1, 2026, at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Greg Fiore/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Justin Herbert turned the ball over in the seventh consecutive game to begin the 2026 season. He ended with a pair of interceptions thrown and another fumble that luckily was knocked out of bounds before the Rams could secure it. Most days, it’s easy to turn around and blame the offensive line who normally puts up an underwhelming performance in pass protection. That wasn’t the case in Week Eight as nearly the entire front five had a decent to great day protecting Herbert. The defense unsurprisingly had some standouts. Holding the Rams to zero first downs through the game’s first 28 and a half minutes is something to be very proud of. Unfortunately the nine points score during that stretch of dominance was nowhere near enough to put the game away. Let’s go ahead and check out the grades from Sunday. Offense Best OT Joe Alt – 77.7 TE Oronde Gadsden II – 74.4 OT Travis Burke – 69.4 WR Tre’ Harris – 66.1 WR Quentin Johnston – 63.1 Alt remains one of the top offensive tackles in the NFL and that didn’t change after missing two games with a nek injury. He returned to be the top player on the offense, posting a pass block grade of 89.9 which fell a hair short of an elite mark. Gadsden had season-high 52 yards receiving against the Rams on five receptions, also tying his previous season high. With eight catches on 10 targets over the past two games, the hope is that McDaniel keeps pushing to get Gadsden back to his rookie season form where he was a surprising standout. The rookie Burke remains one of the Chargers’ best offensive players despite being forced into a starting role much sooner than he likely expected. Behind both Alt and Rashawn Slater, Burke is actually the team’s third-highest-graded player on the year. He had a team-high 67.5 run block grade against the Rams. In his first game back from injury, Harris was the team’s highest-graded wideout after catching three passes for 31 yards. He remains the best run-blocking wideout for the Chargers. Johnston also caught all four of his targets for 37 yards. Worst FB Scott Matlock – 31.9 RB Omarion Hampton – 47.2 OG Cole Strange – 48.6 QB Justin Herbert – 50.2 WR Ladd McConkey – 51.0 After a strong return to the field following his IR stint, Matlock had a rough outing against the Rams where he earned a porous 38.5 as a run blocker and was flagged for a penalty. Hampton’s 30.5 receiving grade sunk his overall mark. He had a very strong 74.9 in pass protection, though. Strange is on pace for the worst overall season grade of his career. His 39.5 pass block grade on the year remains atrocious and he continues to be one of the bottom five Chargers players week-in and week-out. Herbert threw two more interceptions and only grew his league-leading total to 10. McConkey dropped one of the first passes thrown his way on Sunday and his stat line (4-86) would have looked a lot better if he didn’t luck into catching the Hail Mary attempt at the end of the first half (54 yards). Defense Best CB Isas Waxter – 89.0 S R.J. Mickens – 84.2 LB Troy Dye – 82.8 LB Del’Shawn Phillips – 79.8 DT Justin Eboigbe – 73.7 Look at the rookie Waxter go! He was the highest-graded player not only on defense, but the entire Chargers team. He posted an 89.9 in coverage. His 79.6 tackling grade was also third best on the team. This was Mickens’ best game of the year, as well. His 85.6 in tackling topped the team and his 75.1 in coverage was fifth best. Despite playing very few snaps each week, Dye has been impactful. His 80.8 in coverage was second on the team while his 76.9 in tackling was fourth best. Eboigbe was one of the team’s best run defenders (74.5 in run defense) and was sixth in tackling (71.2). Worst LB Daiyan Henley – 27.7 DT Dalvin Tomlinson – 29.8 DT Jamaree Caldwell – 47.4 S Elijah Molden – 53.3 DT Nick Barrett – 55.1 Henley had a very rough outing against the Rams. He was put on his butt more than once and struggled mightily in coverage (27.2). He allowed all four targets his way to be completed and missed a tackle. Tomlinson posted the team’s worst run defense grade with a 29.9. Molden was put one-on-one with a running back in the open field multiple times on Sunday. It never ended well for him and that’s reflected in his run defense (33.0) and tackling (24.6) grades.

title: Chargers sign former Ravens, Titans CB Jalyn Armour-Davis
summary: The Chargers are 0-7 after losing to the Rams on Sunday, but that isn’t stopping the from adding new bodies to the fold in hopes of finally turning the season around. Per NFL insider Jordan Schultz, the Bolts are signing former Ravens and Titans cornerback Jalyn Armour-Davis who last played 10 games in Tennessee before […]
full_text: The Chargers are 0-7 after losing to the Rams on Sunday, but that isn’t stopping the from adding new bodies to the fold in hopes of finally turning the season around. Per NFL insider Jordan Schultz, the Bolts are signing former Ravens and Titans cornerback Jalyn Armour-Davis who last played 10 games in Tennessee before tearing his achilles. Before going down with his injury, Armour-Davis was having a career year with 34 total tackles, a tackle for loss, and a pair of pass deflections. Sources: The #Chargers are signing former #Ravens and #Titans CB Jalyn Armour-Davis. The former Alabama standout started 10 games for Tennessee last season before suffering a torn Achilles. He’s now fully healthy and back in the NFL. pic.twitter.com/AiWargplcr — Jordan Schultz (@Schultz_Report) November 2, 2026 Armour-Davis played collegiately at Alabama and was originally selected by the Ravens in the fourth round of the 2022 NFL Draft. He played in 19 games with three starts during his three years in Baltimore. He had started 10 games and played in 11 with the Titans a year ago. In his three seasons prior, Armour-Davis had totaled just 22 tackles, one tackle for loss, and two pass breakups.
