title: This Can’t Continue (But It Probably Will)
summary: On Sunday afternoon at Ford Field, the Minnesota Vikings finally ran into a situation where their defense couldn’t overcome what is becoming one of the worst offenses in recent team history. The Vikings’ offense had ten possessions on Sunday afternoon in Detroit (excluding their kneel down at the end of the first half). Only two […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - NOVEMBER 1: Kyler Murray #1 of the Minnesota Vikings is sacked by Alim McNeill #54 of the Detroit Lions during the third quarter at Ford Field on November 1, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images On Sunday afternoon at Ford Field, the Minnesota Vikings finally ran into a situation where their defense couldn’t overcome what is becoming one of the worst offenses in recent team history. The Vikings’ offense had ten possessions on Sunday afternoon in Detroit (excluding their kneel down at the end of the first half). Only two of those possessions lasted longer than three minutes. The Lions had a more than eleven-minute advantage in time of possession (35:43 to 24:17). Usually, those sorts of numbers are a recipe for a beatdown. That the margin of victory wound up being four points, and that the Vikings had a lead with five minutes left to go in the game, is a testament to the effort the defense was able to put up before they finally just got worn down. But this offense, quite simply, is just not a serious NFL offense right now. And, unfortunately, the path to any sort of a simple fix for this season just doesn’t appear to be there. There were those of us who spent this offseason screaming into the void that Kyler Murray was not a fit for what the Vikings have wanted to do offensively in the Kevin O’Connell era. Think, for a second, about the two quarterbacks who have really been successful in this offense since O’Connell became the head coach: Kirk Cousins and Sam Darnold. What did those guys do well? Lined up under center, excelled in the play-action game, turned their back to the defense, didn’t run around a lot, manipulated the pocket and fired passes down the field. Or, to put it another way. . .roughly the exact opposite of everything Kyler Murray has done throughout his NFL career prior to now. Per a September article from Garrett Burroughs over at Vikings Wire , during his time in Arizona, Murray was lined up in the shotgun on approximately 85% of the Cardinals’ snaps, per numbers taken from Next Gen Stats. Since O’Connell became the Vikings’ head coach in 2022, only two teams in the NFL had a lower percentage of snaps out of the shotgun than the Vikings’ 53%. The style of offense that O’Connell has wanted to run since he became the Vikings’ head coach is not compatible with Murray’s skill set, and whatever adjustments needed to be made apparently have not been. But, here we are, continuing to attempt to jam the square peg into the round hole with entirely predictable results. And, respectfully, miss me with any sort of “Well, he had to split reps in training camp” excuse. Kyler Murray is approaching 100 career NFL starts. If he looks like this because he had to cede a few training camp reps. . .well, then there are a few other questions that need to be answered. So, what’s the fix? Honestly, I’m not sure if there is one. There probably isn’t a feasible trade scenario. Any quarterback that you’re going to trade for at this point is probably going to require you to pay through the nose and will require an adjustment period of some sort. There is one notable exception, and man, if you think people have thoughts about the quarterback situation now, just wait until the potential premiere of Kirko 2: Kirk Harder . Yes, Kirk Cousins could step into this offense immediately and be an upgrade. . .and, yes, I can’t believe that’s a sentence I’m typing in this, the year of our Lord 2026. But that comes with a hitch as well, that being that the Las Vegas Raiders have had the audacity to go out and actually be a competitive football team this season, largely due to Cousins’ play. Did you know that Kirk Cousins is currently second in the NFL in touchdown passes? He’s thrown more than Josh Allen, more than Patrick Mahomes, more than Matthew Stafford, and more than anyone else not named Joe Burrow. And outside of Brock Bowers, I can’t name three guys he’s throwing the ball to without going to ESPN or Pro Football Reference or something. So while a Cousins trade would help the Vikings. . .do the Raiders even want to move him? (Would it be wrong to point out that the Vikings could have signed Cousins this offseason? That would be wrong of me, wouldn’t it? Okay, then, I won’t do it.) For better or worse, the Vikings may be locked into their current quarterback depth chart for the rest of this season. Maybe I’ll be wrong on that, but I don’t see anything else that does anything for them this season at the quarterback spot. The Vikings have had other trade rumors around them as well, notably for Colts’ running back Jonathan Taylor. Our friends at Stampede Blue have said that the asking price for Taylor is a first-round pick and a defensive tackle, which is a price that the Vikings should absolutely not be entertaining, in my opinion. Jonathan Taylor doesn’t fix this offense if there’s no passing game, and in its current state, the Vikings need to be careful about expending too much draft capital. Why? Well, because this team has zero quarterbacks on the roster under contract beyond this season. Murray is here on a one-year deal and, as we know, hasn’t been making what you’d call a super compelling case for being the long-term guy anyway. Carson Wentz is on a one-year deal and also isn’t the long-term answer. And if you’ve looked at the 2027 free agent pool at the quarterback position, it’s a bit of a wasteland. Even in the aftermath of the J.J. McCarthy situation. . .and don’t get me started on that again. . .this team is probably going to have to take another swing at a quarterback in the draft sooner rather than later, and given that they already have six wins, if they want to make any sort of move for a top quarterback in 2027, they’re going to need picks to do that. I can understand Kevin O’Connell coming to the podium after games each week and telling us that the offense is close and that the breakthrough is coming any time now. I get it, honestly. But, you know. . .we’re halfway through the 2026 season. At this point, you sort of are what you are. And, at this point, the Minnesota Vikings are a bottom-five NFL offense by pretty much any objective measure, and I’m not sure that there’s a fix that’s going to change that for the second half of this season. But, as always, I’m more than open to Nolan Teasley and company proving me wrong.
author: Christopher Gates

title: Patriots injury analysis after Dolphins win in Week 8
summary: Despite playing some bad 30 minutes of football to start their Week 8 game in Miami, the New England Patriots were able to beat the Dolphins with a final score of 24-19. Their ability to overcome a halftime deficit is one of the positive takeaways from the game, but it’s not all sunshine and roses. […]
full_text: Despite playing some bad 30 minutes of football to start their Week 8 game in Miami, the New England Patriots were able to beat the Dolphins with a final score of 24-19 . Their ability to overcome a halftime deficit is one of the positive takeaways from the game, but it’s not all sunshine and roses. The team of head coach Mike Vrabel suffered more injuries to some rather important players. Here is our weekly run-down after rewatching the game. Patriots injury analysis: NFL Week 8 TE Hunter Henry: Catching his third pass of the afternoon in the early second quarter, the Patriots’ starting tight end seemingly slipped and exited the field. He showed some discomfort on the sidelines, headed into the blue medical tent and later the locker room. Originally labeled questionable to return with a foot injury, he did reemerge shortly before the half to test out his foot but did not reenter the contest. He went through the same routine in the early third period but once again departed. This time for good: he was ruled out midway through the fourth quarter. QB Drake Maye: New England’s starting quarterback got his left non-throwing hand taped up late in the first half, but did not miss any time. He ended the game having played all 60 offensive snaps, and completing 16 of 20 throws for 199 yards and a pair of touchdowns. ED Gabe Jacas: Arguably the Patriots’ most impressive rookie so far this season, Jacas came up limping after the first third down of the second half. He was initially rushing the passer on the play and reversed course to pursue where the ball was going, and only then started favoring his right knee. The second-round draft pick entered the blue medical tent and was announced as questionable to return. He didn’t, even though he remained on the sideline for the remainder of the game. CB Charles Woods: Woods entered the blue medical tent midway through the third period, after getting banged up on a punt return rep. Lining up as a vice player, there was no obvious collision or moment he got hurt, and no injury was announced either. He reentered the game on the next occasion — a kickoff coverage play eight minutes of game time later — and finished without any notable hiccups. He did, however, stumble while on coverage on a long Dolphins touchdown late in the fourth quarter. ED Dre’Mont Jones: Jones needed some medical attention on the field after taking a rather violent fall on an end-around halfway through the fourth quarter. He eventually walked off under his own power and ended up missing two plays before a return on the next drive. What this means for the Patriots The Patriots’ skill position depth was already thin before the Dolphins game, and losing Hunter Henry is another blow. To their credit, the unit did adapt and overcome his departure, but there is no denying his importance to the operation either: Henry is one of Drake Maye’s favorite targets, and one of New England’s most reliable players on the offensive side of the ball. With him out, rookie Eli Raridon and an already-depleted wide receiver group saw an uptick in snaps. Whether that will continue heading into the upcoming Week 9 game against the Green Bay Packers will be seen; Mike Vrabel did not provide any updates on Monday. “I don’t have any expectations yet,” he said. “We’ll see how he responds here. He wasn’t able to finish the game. So, we’ll see where he is. I know Hunter will do everything that he can to get back to help us, and we’ll go from there.” The other noteworthy injury coming out of Sunday’s game is the one suffered by Gabe Jacas. The fact that he did not leave the field and was never officially ruled out can be interpreted as a positive sign. However, the first practice of the week on Wednesday will give us further information about the second-round draft pick and the other players listed above. It also will be the first opportunity this week for previously-absent players such as wide receiver A.J. Brown and running back TreVeyon Henderson to return to the field; the same is true for fellow wideout Mack Hollins and fullback Reggie Gilliam, who are now both eligible to return from injured reserve. The Patriots will host the Packers at Gillette Stadium on Sunday, Nov. 8, for a 4:25 p.m. ET kickoff.
author: Bernd Buchmasser

title: Patriots lose practice squad linebacker K.J. Britt to the Lions
summary: The New England Patriots have lost a member of their practice squad to the Detroit Lions. Linebacker K.J. Britt, who has seen action in one game so far this season, has been signed to Detroit’s active roster. The transaction comes in the aftermath of the Lions losing starting linebacker Jack Campbell to a neck injury […]
full_text: The New England Patriots have lost a member of their practice squad to the Detroit Lions. Linebacker K.J. Britt, who has seen action in one game so far this season, has been signed to Detroit’s active roster. The transaction comes in the aftermath of the Lions losing starting linebacker Jack Campbell to a neck injury on Sunday. Adam Schefter of ESPN was first to report the news, which were also shared in the Pats Pulpit Feed by community member Matt Monitto. Britt, 27, originally joined the Patriots on a one-year free agency deal in March. He did appear in all three preseason games on defense and special but ultimately was released ahead of late August’s roster cutdown deadline. He was brought back via New England’s practice squad the next day, and spent the entire season so far there. He played 14 kicking game snaps and registered one tackle is his lone regular season appearance. Britt was one of six linebackers on New England’s pay roll entering this week, and the only one on the practice squad. The active roster features starters Robert Spillane and Christian Elliss as well as backups and special teamers Darius Muasau, Namdi Obiazor and Erick Hunter. With Britt now off to Detroit, New England will have an open spot on its practice squad . Recently-released safety Elliott Davison appears to be a realistic candidate to fill it . The Patriots will host the Green Bay Packers at Gillette Stadium this coming Sunday. They will play the Lions the following week in Munich, Germany.

title: What waiving Elliott Davison means for the Patriots
summary: One day after their win over the Miami Dolphins, the New England Patriots decided to part ways with a member of their safety group. Elliott Davison, who had originally joined the 53-man roster from the practice squad in mid-October, was waived. Let’s assess what the move means for the Patriots from a big-picture perspective. Unsurprising […]
full_text: One day after their win over the Miami Dolphins, the New England Patriots decided to part ways with a member of their safety group. Elliott Davison, who had originally joined the 53-man roster from the practice squad in mid-October, was waived . Let’s assess what the move means for the Patriots from a big-picture perspective. Unsurprising move When the Patriots announced their inactives on Sunday, the six-players list included four healthy scratches. Davison was one of them, reflecting his position near the bottom of the roster and the volatile status of his spot on the 53-man team. From that perspective alone, him getting the axe on Monday was no particular surprise — and that’s before putting injured reserve into consideration as well. After all, wide receiver Mack Hollins and fullback Reggie Gilliam are both eligible to return to practice and subsequently off IR this week, while offensive tackle Marcus Bryant’s 21-day window for activation is set to close on Wednesday. New England had no openings on its roster coming out of Week 8. It now has one, and it is likely to be used sooner rather than later. Safety shakeup The Patriots have had to deal with their fair share of depth questions across the roster this season, but the safety spot has been in relatively good shape. Led by team captain Kevin Byard and sophomore starter Craig Woodson, the group has enjoyed a level of stability others on the team can only dream of. Removing Davison from the equation does little to change that, given that he was the sixth option and played only 10 defensive snaps — all late during a blowout win over the Raiders in Week 5. 53-man roster (5): Kevin Byard III (31), Craig Woodson (4), Jaylen Reed (23), Brenden Schooler (41), Mike Brown (33) Injured reserve (1): Dell Pettus (24) The big question mark among the group is Dell Pettus, who remains on injured reserve despite being eligible to come back since Week 7. Should he be cleared for a return, he and Mike Brown might end up competing for one spot on the team as a backup/third safety and personal punt protector. Special teams impact Before being made inactive for the Dolphins game on Sunday, Davison saw most of his action on special teams. He played 57 combined snaps during his three active games, a share of 67% over that span. He lined up on kickoff coverage, kickoff return, punt return and field goal/extra point block — roles that were already redistributed versus Miami. From that point of view, his removal from the 53-man roster will not have a notable impact: he already had been replaced in that regard. Return possible An undrafted rookie in 2025, Davison will have to pass through the waiver wire before entering the open market. There is a theoretical chance that a team ends up putting in a claim on the 24-year-old to bring him aboard, but the expected outcome is that he won’t be picked up that way. If so, the Patriots re-signing him to their practice squad seems like a realistic option. Davison already spent most of the early parts of the regular season on New England’s “second roster.” If such a move were to happen, however, a follow-up would be necessary. The addition of running back Terrell Jennings on Monday means that the club currently has a full 16 players — not counting offensive tackle Lorenz Metz, who is exempt — signed to the practice squad.

title: Patriots waive safety Elliott Davison, bring back running back Terrell Jennings on practice squad
summary: The New England Patriots head into November with an opening on the 53-man roster. full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - OCTOBER 22: Elliott Davison #27 of the New England Patriots warms up prior to an NFL football game against the Chicago Bears at Soldier Field on October 22, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New England Patriots head into November with an opening on the 53-man roster. The organization waived safety Elliott Davison on Monday and also announced the re-signing of running back Terrell Jennings to the practice squad. Davison, 24, had been promoted to the active roster midway through October after twice serving as a standard elevation . The 6-foot, 190-pound safety first arrived on the practice squad in September before being released and re-signed. His stay has brought two tackles and one pass deflection through three appearances spanning 10 snaps on defense and 57 snaps on special teams. Entering the NFL as an undrafted free agent in 2025, Davison spent the entirety of his rookie year on the practice squad of the New Orleans Saints and reached a futures contract in January. The UTSA product checked in as the sixth safety on the 53-man roster in Foxborough alongside Kevin Byard III, Craig Woodson, Jaylen Reed, Mike Brown and Brenden Schooler, yet was a healthy scratch last weekend. Jennings, 25, officially returns to the Patriots on the practice squad after three months as a free agent. The 6-foot, 222-pound rusher had been waived off injured reserve in August with an injury settlement that expired after the initial six weeks of the regular season, as the Boston Herald’s Doug Kyed reported. He was among three backs in for workouts in October. A former rookie minicamp tryout, Jennings first agreed to terms as an undrafted free agent in 2024. The Florida A&M alum went on to spend parts of the two campaigns on the 53-man roster after reaching the league limit in standard elevations from the practice squad. And in 2025, he rushed for his first NFL touchdown before finishing the road to Super Bowl LX on injured reserve. Standing 10 appearances into his career with 77 snaps on offense and 69 snaps on special teams, Jennings has totaled 115 yards from scrimmage across 37 touches. New England’s practice squad now returns to capacity after the recent promotion of running back Lan Larison to an active depth chart also featuring Rhamondre Stevenson, Corey Kiner and TreVeyon Henderson. Also on Monday, wide receiver Ryan Miller reverted to the 17-man scout team after facing his previous team as a standard elevation . Miller, 26, played five offensive snaps during what became a 24-19 win at Hard Rock Stadium. The 6-foot-2, 221-pound target entered Sunday’s AFC East meeting ranked fifth on the Miami Dolphins in receiving yards. That was the case despite being waived from the 53-man roster midway through October and signing to the practice squad in Foxborough. A 77-yard touchdown was reeled in during the initial weeks of the season after arriving as a waiver claim at the end of training camp. Undrafted out of Furman in 2023, Miller spent three campaigns between the active roster and practice squad of the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. He would finish 2025 with the New York Giants and now stands 31 games into his career. A six-game starter, his odometer includes 17 receptions for 254 yards and four touchdowns through 449 downs on offense and 421 downs on special teams. The Green Bay Packers visit Gillette Stadium next Sunday. Kickoff is set for 4:25 p.m. ET.

title: Packers star Micah Parsons set to return to practice ahead of Patriots game
summary: The Green Bay Packers are getting some reinforcement ahead of their upcoming game with the New England Patriots. Micah Parsons, the four-time All-Pro edge rusher, is set to return to practice this week. Packers head coach Matt LaFleur announced the news on Monday. “That would be the intention,” he said during a press conference. “It’s […]
full_text: The Green Bay Packers are getting some reinforcement ahead of their upcoming game with the New England Patriots. Micah Parsons, the four-time All-Pro edge rusher, is set to return to practice this week. Packers head coach Matt LaFleur announced the news on Monday. “That would be the intention,” he said during a press conference. “It’s going to be a process trying to get him back. We’re hopeful. It’s going to be dependent on the next couple of days, but we’re hopeful it’s going to be sometime this week.” Parsons, 27, started the regular season on the physically unable to perform list after tearing his ACL last December. When he went down, the Packers’ high-profile trade acquisition via the Dallas Cowboys had 12.5 sacks and a pair of forced fumbles on his 2025 résumé. While Parsons returning to practice opens the window for his return to Green Bay’s active roster and would make him eligible to play in Sunday’s contest in Foxborough, an immediate return to game action is not a guarantee. Last week, Rob Demovsky of ESPN noted that “[e]ven if Parsons practices next week, it would be highly unlikely he could play in the Week 9 game at the Patriots.” According to a report by NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport, Nov. 25 against the Los Angeles Rams is Parsons’ targeted return date. LeFleur hinted at that approach as well on Monday. “Like everything around here, it’s pretty fluid in terms of how he responds and just the progress he’s going to, hopefully, continue to make leading up to when he’s available,” he said. “If I had a bet on it, it’s going to be more toward the longer end than the shorter end.” For the Patriots, facing a Parsons-less Packers team is the preferred scenario. Even if not at a 100%, he has the ability to make game-changing plays against an offensive line that has had to deal with its fair share of injury questions this season. The Patriots have lost both of their starting guards to injury, while both of their tackles also got banged up at one point. Heading into Sunday’s game, New England’s projected O-line will feature Will Campbell and Morgan Moses at tackle, with two of Ben Brown, Matt Pryor and Walter Rouse flanking center Jared Wilson at the guard positions. Kickoff between the two storied franchise is scheduled for 4:25 p.m. ET on Sunday, Nov. 8.

title: Mike Vrabel remains confident in Andy Borregales despite missed kicks
summary: Andy Borregales made just one of his two field goal attempts in the New England Patriots’ Week 8 victroy over the Miami Dolphins on Sunday. The miss came from just 40 yards out, marking Borregales’ third missed field goal of the season from inside 50 yards. Through eight games, the second-year kicker is now 10-of-13 […]
full_text: Andy Borregales made just one of his two field goal attempts in the New England Patriots’ Week 8 victroy over the Miami Dolphins on Sunday. The miss came from just 40 yards out, marking Borregales’ third missed field goal of the season from inside 50 yards. Through eight games, the second-year kicker is now 10-of-13 on field goals and 20-of-21 on extra points. Head coach Mike Vrabel, however, still has belief in his kicker. “That needs to get corrected,” Vrabel said Monday. “I’ve got a lot of confidence in Andy. I think when you see the timing and when the approach is in rhythm, it looks really good. We have to make our kicks. Everybody has a job here. There’s no real message. It’s, ‘Hey, we’ve got to make them.’ But I’ve got a lot of confidence. “I thought he did a really nice job on the kickoff with the ball placement. Hopefully, he’s making a lot of extra points and not having to kick a lot of field goals.” The Patriots selected Borregales in the sixth round of the 2025 NFL Draft out of the University of Miami. His rookie season got off to a slow start, including a pair of missed extra points in Miami in Week 2. However, he missed just three kicks over the remainder of the regular season. During his weekly appearance on WEEI’s The Greg Hill Show , Vrabel also poked fun at how quickly analysts and fans call for players to be benched or released after making mistakes, referencing both Drake Maye and Rhamondre Stevenson as examples. The Patriots have not had internal competition on the roster for Borregales since his rookie season, when John Parker Romo competed with him during training camp. For now, Vrabel appears content to stick with his kicker while emphasizing the need for better results.
author: Brian Hines

title: Patriots vs. Dolphins: Fan observations from Week 8
summary: Allow me to be the first to welcome everyone to the best time of the year! 3:30 p.m. sunsets and constant darkness, here we come! It’s wild how I used to actually enjoy the first night of Daylight Savings Time starting, or ending, or whichever one this one is. You’re out at the bars, they’re […]
full_text: Allow me to be the first to welcome everyone to the best time of the year! 3:30 p.m. sunsets and constant darkness, here we come! It’s wild how I used to actually enjoy the first night of Daylight Savings Time starting, or ending, or whichever one this one is. You’re out at the bars, they’re about to close…and then all of a sudden, you get an extra hour to make bad decisions. But I’ve aged out of all that, alas, so now I’m taking up the mantle of the crotchety middle-aged man who likes to complain about everything. At least I’m not complaining about a Patriots loss, though, as New England took care of business to the tune of a 24-19 victory to move ahead to 5-3, 3-0 in the AFC East . I had absolutely no idea what to expect coming into this game. Sure, the Fins stink, but nothing is as it seems when the Patriots head down to Miami. Compound that with rainy conditions, an oddly-positioned 4:25 slot for a game that certainly didn’t deserve a late window, and an absolutely decimated Patriots team, and this just seemed to have all the makings of a trap game. And for the first half, that’s exactly what seemed to be happening. New England couldn’t move the ball at all, the defense was oddly off, and the whole game just seemed like holiday commercials before Halloween even hits; nobody wants to see that. But something happened in that locker room at halftime, because the Patriots came out and scored on three consecutive drives to open this one up. But I’m getting ahead of myself. I have a few more complaints to lodge before I break this game down in earnest. As the Patriots played in the late window for the first time this year, I watched the 1 p.m. games for the first time all season. And I wish I was saying differently, but the NFL is becoming completely unwatchable. The games have zero flow to them. The officiating somehow seems to be getting worse every year as opposed to better, and everyone just kind of stinks. As a product, it has been trending in the wrong direction for years now, and I’m starting to wonder when I’m going to just stop watching altogether. Probably when the NFL inevitably starts offering Tuesday Night Football, Wednesday Night Football, and Friday Night Football to completely oversaturate the market. Children would love to eat chocolate and candy with every meal, but normal adults don’t allow that. You need to limit things. OK, enough of that. Sorry to open on a downer. I just used to love the NFL so damn much, and it’s losing me, and that makes me sad. On the plus side, the horrendous officiating and terrible refs blessed us with what might be the most spectacular display of infathomable incompetence we’re going to see this year. On New England’s second possession of the third quarter, Drake Maye hit Kyle Williams for what turned out to be a 43-yard touchdown. Williams caught the ball at the five-yard line, took four or five steps, crossed the goal line, then his knee hit the ball and came loose. The goal-line referee threw a blue beanbag to indicate a loose ball/fumble, and then ruled the pass incomplete. The result was Mike Vrabel suddenly finding himself on the radar of no fewer than six QB-needy teams as he threw an absolute laser of a challenge flag 65 yards in order to get the call…I don’t even want to say “reversed,” as there were about six different things that went wrong for the refs there. Just pure, unadulterated comedy. What isn’t funny, though, is playing a game without your WR1, WR2, TE1, LG1, LG2, RB2, RG1, and RG2. I don’t know who any of these people are. I’m just going to hope that the Patriots were being extra cautious with these guys and were confident that they could beat Miami wildly short-handed, because the Packers and Lions are coming up and this simply isn’t sustainable. Thank Tebow that we have Drake Maye, as that man put the franchise on his back yesterday and didn’t look back. He’s finding ways to make plays and extend drives with the guys he has. I’d be lying if I said that I didn’t think that New England was done for once Hunter Henry went back to the locker room, but New England dug deep into the well, operated out of a lot ot Jumbo sets featuring tight end extraordinaire Caleb Lomu on the end, ground it out with Stevenson, and utilized the run to open up the big play. The Williams and Pop Douglas catches ended up being what decided this one. Was it the Williams touchdown where a Dolphins defender had Maye dead to rights on an unimpeded blitz, but instead just kind of fell down and didn’t even touch him? Or maybe it was the fourth-down conversion to Efton Chism that could have completely changed the momentum of the entire game if he had just done anything besides fall down. Dolphins gonna Dolphin, I guess. Though I don’t know how the refs were able to overturn that DeMario Douglas fourth-down conversion that was/wasn’t/was. I’m always blown away by how different my interpretation of the phrase “incontrovertible evidence” is from the NFL’s. My favorite play of the game had to be Maye’s TD run, a read-option where he completely froze Willie Gay and Rajon Rondo’d his way into the end zone. Just a beautiful read, pump fake, and play design. Morgan Moses knew Maye could handle Gay, so he bumped up to chip block Uche and leave a wide open lane. These jumbo packages are going to be a lot of fun when the Patriots actually have some receivers in there. Was anybody else screaming a combination of “Don’t fall down!” and “Hang onto the ball, dammit!” as Douglas was weaving his way towards the end zone? You know who I don’t want or need to talk about this morning? Will Campbell. Who played half of the game next to Walter Rouse, who was pulled for a Ben Brown who basically had to get in and out of a hospital bed in between drives. 27 passing snaps, just one hurry allowed. There’s a very large faction of fans out there who lament the fact that the Patriots got Campbell instead of trading down and taking Tetairoa McMillan… but if Campbell wasn’t out there, this 2026 unit would probably have Milton Williams trying to set the edge on offense. Who I do need to talk about, though, is Jared Wilson. I’m going to be nice and chalk yesterday up to a combination of the wet weather and the rain shrinking that protective layer on Wilson’s helmet, which restricted blood flow to his brain, because he seemed to think he was playing Bocce instead of snapping a football on multiple occasions. This is one of those offensive performances where you’re able to be happy with what you saw, acknowledge that it could have been better, and also acknowledge that this isn’t sustainable with the current roster. Mack Hollins should be eligible to return this week, and hopefully the Patriots just held AJ Brown out this week as a precaution. Oh, and hopefully Hunter Henry is OK. And Gabe Jacas. Speaking of Jacas, who continues to be a disruptive force… this was a weird game for the defense. They were well-disciplined and decisive up front, but still allowed Malik Willis to move the ball. No Miami receiver eclipsed 50 yards… but the D gave up key plays in big moments. I haven’t watched any replay footage, but this team seems to feast in man and famine in zone. If I had to guess, I’d say that Zak Kuhr called a lot of zone looks yesterday. The Dolphins responded with underneath routes and sit-down routes to efficiently move the chains. New England gave up completions of 35, 23, 19, and 18 yards. I have always been of the opinion that the only place you want to see a soft cushion is on a chair, but I know multiple DCs that disagree with me. I’d like to show Logan Ryan some love, as I think he was a very underrated Patriots DB and had some great moments in New England. And as a commentator, he’s still pretty green with plenty of time and room to find his footing. But I don’t think you’ll be seeing him call any of the bigger games anytime soon. I have about as much faith in Andy Borregales as I do in men whose Halloween costume is an oversized gift…
author: Alec Shane

title: Drake Maye provides the answer for shorthanded Patriots in Miami
summary: The New England Patriots entered the visiting locker room inside Hard Rock Stadium at halftime trailing 13-3 to the one-win Miami Dolphins. It was a sluggish start offensively for a group that was down multiple offensive lineman and three of their top pass catchers before losing tight end Hunter Henry early in the second quarter. […]
full_text: The New England Patriots entered the visiting locker room inside Hard Rock Stadium at halftime trailing 13-3 to the one-win Miami Dolphins. It was a sluggish start offensively for a group that was down multiple offensive lineman and three of their top pass catchers before losing tight end Hunter Henry early in the second quarter. It was a sluggish start offensively for a group missing multiple offensive linemen and three of its top pass catchers, before they then lost tight end Hunter Henry early in the second quarter. But the group still had Drake Maye, and that proved to be enough to mount a comeback. “You want to be a great quarterback in the National Football League, there’s not a whole lot of excuses,” head coach Mike Vrabel said post-game. “You go out there and you find ways to win for your football team. And I know that that’s one who he is and that’s what he wants to continue to be. So, he just throws to the open guy and controls our offense and gets guys in the right spot. That’s being one of the best quarterbacks in the league, that’s what the job description requires.” After scoring just three first half points in a rainy Miami, Maye went on to lead three consecutive touchdown drives in the second half to put the Patriots in front. The turnaround began with a 43-yard touchdown pass to Kyle Williams on a deep post, as Maye and the offense began pushing the ball downfield more aggressively. “The touchdown, yeah, I think it was huge. We kind of needed to open it up a little bit and kind of break the barrier of getting in the end zone. I think we did that,” Maye said. “I think Coach was just kind of on us a little bit to stop hurting ourselves, Coach Vrabes and Coach McDaniels. So we were just kind of hurting ourselves and killing drives.” Maye continued to deliver in the second half , capping off the comeback with a two-yard rushing touchdown and a 48-yard touchdown pass to DeMario Douglas. He finished the final two quarters 9-of-10 for 146 yards, with three total touchdowns and a perfect 158.3 passer rating. As Vrabel noted, it was the kind of performance expected from an elite quarterback. With key contributors sidelined and the offense struggling to find its rhythm early, Maye gave the Patriots the spark they needed to leave Miami with a 24-19 victory . “Go be the answer,” Maye said. “Don’t wait around for anybody else, go make it. And I think that was kind of the message everybody took in, and we just felt like we did that. It was good to see from those guys.”

summary: A win is a win is a win. I’ve long said division games are different animals and any road win in Miami is a “take it” and ask no questions scenario. That said, the crowd in my living room had a lot of questions (and statements) yesterday during the game. Mistakes and drive-killing turnovers were […]
full_text: A win is a win is a win. I’ve long said division games are different animals and any road win in Miami is a “take it” and ask no questions scenario. That said, the crowd in my living room had a lot of questions (and statements) yesterday during the game. Mistakes and drive-killing turnovers were the only variable that could have sent this game overboard, and the first half had a bucketful: Hunter Henry’s injury, Efton Chism’s fumble, Maye getting sacked, the secondary playing too soft, Andy Borregales’ missed field goal all contributed to the three-phase slop that kept the team stalled. Even with all that, it never really felt as if the Patriots would lose. So this indeed was a tale of two halves. New England woke up after going three-and-out in the first series coming out of halftime. And they are a good enough team all-around to be able to come from behind. The Packers may not be so forgiving next week, but for now I’ll just enjoy the win and being up on the division games 3-0. title: Saints guard David Edwards takes responsibility following T.J. Paganetti’s firing
summary: The New Orleans Saints are making changes to their coaching staff after a disappointing start to the season, with run game coordinator T.J. Paganetti being relieved of his duties. While coaching decisions are part of the business, Saints guard David Edwards believes the players also need to take responsibility for the offense’s struggles. Speaking with […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LA - OCTOBER 11: David Edwards #76 of the New Orleans Saints looks on from the field during an NFL football game against the Minnesota Vikings at Cesars Superdome on October 11, 2026 in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New Orleans Saints are making changes to their coaching staff after a disappointing start to the season, with run game coordinator T.J. Paganetti being relieved of his duties. While coaching decisions are part of the business, Saints guard David Edwards believes the players also need to take responsibility for the offense’s struggles. Speaking with the media on Monday as the Saints returned from their bye week, Edwards expressed disappointment over Paganetti’s departure, acknowledging that the players could have done a better job executing the offensive game plan. “You know, I wish we as players, everybody, did a better job for him. And again, it’s just like the hard part of this business is it’s performance-based, and we haven’t gotten it done to a point,” Edwards said. The Saints’ inability to establish a consistent rushing attack has been one of the biggest issues surrounding the offense. Those struggles ultimately cost Paganetti his job, but Edwards made it clear that the problems extend beyond one person on the coaching staff. He pointed to execution and communication as two major factors that go into building a successful rushing attack, stressing that the players have to do their part to make the system work. “There’s an execution part, there’s a communication part. There’s so many things that go into the run game, having a successful run game,” Edwards said. Rather than focusing on the coaching change, Edwards wants his teammates to concentrate on the things that they can control. That means improving their preparation, maintaining a positive approach and making sure they are practicing at the level necessary to produce better results on Sundays. The Saints are coming out of their bye week with an opportunity to reset and address some of the problems that have plagued them throughout the season. For Edwards, the time away was beneficial, but the focus now needs to shift toward getting back to work and getting back to winning football games. The coaching change will not automatically fix New Orleans’ rushing attack. The players still have to execute, communicate and create opportunities for the offense to find consistency. Edwards’ comments reflect an understanding that Paganetti’s departure does not eliminate the responsibility of those still in the building. If the Saints want to improve their running game, the players will have to show it through their improved performances.
author: Nic Jennings

title: Should the Saints be buyers or sellers at the trade deadline?
summary: The season for the New Orleans Saints has not gone as the organization had planned so far, and coming off a bye week, the Saints are in a very precarious situation. As the division stands right now, the Saints are only one game out of first place. Every other team has three wins, with the […]
full_text: The season for the New Orleans Saints has not gone as the organization had planned so far, and coming off a bye week, the Saints are in a very precarious situation. As the division stands right now, the Saints are only one game out of first place. Every other team has three wins, with the Panthers, who have already had their bye week, sitting at four losses while the rest of the division has five. This puts the Saints in a difficult situation. Do they make a move at the trade deadline to try to go all in and win the division, or do they punt on the 2026 season because of the systemic issues and the need to acquire more young talent on cheap contracts for the long-term challenges ahead? Looking at the roster as it stands right now, if the Saints wanted to bring in some players to help them win, they would have to spend future draft capital on the defensive side of the ball. The Saints spent the entire offseason ignoring some major issues on defense, especially their inability to stop the run. They would have to start there, focusing on the line of scrimmage. The first player to explore would be Grover Stewart, the interior defensive tackle for the Colts. Stewart is one of the best run-stuffing tackles in the league. During his NFL career, he has recorded over 400 total tackles and 13 sacks. The issue with Stewart is that he has now been in the league for nine years. Do you feel comfortable with the Saints sending draft capital in exchange for a veteran who has been in the league this long? Other options include Daron Payne of the Commanders, an eight-year veteran who can defend the run and add valuable interior pass-rushing ability, with 38 sacks over his career, and Dalvin Tomlinson. Tomlinson is not as accomplished as Payne and Stewart, but he is a player known for his play and durability. He has not missed a start over his nine-year career, and on a team that struggles with health issues, this would be an immediate upgrade. The Saints could also look at linebackers like Cody Barton of the Titans and Daiyan Henley of the Chargers. But at this point, the Saints should not be comfortable giving up draft capital in a season like this one. This is not a team that is just a single player away from making a run. It’s one thing to consider going on a championship run with the playoffs in sight, but this team is trying to make a run to win a poor division. This is a team trying to make a run to win eight or nine games. This is not an acceptable position to be in when it comes to trading away future assets just to finish a season with fewer than double-digit wins. As the trade deadline approaches, the Saints may want to consider trading players to acquire more assets. But the issue is that the Saints don’t really have a roster constructed in a way that could bring back a haul like the Titans just received, which included two first-round picks and a fourth-round pick. The best available player who could potentially bring back a high draft selection would be Chase Young. With the way Young is playing right now, the best the Saints could potentially get in return for him would be a second-round selection, primarily because this is his first year playing well and staying healthy. At this point, Young is looking more and more like the heir apparent to Cam Jordan at edge rusher, and Carl Granderson has been able to complement him in a truly special way. However, Granderson’s play over the past few seasons has been up and down as well. The Saints just signed Chris Olave to a top-10 contract extension among receivers in the league, so another team may not be willing to take on that contract. Realistically, the Saints should look to move players like Justin Reid, Pete Werner, Spencer Rattler, Kendre Miller, and Cesar Ruiz. These players are all playing in position groups that the Saints need to upgrade. Without them on the roster, it would not necessarily create massive holes that would be difficult to fill. Whatever compensation the Saints could get in return might potentially be more valuable than what they are currently getting out of those players. It’s very interesting situation the Saints have put themselves in. Do they build for a nine-win season now and make building something better in the future more challenging? Or do they try to build for the future, knowing they don’t have enough valuable assets to make the moves necessary to elevate the roster and improve the many different position groups that need attention? Also, do you trust this coach and the vision he has for the roster at any point during this reconstruction? Can he properly utilize the players to get the most out of them? The next few weeks will be very telling for this franchise, and the decisions made will have implications not only for the 2026 season but also for the foreseeable future in New Orleans. What do you think the Saints should do at the trade deadline? Who do you think they should trade, or who should they trade for?

title: Fantasy Football 2026: Waiver Wire, Week 9 edition
summary: Welcome to the Fantasy Football Waiver Wire for Week 9. Week 8 was a strange one, through and through. Can we chalk that up to Halloween? Maybe. Perhaps the biggest headline is that Lamar Jackson came back after missing three games with an ankle injury and his return lasted all of one play, and now […]
full_text: JJ is getting it done | Getty Images Welcome to the Fantasy Football Waiver Wire for Week 9. Week 8 was a strange one, through and through. Can we chalk that up to Halloween? Maybe. Perhaps the biggest headline is that Lamar Jackson came back after missing three games with an ankle injury and his return lasted all of one play, and now he’s on IR and might miss the rest of the season with a thumb injury. That’s going to negatively impact all of the Ravens. Throw in other injuries and the steady drumbeat of bye weeks, and the waiver wire is once again going to be busy this week. Unfortunately, it’s one of the weaker free agent crops of the season – so far. The Process : Each week, I try to identify the top Waiver Wire targets and evaluate the short- and long-term prospects of those players. I also do my best to reveal which players who are coming off a big week are fool’s gold. Finally, I look at streamers who might help you in a pinch (this is usually more important during Bye weeks). Some players discussed won’t be available in your league. I try to list players who are available in more than 50% of leagues. But what does that even mean? A 10-team league with six bench spots will have a much larger Free Agent pool than a 14-team league with eight. Most leagues fall somewhere in between. This isn’t “one size fits all.” By way of example, I won’t list Kirk Cousins , Jonah Coleman , Rachaad White , Makai Lemon , Jordyn Tyson , DeVaughn Vele , T.J. Hockenson , or Brenton Strange , among others who probably aren’t available in any of your leagues. Note that I’m writing this column BEFORE the Week 9 Monday night game (CHI @ SEA). WEEK 9 BYES: Steelers and Titans Week 9 Waiver Wire Quarterback: Geno Smith makes my list again, and the veteran QB is delivering in his return to the team that drafted him. His last two outings: 24.5 and 19.0 fantasy points. Kansas City in Week 9 isn’t a good matchup, but the schedule is favorable for the following three games (Bills, Chargers, and Dolphins). Let’s stay in New York (OK fine, New Jersey). J.J. McCarthy has looked outstanding through five quarters as a Giant. As in, he’s completely unrecognizable – so far – from the quarterback who was so atrocious on Minnesota last season. That excellence didn’t translate to big fantasy points in their last game (an OT upset win in Houston), but those will come if he keeps hitting his weapons all over the field, and using his legs as needed. If you need a second QB in a Superflex he’s a good target, as the first-place Giants have been moving the ball and scoring. And if he turns back into a pumpkin, it was worth the risk (same as for Big Blue). Jacoby Brissett and Daniel Jones got benched in Week 8. I don’t know what that means long-term, but Gardner Minshew and Anthony Richardson could be in line for some starts for at least a little while. Minshew has already been named the starter for Week 9. The Colts are in free-fall, and maybe the whole team should just be avoided, minus Jonathan Taylor if he’s still there. Richardson — if he starts some games —can run and that always has value. The Cardinals throw the ball a ton and Minshew has produced at times in the past. Arizona is at Seattle this week, so you won’t want to start Minshew in Week 9. But the Colts host the Cowboys and their terrible defense, so if you really want to gamble…Anyway, of the two, I prefer Minshew. Need a Week 9 streamer? Malik Willis gets the Lions and their generous defense. Running Back: There are some very good options here, but availability will vary a lot. Some of the publicly available roster percentages on the guys I’m about to list feel lower than they actually are, in practice. Mike Washington, Jr. got the first six touches in the Raiders’ win over the Jets on Sunday and ended up with 25 carries to just two for Ashton Jeanty. He didn’t have any catches, though, and Jeanty (who may have been in the doghouse) is still dominating the third down and passing game work. This is a situation to watch. Washington is a high priority add if he’s somehow available in your league. Tyler Allgeier had a monster game on Sunday (RB1 for the week!). It was against Dallas (the league’s worst run defense), and Jeremiyah Love is still not at 100%. It was Allgeier’s first game with more than more than 6.5 fantasy points in a month. So yeah, it’s an outlier performance. Still, he’s a very capable back, and Arizona can score. He’s a good player to have on you roster for spot starts and maybe more. Seth McGowan should be rostered everywhere, while we all wait and see whether Jonathan Taylor gets moved. It might just get so ugly in Indianapolis that it’s an offense to completely avoid, but “first string” running backs should always be rostered. In the same vein, both Tyjae Spears and Nick Singleton are speculative adds, as Tony Pollard could possibly get traded as well. Kenny Gainwell erupted for a monster game Sunday, but the Bucs only attempted three passes in the rain and ran both of their backs down Atlanta’s throat. I don’t think this performance is all that repeatable, and Gainwell has mostly disappointed this season after his mini-breakout last season. Still, he should be rostered. Devin Singletary is worth a roster spot. It’s possible that New York could be adding a back via trade, but with Tyrone Tracy, Jr. on IR and Cam Skattebo straining his hamstring at the end of the Week 7 game, Singletary should be in for more work on a productive rushing offense. Emmett Johnson and Kaelon Black are exciting rookie backups who’ve shown plenty of burst when given the chance and are in great handcuff situations. Did you see Johnson’s long TD catch-and-run at Denver? Wow. Both can be flexed in an emergency and are lottery tickets that should be rostered. Jonathon Brooks (IR stash) is another to consider if you want to speculate. Wide Receiver The cupboard is pretty bare at receiver this week. Here’s something I thought I’d never write: The Jets have a lot of weapons. A week after everyone ran out to get Omar Cooper, Jr. , Cooper goose-egged and Adonai Mitchell , who put up zero points the week before in his return from injury, exploded for 7-142-1. Welcome to fantasy football! It’s going to be frustrating at times, but both players will have good games, and bad ones, on an offense that’s constantly chasing points. Cooper probably isn’t available in your league, but Mitchell might be. De’Zhaun Stribling is an intriguing IR stash, given how banged-up the 49er receivers are. DeMarcus Robinson is too, for that matter. Need depth? I’ll repeat a bunch of names I’ve listed in recent weeks, together with some new ones: Antonio Williams , DeMario Douglas , Keenan Allen , Malik Washington, Jahan Dotson, Caleb Douglas, Travis Hunter, Jakobi Meyers, Savion Williams , and Tank Dell. Speculative stashes: I’m slightly intrigued by Treylon Burks , who is getting deep shots and has the frame and high catch point to be useful in the red zone, and Kyle Williams , given all the injuries to New England’s receivers. I don’t think I’d chase Chimere Dike’s big Week 8, unless you get points for return yardage. He’s likely to go back to a very part-time role in the offense once Carnell Tate is back, and the Titans are on a bye this week which gives Tate another week. Tight End: Mike Gesiscki has a TD in five straight games, and six on the season. We can’t continue to ignore this. A bonus: This week he even caught a few other passes. Joe Burrow is playing out of his mind. The volume is low, and maybe the TD production isn’t sustainable, but Gesicki is scoring more fantasy points than a lot of guys who are in fantasy starting lineups each week. Eli Raridon gets a nice bump if Hunter Henry misses time, and especially with so many New England receivers banged up. Chig Okonkwo is now a mainstay in this column. He’s making plays, even if the volume isn’t great. Terry McLaurin’s injury has opened the door for multiple players to see more targets. Terrance…

title: NY Giants John Harbaugh: Team ‘open for any call’, and will make any call
summary: New York Giants head coach John Harbaugh unapologetically admitted on Monday that he did call Tennessee Titans owner Amy Adams Strunk about the possibility of trading for defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons. “I left a message [with Strunk] because you’re turning over every stone, going to try everything,” Harbaugh said. “I mean, I’ll put it out […]
full_text: John Harbaugh | Getty Images New York Giants head coach John Harbaugh unapologetically admitted on Monday that he did call Tennessee Titans owner Amy Adams Strunk about the possibility of trading for defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons. “I left a message [with Strunk] because you’re turning over every stone, going to try everything,” Harbaugh said. “I mean, I’ll put it out there, man. We’re open for any call. Anybody who wants to call us or call anybody, call. “It was kind of like fun to see the outpouring of interest in that. I enjoyed it. We’re not part of any secret society oath that says you can only talk to somebody. We’re not in that. We didn’t get memoed on that. We’re not in that agreement. So, like I said, anybody can call us. We won’t be adhering to that particular agreement.” Harbaugh said the Giants are “not apologizing” for aggressively trying to do what is best for them. “It’s a small world, so people call people. So, to say that only these two people can talk to each other, it’s not how it works. It’s false, it’s incorrect. People on every level make calls to people on every level because they know them,” Harbaugh said. “And how we do it here, and how we did it in Baltimore, and I love the way it’s done here, and the way they’ve done it here in the past too, is it’s transparent in our building. We’re all talking to each other, we all know what each other’s doing, we all know. I know who Joe’s calling, Joe knows if I’m calling somebody, Joe knows who I’m calling. “We’re turning over every stone, we’re making every call. We’re getting all the information we can possibly get at all times, and we are not apologizing for that at any point in time ever. We’re going to do the most we can possibly do to try to get some things done. It’s hard to get deals done. It’s hard, you can see how hard it is, but we’re going to do our best and what’s for our team.” "We're all talking to each other. We all know what each other's doing." John Harbaugh talks about the Giants' trade deadline process and his communication with Joe Schoen: pic.twitter.com/2hbX1F1s8Q — SNY Giants (@SNYGiants) November 2, 2026 The Giants are 4-2-1 and in first place in the NFC East. With the Dallas Cowboys, Philadelphia Eagles, and Washington Commanders all floundering and under .500, the Giants have an opportunity to win the division for the first time since 2011. That, coincidentally, is the last time the Giants won the Super Bowl. With the Nov. 10 NFL trade deadline just a week away, Harbaugh said the Giants will “always” look to upgrade the roster. “That’s always the goal,” Harbaugh said. “Easier said than done. And it’s hard to find players that can make you better, because we have good players. Very good players. “So, it’s got to be something that is a need, that fits your financial profile, that fits your price tag. I mean, it’s not like we have a bunch of draft picks either. We’re not loaded with 12 or 13 draft picks where we’ve got draft capital to burn. We don’t. So, we have to be smart shoppers that way.” "It's got to be something that is a need, that fits your financial profile, that fits your price tag. It's not like we have a bunch of draft picks, either. We're not loaded with 12 or 13 draft picks where we've got draft capital to burn. We don't, so we have to be smart shoppers… pic.twitter.com/hrkRduSX4c — SNY Giants (@SNYGiants) November 2, 2026 Harbaugh said that if the Giants surrender draft capital they want to do it with more than just this season in mind. “It would have to be, though, honestly, it wouldn’t have to just be a short-term thing, for me, it wouldn’t want to be a one-on-one kind of thing,” he said. “You want to have a short-term and a long-term win if you’re going to do it with draft capital.” Harbaugh admitted that locker room acceptance would be a consideration in any proposed deal. “Yes, absolutely, very important. We got a great camaraderie, a great brotherhood, synergy,” Harbaugh said. “All those things is really, really good right now, and you want to take that into account, even to the point where you probably talk to some of your guys before you did something like that. Make sure that everybody understands, and they’re kind of on board with it.”

title: NY Giants add a familiar running back to the practice squad
summary: The New York Giants made a move at running back coming out of their bye week, but it’s probably not the move everyone was waiting on. The Giants have signed Eric Gray to their practice squad, per reports. The move reunites Gray with the team that drafted him and comes as the Giants are short-handed […]
full_text: ﻿New York Giants running back Eric Gray carries the ball durring warmups | Getty Images The New York Giants made a move at running back coming out of their bye week, but it’s probably not the move everyone was waiting on. The Giants have signed Eric Gray to their practice squad, per reports . The move reunites Gray with the team that drafted him and comes as the Giants are short-handed at running back. Starter Cam Skattebo is nursing a hamstring injury, while Tyrone Tracy is on IR with his own hamstring injury. The Giants originally selected Gray out of Oklahoma in the fifth round of the 2023 NFL Draft. The 26-year old is familiar with the Giants’ offense and blocking scheme, having been with the team throughout the off-season program and training camp. The Giants cut Gray in the final cut-down to their initial 53-man roster, after which he landed on the Cleveland Browns practice squad. Gray has appeared in 34 career games for the Giants, serving as a depth player in their backfield as well as a kick returner. He had 21 kickoff returns in 2024, averaging 26.4 yards per return. Gray has a similar skill set as both Tracy and Gregory Desrosiers, whom the Giants signed off of the Los Angeles Chargers practice squad last week. The Giants released DL Josh Topou from the practice squad to make room for Gray.
author: Chris Pflum

title: NY Giants trade candidate: DT Christian Barmore
summary: The New York Giants need defensive tackle help. Badly, enough, in fact, that head coach John Harbaugh recently took the unusual step of calling Tenneessee Titans owner Amy Adams Strunk directly to find out if the Giants could get Jeffery Simmons. That, of course, did not happen. There are other fish in the defensive tackle […]
full_text: Christian Barmore | Getty Images The New York Giants need defensive tackle help. Badly, enough, in fact, that head coach John Harbaugh recently took the unusual step of calling Tenneessee Titans owner Amy Adams Strunk directly to find out if the Giants could get Jeffery Simmons. That, of course, did not happen. There are other fish in the defensive tackle sea, however, though none would be a prize the size of Simmons, who was dealt to the Chicago Bears for two first-round picks and a fourth-round pick. One defensive tackle who is apparently available, and might help the Giants, is Christian Barmore of the New England Patriots. According to Sports Illustrated NFL insider Albert Breer, the veteran defender “ could be had” by a willing trade partner , and the price to get him would be about a fourth-round draft pick. “My understanding is the price would be about a fourth-round pick, and he may be tradable because if you look at his contract, he’s making $13.3 million this year,” Breer said on NBC Sports Boston . “So you’d be taking on a prorated number off of that if you did trade for him. His numbers balloon after this year. …Those numbers aren’t guaranteed. “So, a team could wind up walking away from that if they did trade for him. But this is a player that very clearly is available. And if somebody’s willing to swing the Patriots a fourth-round pick, I think something could happen.” Should the Giants be interested in the 6-foot-5, 315-pound 27-year-old? Why it would work The price would not be that high. Even though Barmore is in the midst of a four-year, $84 million contract nothing beyond this season is guaranteed. So, if you don’t like what you see over the remainder of the year, moving on is not an issue. Barmore is a former second-round pick with 19 career sacks, so there is clearly talent there. If he plays well, maybe he could be a piece of the defensive line going forward. Why it wouldn’t work There is a reason why Barmore has been losing playing time in New England to former undrafted free agent and one-time Giant Cory Durden. His run defense has been atrocious. “He’s been used more as a situational pass rusher than the three-down impact player he’s being paid to be,” said Bernd Buchmasser of SB Nation’s Pats Pulpit . “He also was extended by the Patriots before Mike Vrabel arrived and had some off-the-field and medical issues. Rumor has it a mid-round pick could be the price.” In his seasons, Barmore has had a Pro Football Focus run defense grade above the 60.0 average score just one time. Last season, his run defense grade was a miserable 33.6. This year, it is 44.8. By PFF grade, the Giants are getting far better play from the much-maligned Darius Alexander (59.6). Barmore’s Pro Football and Sports Network Impact Scores aren’t any more encouraging. PFSN gives him a 90.3 pass-rushing score, No. 7 among defensive tackles. Run defense? His PFSN score is 68.3, 106th among defensive tackles. “I don’t think it’s [Barmore’s run defense] necessarily that he’s bad, but he’s better attacking upfield than controlling his gap, for example,” Buchmasser said. “I think if you have a big nose to occupy the 0/1-tech spot and line him up at 3T, he can certainly be a serviceable run defender; he was at times last year when the Pats had Khyiris Tonga available. They don’t have anybody like that at the moment, and therefore nobody to lift some pressure off of Barmore when he is asked to do early-down run work.” The Giants need defensive tackles who help the run defense, not add more questions to it.

title: The Jets aren’t good enough to overcome the mistakes they made against the Raiders
summary: I have said it before. I will say it again. There are different types of bad teams in the NFL. For much of 2025, particularly at the end of the season with Brady Cook at quarterback, the Jets were a comedically mismatched bad team. They didn’t have the talent or the coaching necessary to be […]
full_text: Nov 1, 2026; East Rutherford, New Jersey, USA; Las Vegas Raiders tight end Michael Mayer (87) makes a catch against the New York Jets in the second half at MetLife Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Robert Deutsch-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect I have said it before. I will say it again. There are different types of bad teams in the NFL. For much of 2025, particularly at the end of the season with Brady Cook at quarterback, the Jets were a comedically mismatched bad team. They didn’t have the talent or the coaching necessary to be competitive with practically any of the other 31 teams. In 2026 the Jets are also a bad team, but they are a different type of bad. The talent level is better. Of course, that isn’t saying much. The Jets could be putting practically any sort of roster on the field and still be much better than what we saw at the end of last season. The 2026 Jets still rank fairly low on talent relative to the rest of the league. That is particularly true on defense. I’m not sure many of the players who took the field in yesterday’s game against the Las Vegas Raiders would see much playing time on a Super Bowl caliber defense. Even most of those who would make the cut almost certainly would have smaller roles than they have with the Jets. There are any number of reasons the Jets are so low on talent on the defensive side of the ball. Teams do have to prioritize which areas they want to improve first in a rebuild, and the Jets have sunk many resources into their offense. There also have been a number of personnel miscalculations, particularly in free agency in 2026. I would also argue that the way the defense was built shows fundamental flaws. The pass rush seems entirely structured around one player, David Bailey, a developing rookie. We have seen the sort of up and down season we might expect from a rookie. When said rookie is out of the lineup, it makes things even more challenging, impossible even. Things look brighter on offense where the Jets do have a number of young players showing real talent, but on the whole it would be fair to state that this remains a roster closer to the bottom than the top. Teams like I just described can still win in the NFL. It requires them to be opportunistic. They need to find ways to equalize games. Being efficient in the red zone on offense and stingy in the red zone on defense is important. Ditto to protecting the ball and forcing turnovers. Playing top notch special teams also helps a lot. And through these things and more, quality coaching has a way of making up the gap. Unfortunately, the Jets are poor in most of the aspects I just mentioned. Avoiding turnovers is really the only thing they are doing well at that point. These flaws all manifested themselves in the team’s 38-33 loss to the Raiders. Teams like the Jets just don’t have a margin for error, even against an opponent like the Raiders. Most of the attention will rightly be given to a putrid defensive performance. There isn’t anything you can say to sugarcoat a game like that defensively. The Jets’ lack of defensive talent showed, but it wasn’t just that. Even basics of defense were a struggle. It seemed like on a number of occasions they lost track of Brock Bowers, which you just can’t do considering how important he is to the Raiders offense. And for a third straight week, the unit allowed the opponent to grind out the clock with a time consuming drive late in the fourth quarter. This was a team loss, though. A special teams unit that was the league’s best in a dismal 2025 has completely regressed. Week 8 was another ugly day for Chris Banjo and his group as they allowed a kickoff return touchdown. On offense the day was a bright spot for the most part. The Jets put a season high 33 points on the board. Still, they left points on the field, settling for a field goal four times in the red zone. This included three stalled drives in the first half. There were stretches where the Jets might have been able to seize control of the game had they made plays. The three first half red zone drives ending in field goals produced 9 points instead of 21. The touchdown gave the Raiders 7. Adding even some of those lost 19 points could have taken a 23-14 halftime lead into a territory where the Jets were in total control of the game. Geno Smith misfired on two would be touchdown passes to Garrett Wilson in the first quarter. In the context of what turned into a superb day for Smith throwing the ball, I think we can give the quarterback some grace. A drive that stalled before halftime, though, is tougher to defend. That drive stalled just before and after the two minute warning as Frank Reich called seven consecutive runs. It felt like Reich was prioritizing running out the clock so the Raiders couldn’t get the ball at the expense of scoring an important touchdown. Given how publicized the cartoonish point differential the Aaron Glenn Jets in the last two minutes of the first half has been over the last two weeks, it almost seemed like the Jets coaching staff was prioritizing not giving the Raiders a chance to score and make that differential worse over winning the game. As I have mentioned in this space before, the best two minute drills find the right balance between maximizing points and leaving as little time as possible on the clock for the other team. Of the two, maximizing points should be the higher priority. The Jets can win games, but they just aren’t good enough to overcome their inability to do the little things. That goes for their players and their coaches. And because these mistakes are made over and over, it seems increasingly likely the Jets will have a lot of new players and new coaches sooner rather than later.

title: New York Jets News: Aaron Glenn is Dying by the Sword
summary: During the offseason, New York Jets head coach Aaron Glenn decided to take over defensive playcalling. He called it his “superpower.” I respected the decision. Had Glenn hired someone else to do it and it failed, Glenn would have been fired. For the rest of his life, he’d be filled with regret and wondering what […]
full_text: New York Jets head coach Aaron Glenn talks with a referee after a flag is thrown as the New York Jets play Las Vegas Raiders in a week 8 NFL football game at MetLife Stadium on Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026, in East Rutherford, NJ. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co During the offseason, New York Jets head coach Aaron Glenn decided to take over defensive playcalling. He called it his “superpower.” I respected the decision. Had Glenn hired someone else to do it and it failed, Glenn would have been fired. For the rest of his life, he’d be filled with regret and wondering what could have happened had he taken over playcalling, considering that was a big reason he got the Jets job anyway. Glenn chose to live and die by the sword. If he was an excellent defensive playcaller, he would have received flowers and all of the credit. However, if it failed, Glenn would die by the sword and have no regrets. Well, eight games into the 2026 season, the Jets sit at 2-6. According to ESPN’s Rich Cimini , the Jets are only the third team in the last 45 years “to lose after scoring on their first six possessions.” How did that happen? The Jets’ defense collapsed like a used lawn chair. The Jets’ defense has served as the perfect antidote for ailing teams. Miami was 0-5 and never held a lead all season until they played the Jets and were cured. Las Vegas had lost four in a row, and suddenly the Jets cured their problems. Glenn getting fired is no longer a question of if, but rather when. Whenever that time comes, Glenn will have died by the same sword he wielded, promising that things would turn around. J-E-T-S!
