title: Eagles-Commanders snap counts: Makai Lemon seeing more opportunity
summary: The official snap counts from the Philadelphia Eagles’ Week 8 loss to the Washington Commanders are in. Does anyone actually care? Regardless, let’s take a look and run through some analysis. OFFENSE DEFENSE SPECIAL TEAMS DID NOT PLAY ACTIVE: Joe Milton, Cole Payton INACTIVE: DeVonta Smith, Jihaad Campbell, Dontayvion Wicks, Jonathan Jones, Lane Johnson, Jake […]
full_text: LANDOVER, MARYLAND - NOVEMBER 1: Trey Amos #23 of the Washington Commanders breaks up a pass intended for Makai Lemon #9 of the Philadelphia Eagles during the second quarter of an NFL football game at Northwest Stadium on November 1, 2026 in Landover, Maryland. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The official snap counts from the Philadelphia Eagles’ Week 8 loss to the Washington Commanders are in. Does anyone actually care? Regardless, let’s take a look and run through some analysis. OFFENSE Jordan Mailata is the only player who’s played 100% of the Eagles’ offensive snaps this season. He’s also played 11.79% of the Eagles’ special teams snaps. The Eagles’ starting offensive line configuration in each of their last three games has played 100% of the team’s snaps on offense. The continuity doesn’t really seem to be helping, though. Darius Cooper played the most snaps of any Eagles wide receiver for the second week in a row. He ranked second on the team in targets with six but only logged two receptions for 19 yards. Makai Lemon was one snap behind Cooper for the second game in a row. The Eagles’ 2026 first-round pick saw a team-high nine targets for six receptions and 57 yards. It’s been good to see Lemon getting more involved … but I do think some of the praise seems to be overboard? He’s been taking a step in the right direction, for sure. But I don’t think 17 targets resulting in 13 catches for 124 yards (9.5 average) and a touchdown is any indication that he’s a flat out stud. Great route but when it happened my immediate thought was this is a catch Lemon must make to be an impactful NFL WR – high level of difficulty but a perfect throw from QB b/w defenders dropped right into his hands on 3rd down, gotta have it play. Punt -> Commies get 3 before half https://t.co/HNSGpHRM7D — Dan (@snaxonly) November 2, 2026 The Commanders’ defense has allowed the second-most fantasy points to tight ends this season. Naturally, Dallas Goedert saw just four targets for four receptions and 30 yards. Sure. Elijah Mitchell ended up as the top running back with Saquon Barkley’s workload limited due to his hamstring and back injuries. He saw two fewer carries than Barkley while producing four more yards. His six targets resulted in four catches for three yards. Brutal. Hollywood Brown: two targets, two catches, 17 yards! Awesome player! Man, wouldn’t it be a smart move for another team to make a big offer to the Eagles in order to get Brown before the NFL trade deadline? The Eagles will have a hard time letting him go … but the price just might be right. Elijah Moore has seen zero targets in four of his six games played this season. Just doing cardio out there. Dating back to Week 5, Johnny Mundt’s snap count percentage has progressively decreased each week: 32.3% to 29.7% to 24.2% to 18.8%. Just cut him and put Zach Ertz on the roster at this point. Eli Stowers had the fakest three receptions for 53 yards stat line that you’ll ever see. 46 of those came in garbage time on the final two plays of the game with the Commanders playing prevent defense. Good on the rookie tight end for a real seven-yard reception (where it looked like he really fought the ball as it came in) when the game was actually still competitive. Nice for him to get that experience under his belt. The Eagles should find more playing time for him as they eventually shift into evaluation mode. Why is Grant Calcaterra on this team? You know you are simply the smartest person in the room when you line up Grant Calcaterra at FB. Next level thinking! He not only fails to disrupt #45 when he slants outside he also whiffs on #2 after that and then pushes him in the back for good measure. pic.twitter.com/Z9HzeLXUin — Shane Haff (@ShaneHaffNFL) November 2, 2026 Jaydon Blue saw some offensive snaps in garbage time in addition to looking ineffective as a kick returner. Willie Lampkin lined up as a fullback on Saquon Barkley’s rushing attempt. That was cool! His block wasn’t great but they should experiment with him in that role more often. Fred Johnson came in as a sixth offensive lineman for Barkley’s touchdown run. DEFENSE Andrew Mukuba briefly missed some time after getting evaluated for a concussion. Jeremiah Trotter Jr. got the start in place of an injured Jihaad Campbell and led the Eagles in total tackles. He graded out well by Pro Football Focus. Jalen Carter was more productive than he was against the Cowboys in Week 7. Good to see him bounce back a bit. Still not as dominant as the Eagles need him to be. Nolan Smith was the Eagles’ top edge rusher after missing Week 7. He’s tied with Carter for a team-leading four sacks this season. Jordan Davis has logged the two highest snap count percentages of his season over the past two weeks. But he’s not exactly showing up much in the box score with just a single solo tackle from those games. In a sign of how bleak this season is, the Eagles’ social media team (not a criticism of them, to be clear, just a commentary on how there’s not much positive to share) posted a brag about Moro Ojomo’s TFL from Sunday night: Playing behind the line @novonordisk | #FlyEaglesFly pic.twitter.com/IBGpPNPxgM — Philadelphia Eagles (@Eagles) November 2, 2026 Jonathan Greenard played his highest snap count percentage of the season! He had a solo tackle and zero other stats. He’s logged just one quarterback hit this season. I liked the Eagles acquiring him, to be fair, but he’s just been a total zero for them thus far. I do think it could just be a lost season for him since he’s been hampered by injuries. But perhaps he’ll continue to struggle to stay healthy since he’s turning 30 this offseason. Arnold Ebiketie was back to being a rotational edge rusher instead of the top guy at the position after injuries forced him into the latter role. Jalyx Hunt’s playing time continues to be limited due to his injuries. Kenny Moore and Marcus Epps, who had been demoted out of a defensive role, shared some playing time. Ty Robinson warrants more playing time simply because the Eagles need to see what they have in him. Michael Carter II seemingly re-aggravated his abdomen injury in this game. SPECIAL TEAMS Mason Reiger saw a good deal of special teams duty after being temporarily elevated from the practice squad. This was his NFL regular season debut. A.J. Epenesa was demoted to special teams duty only after previously having a rotational role on defense. Wonder if the Eagles might try to trade him, albeit for very little? Or just cut him and sign Reiger or Keyshawn James-Newby to the roster. DID NOT PLAY ACTIVE: Joe Milton, Cole Payton INACTIVE: DeVonta Smith, Jihaad Campbell, Dontayvion Wicks, Jonathan Jones, Lane Johnson, Jake Majors, Britain Covey There have been calls for Milton to replace McKee. I’m not going to say no … but I don’t think it would make much of a difference. Although … Nick Foles made a good point: EVAN MOORE: “It’s at least intriguing to consider [Joe Milton over Tanner McKee.] And I realize he probably doesn’t know the offense […] NICK FOLES: “That might actually be a good thing that he doesn’t know the offense that well.” Via “The SZN” 💀💀💀 pic.twitter.com/iaVhbXsiGK — Brandon Lee Gowton (@BrandonGowton) November 2, 2026 Payton was active but the Eagles did not use him on special teams like they did earlier this season. We’ll see if any of the injured players are able to return to practice this week. As a reminder, Johnson is set to remain on the Eagles’ roster until June 2027 , even though he retired.

At 2-6 and languishing at the bottom […]
full_text: Photo by Patrick Smith/Getty Images | Getty Images Now, there can be no false hope. After their 27-10 defeat at the hands of the Commanders in Maryland on Sunday Night Football, their second prime-time humiliation against a divisional opponent in six days, there can be no rationalizing making a push for a sixth straight postseason appearance. At 2-6 and languishing at the bottom of a laughably bad NFC East, the Eagles’ 2026 season is done. We should be thankful for the closure. Over the next two weeks, general manager Howie Roseman will work to sell off starters on expiring contracts. Those of you with Dallas Goedert, Riq Woolen and/or Hollywood Brown jerseys, tough luck there. He’ll certainly listen to offers on everyone else. Yes, even Saquon Barkley, who it was reported on Sunday the Eagles would not trade as they look to contend in 2027. It’s hard to believe Roseman would shoot down an obscene offer for anyone on his roster at this point, although it’s highly unlikely Barkley wears another uniform this season. The big question left after another dreadfully sloppy performance on Sunday night is whether Nick Sirianni, Sean Mannion, Vic Fangio and the rest of the current coaching staff will be around to coach Barkley and his teammates on next year’s Eagles squad. It’s no surprise the Eagles are losing right now, and Roseman deserves as much of the blame for what’s happened this year as any of his coaches. Roseman and Lurie, after all, are the ones who hired Sirianni’s offensive coaching staff. But mirrors can be difficult to look into, and Roseman and Lurie aren’t firing themselves. Injuries cannot be helped. If Jalen Hurts had been on the field last night instead of overmatched back-up QB Tanner McKee, it’s likely the Eagles would have won. That he was lost for the season with blood clots is an unfortunate bit of bad luck, as are the injuries to DeVonta Smith and Tay Wicks, the retirement of Lane Johnson, and Barkley’s inability to stay 100% healthy this year. But it’s possible to play a cleaner brand of football with mediocre talent than what we’re seeing out of the Birds over the last few weeks. The highly-paid and supposedly talented defense knows the offense has no chance and appears to have given up. Vic Fangio was reportedly thinking about retiring this past off-season, and one has to wonder if this nightmare won’t accelerate those plans. But there’s no excuse for the kinds of mistakes (off-sides penalties, personal fouls), and inability to generate splash plays that we’ve seen from the defense this year. That side of the ball is relatively healthy. After Sunday’s night’s debacle just outside the nation’s capital, Sirianni shouldered the blame for his team’s brutal display. “I know I’ve said this: Until we coach better, until we have better detail as coaches, until our players play with better detail, then we’re gonna see the same results,” he said. “And that falls on me. I feel like with all the detail that’s not happening right now, I got to try a different approach. And so that’s 100 percent on me. With how many of those issues are happening right now, I’ll do everything I can to try different things to make sure that we’re getting that point across.” There is little doubt Sirianni is preaching the right messages to his players. They just may not be listening. And that is usually the death knell of a coaching tenure. Sirianni’s message has helped compile one of the most impressive resumes of any head coach in the history of the NFL. In his sixth year with the team, he entered 2026 with a 59-26 record, the third-highest career winning percentage (.694) in the Super Bowl Era (min. 50 games). Among Super Bowl-winning head coaches, only John Madden (.759, 1969-78) and Vince Lombardi (.738, 1959-67 and 1969) have a better winning percentage. He’s also the first coach to reach the playoffs in each of his first five seasons, with three division titles, two trips to the Super Bowl and one Super Bowl victory. But every coach has a lifecycle, and most don’t last as long as Andy Reid’s did at the beginning of Lurie’s tenure, or Mike Tomlin’s in Pittsburgh. Despite preaching the mantra “tough, detailed, together” ad nauseum to his players, these Eagles are none of those things. They are getting bullied. They are exceedingly sloppy. They do not communicate or function well as a unit in any phase of the game. It’s not necessarily his fault when Markel Bell commits a false start on a 4th-and-4 with the game on the line in the 4th quarter, nor is it his fault when former All-Pro offensive tackle Jordan Mailata lines up wrong on a late game field goal that is negated and then subsequently missed. But when you have a string of incidents like this, game after game, that’s less about talent and more about competency of coaching. While the Eagles are much less talented than they have been over the course of Sirianni’s tenure, there are enough good players on the roster that they should not be embarrassed by the likes of the Cowboys and Commanders. They should not be a bottom-feeder. Andy Reid went 5-11 in his first season with the Eagles. It was exceedingly ugly early on, but it was clear he was building something. The team had a young quarterback in Donovan McNabb they were excited about, and pieces were being put in place. The team looked more cohesive than they had in Ray Rhodes’ disastrous 3-13 disaster in 1998. Despite having an awful record, the difference in play between the two regimes was obvious. So, what are we witnessing here? Are we watching a Rhodes’ 1998 season, or will Sirianni’s group get it together over the second half and at least put on a good show, like the ‘99 Reid squad did? Obituaries for Sirianni have been written before. There are probably a number of Eagles beat reporters that had one ready to go in the can in the middle of the 2021 season, following the 2023 season, or at the bye week in 2024. Every time Sirianni has been written off for dead, he’s resurrected the team and his job security. And maybe that will happen again this off-season. He can fairly point to injuries on offense, specifically the loss of his star quarterback, and the growing pains of an offensive coordinator that he did not hire. He can point to a defense that has not played anywhere close to its potential. He can point to bad luck, bad bounces, and the realities of the cyclical life of the NFL. But one has to wonder if Sirianni has the skills to actually turn things around this time. He doesn’t have an offensive scheme that works anymore. He doesn’t call plays. He’s not an offensive mastermind. He’s completely uninvolved with the defense. He doesn’t have the power to hire his own coaching staff, and the player/personnel decisions are all handled by his bosses, albeit with his input I’m sure. Sirianni’s lone job is to rally the troops, keep the messaging going, and get his players to buy in and believe they can overcome the many obstacles put in front of them. That may not mean making the playoffs or winning a lot of games this year, but it would mean being competitive, avoiding stupid penalties at inopportune times, and other unforced errors that give off the appearance the team is badly coached. If you’re Roseman and Lurie, what makes more sense to you? Would it make more sense to give this current group another season as Jalen Hurts, Saquon Barkley and everyone on defense loses another year of their prime? Or should they wipe the slate clean and hand an offensive-minded guru the keys, let him call plays and hire his own staff? There comes a time when every head coach’s message loses resonance. Players hear it, but tune it out come game day. Players start to play for themselves and their numbers, and aren’t willing to sacrifice for a team that may only win five games. That appears to be what we’re witnessing here as the 2026 season develops. And if it persists, it’s hard to see how Roseman and Lurie decide to give this coaching staff another bite at the…

title: Eagles News: Nick Sirianni’s seat is getting hotter
summary: Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation! The Eagles certainly have issues that go beyond their head coach. But if you’re not part of the solution, you’re part of the problem. And Nick Sirianni doesn’t seem to have answers. This is a poorly coached team. I struggle to […]
full_text: LANDOVER, MARYLAND - NOVEMBER 01: Head coach Nick Sirianni of the Philadelphia Eagles looks on during the second quarter against the Washington Commanders at Northwest Stadium on November 01, 2026 in Landover, Maryland. (Photo by Patrick Smith/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation! The Eagles certainly have issues that go beyond their head coach. But if you’re not part of the solution, you’re part of the problem. And Nick Sirianni doesn’t seem to have answers. This is a poorly coached team. I struggle to see Sirianni returning in 2027 if the team helplessly continues their downward spiral. Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links … Nick Sirianni’s Eagles are burning. Jeffrey Lurie may prefer his Eagles rise from the ashes of Sirianni’s tenure. – Inquirer Sirianni, meanwhile, has nine games left to salvage this season and save it from becoming a referendum on his ability to lead the Eagles out of their doldrums. Lurie may not want to live through a repeat of 2012, 2015 or 2020. But each lost season resulted in him firing his coach, and if he’s being honest with himself, a rebirth. That isn’t an endorsement to get rid of Sirianni. But Lurie entertained the idea before (see: after the 2023 season and during the 2024 bye), and it’s just difficult to see another offseason of the Eagles explaining another change at offensive coordinator. They may end up doing that, but with a new head coach who is also their preferred coordinator. Doug Pederson lost his job partly because he refused to alter his coaching suggestions following the 2020 season. Sirianni has allowed Lurie and Roseman to influence some of his hires. It’s hard to believe they didn’t have some say in him bringing Sean Mannion and his scheme to Philadelphia. But Sirianni said he is still sticking by Mannion and his assistants. 10 Eagles things I think I think from the loss to the Commanders – BGN 9) This team quit for the second straight week. Nick Sirianni protected his players last week by saying he didn’t see an effort issue against the Cowboys. Even if Sirianni fudged the truth to the media, that was the right thing to do as he likely spoke to his players about the lack of effort when evaluating the film. The Eagles demonstrated a lack of effort again with 1:52 left in the game, when the Commanders went for two in a 25-10 game that was all but decided. The decision was wise by the Commanders, as a conversion gets them up three scores with barely any time left — an outcome that would make it basically impossible for the Eagles to tie the game (yet alone win). The defensive line didn’t even try to stop Austin Ekeler from going into the end zone. They checked out, much like the team did on several plays throughout last week’s game. This is a culture problem for the Eagles, and a bad look for a head coach that prides himself on culture. The film doesn’t lie regarding the Eagles’ effort over the last two weeks. Eagles-Commanders Postgame: Tanner McKee, Eagles DUMPED ON, Lose Sixth Straight – PHLY Eagles Despite squirreling out to an early 10-0 lead, the Philadelphia Eagles lost their sixth straight game to the lowly Washington Commanders in a game filled with familiar F-ups, like pre-snap penalties, bewildering play-calling, bizarre injury mismanagement, sloppy defense and more. Let’s talk about it with Brandon Lee Gowton, Bo Wulf, Miles Johnson, Fran Duffy, Vinny Curry and EJ Smith. Handing out 10 awards from the Eagles-Commanders game – PhillyVoice Anytime the team — maybe more specifically the offense — has gone through some rough patches, Sirianni has maintained positivity. Some go-to phrases might include “We’re close,” or “We have to lean on the things we do well.” But not after this game. Not after this six-game losing streak. Sirianni couldn’t muster any positivity. His candor was refreshing in a way, but also perhaps confirmation of what many have seen from this team all season… that nobody has any answers, and it doesn’t feel at all like any are forthcoming. Another L – Iggles Blitz Nick Sirianni looked like a beaten down man in his press conference. He is unbelievably frustrated by all the mistakes this team makes. He can live with talent issues. That is what you have to deal with when backups get on the field. But guys not getting line up correctly is unacceptable. Defenders not setting the edge is unacceptable. Missed blocking assignments are unacceptable. Sirianni likes his teams to be great at the things that don’t require talent. This group isn’t close to great when it comes to that stuff. They make dumb mistakes, often at the worst times. Something is just off. There are a ton of questions, but very few answers right now. Sirianni and his staff need to keep searching for solutions. There is still a lot of football left to play. It would certainly help to get some injured players back. Still, as I mentioned earlier, the problems go well beyond injuries If Eagles fire Nick Sirianni, here are 5 candidates to replace him, including ex-Philly coach – NJ.com Grant Udinski will be one of the top head-coaching candidates during the 2027 interview cycle. At 31, he would be the youngest head coach in the NFL. The Eagles would be taking a big risk hiring the league’s youngest head coach, but the reward could be great. The Rams hired Sean McVay at age 30 — and look at how that turned out. McVay has become one of the NFL’s best head coaches and one of the best offensive coaches in league history. He’s been to two Super Bowls, with one title. Udinski could solve the Eagles’ offensive problems in a way no other coach has. He has learned from Vikings head coach Kevin O’Connell and Jaguars head coach Liam Cohen, two of the league’s elite offensive play callers. He could help the Eagles install a better version of the Kyle Shanahan-McVay system. Nick Sirianni: I am not doing a good enough job, I’ve got to do better – PFT Eagles coach Nick Sirianni took the blame after Sunday night’s loss to the Commanders. The Eagles, who started the season 2-0 and had Super Bowl aspirations, lost their sixth consecutive game to fall to 2-6. Sirianni said the head coach deserves the blame when that happens. “I take everything as my responsibility that happens out on that field. Everything. Obviously I am not doing a good enough job right now. I’ve got to do better,” Sirianni said. Asked if offensive coordinator Sean Mannion will remain the play caller, Sirianni didn’t answer directly. Eagles-Commanders instant takeaways: Mental miscues extend losing streak to six … is this rock bottom? – PHLY Sports Mixed McKee. This was an uneven game for Tanner McKee. The backup quarterback had stretches where he seemed more settled operating Sean Mannion’s system and there were even some glimpses of an identity forming with him under center on the Eagles’ opening series. He found Saquon Barkley for a chunk gain thanks to a well-designed pass play to Barkley on a wheel route out of a “spinner-series” play-action fake out of the backfield. He also managed a well-layered throw to Makai Lemon on a deep crossing route. That was the good. The bad came mostly from McKee navigating muddy pockets. He can be absolved for a handful of errant throws with things collapsing around him and a steadier-than-ideal number of unblocked rushers making things complicated. But with the Eagles on the edge of field-goal range late in the third quarter, McKee not only took a sack in a clear “can’t take a sack here” scenario, he lost the ball as well. Overall, McKee finished 18-for-28 with 139 yards, one interception and one lost fumble. One week after seemingly making some progress, this was about as ugly as it’s been for McKee in another peformance mostly defined by mistakes. title: Saquon Barkley admits his injuries are holding him back
summary: After missing several games due to a hamstring injury, Eagles running back Saquon Barkley hurt his back on his first play against the Cowboys in Week 7. He was able to play 10 total snaps that game, and was adamant in the days after that he was committed to playing on Sunday night against the […]
full_text: Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images | Getty Images After missing several games due to a hamstring injury, Eagles running back Saquon Barkley hurt his back on his first play against the Cowboys in Week 7. He was able to play 10 total snaps that game, and was adamant in the days after that he was committed to playing on Sunday night against the Commanders, even if he wasn’t fully healthy. How much the back injury was impacted Barkley was highlighted after the Eagles second offensive drive in Washington, which ended with the RB taking a direct snap and running it three yards into the endzone for the first TD of the game. After his score, Barkley was moving and stretching non-stop on the sidelines, with the broadcast noting that he couldn’t sit down as he tried to stay loose. It doesn’t seem ideal to be playing a running back who can’t stop stretching his back muscles. He stayed off the field for the rest of the first quarter, but did start taking snaps again in the second — and was even inexplicably used to run out the clock near halftime. Barkley was already on a pitch count heading into the game, and played 22 snaps with 13 carries for 30 yards and a touchdown. After the loss, the RB admitted that while he’s mentally where he needs to be, with the hamstring and back injuries, he’s not physically where he wants to be. Saquon Barkley: “I’m just frustrated because my mind is there, but with the hammie and the back, my body isn’t right now.” #Eagles pic.twitter.com/7mOD7fR8Vh — EJ Smith (@EJSmith94) November 2, 2026 According to reports, and to Barkley himself, the Eagles have stated they are not moving the running back ahead of the trade deadline next week , Nov. 10. With that in mind, and his future still in Philly, the team really needs to consider shutting him down for a little while and give his body a real chance to heal, instead of making things worse for a season that isn’t turning around.

title: Steelers have built the NFL’s most dangerous rushing attack
summary: I can’t remember a time in my life when the Pittsburgh Steelers had as dominant a run game as they do right now. Jaylen Warren had another monster performance in Pittsburgh’s 27-6 win over the Cleveland Browns, rushing for a career-high 143 yards and a touchdown on over eight yards per carry. Rico Dowdle added […]
full_text: (Photo by Lauren Leigh Bacho/Getty Images) | Getty Images I can’t remember a time in my life when the Pittsburgh Steelers had as dominant a run game as they do right now. Jaylen Warren had another monster performance in Pittsburgh’s 27-6 win over the Cleveland Browns, rushing for a career-high 143 yards and a touchdown on over eight yards per carry. Rico Dowdle added 56 yards and a touchdown in his best game as a Steeler thus far. A Pat Freiermuth one-yard tush push touchdown gave the Steelers an even 200 yards against the Browns, and when you look at how the Steelers have performed over the course of their win streak, it’s safe to say they comfortably have the NFL’s top rushing attack. Despite a slow start in the first two games of the season, the Steelers currently rank third in EPA per rush behind only the Buffalo Bills and Kansas City Chiefs, and they are ninth in rush success rate over the course of the season. However, if you look at those numbers since Week 3 – or after Pittsburgh’s pair of poor performances offensively when the season began – they lead the NFL in EPA per rush and yards per carry. And not only are they efficient in the run game, but they are the NFL’s most explosive run game. Since Week 3, the Steelers led the NFL in yards after contact per rush attempt. Jaylen Warren leads all running backs in yards after contact per attempt at 4.24 (min. 50 touches) and he has the fifth-most 10+ yard runs since Week 3 when the Steelers made their offensive line changes on the right side. Maybe the most telling stat, though, is this one from Derrick Bell of Steelers Now. Since Week 3, the Steelers are lapping the NFL in rushing EPA per play. The difference between the Steelers and the second-place Falcons is the same distance as the margin from Atlanta to the 19th-best team. Since the offensive line changes, the Steelers are basically lapping the field in rushing EPA/play. The difference between Pittsburgh and Atlanta is equivalent to the distance between the 2nd and 19th best run games in the league. https://t.co/onNgVGSuPx pic.twitter.com/DlLV6B4uaU — Derrick (@Steelers_DB) November 2, 2026 The Steelers have mastered the art of being explosive in the run game, which certainly does a lot to take the pressure off the shoulders of a soon-to-be 43 year-old quarterback whose receivers are still lacking in terms of explosive play ability. Should the Steelers be able to lean on this run game into January, they can beat anybody. It’s the morning after game day, and the Steelers are a half game out of the top seed in the AFC. Welcome back, T.J. Watt The last two seasons have been down ones for T.J. Watt. After leading the NFL in sacks for a record third time in 2023, Watt combined for just 18.5 sacks over the last two seasons, including just seven in 2025. If there is one person who has greatly benefitted from the Patrick Graham defense, though, it’s been No. 90. Watt put up two sacks on Deshaun Watson on Sunday, taking his season total to 7.5, which tops his season total from a year ago just eight weeks into the season and puts him at the top of the NFL in sacks – a place he hasn’t been in quite a long time at this point in the season. Among all players to play 100 pass rush snaps, he is fourth in pressure percentage, and his pressure to sack ratio is also fourth in the league. And it’s not just sacks that Watt is getting. He’s second in the NFL among edge rushers in tackles for loss (9), and his six stuffed runs are third among edge rushers. Watt has successfully turned back the clock. And at age 32, he’s playing like he’s in his prime. Patrick Queen and Payton Wilson continue their excellent run After a very up-and-down first month of the season for the Steeler’s linebacking corps, Patrick Queen and Payton Wilson have been on a tear during Pittsburgh’s winning streak. Over the course of the Steelers’ four-game win streak, Wilson and Queen are sixth and ninth in the league in tackles, respectively. Wilson’s three tackles for loss in that span are tied for second in the NFL, while Queen is right behind him with two. The duo are also both in the top five in stuffed runs over the last moth, with Queen totaling five and Wilson putting up four. Finally, their impact plays are third in the league with 12 apiece, and no other duo in the NFL matches their 24 combined impact plays since Week 5. Considering how much flack these two have gotten over the last year, seeing them rise to the occasion and become arguably the top linebacking duo in the NFL right now is such a breath of fresh air for a defense that, as a whole, has been dominant. Quick hitters Since Week 5, the Steelers are third in defensive success rate, trailing only the Seattle Seahawks and Denver Broncos. A true elite unit. Rico Dowdle had his best game as a Steelers. Pittsburgh’s backfield duo has become very dangerous. DK Metcalf: one catch, four yards. Pittsburgh should take a big swing ahead of the trade deadline for a difference-maker at receiver. Alex Highsmith was tremendous. Only recored 0.5 sacks, but had five pressures. Really good day from No. 56. Eight sacks is insane. The Steelers now lead the NFL with 26. title: 5 takeaways from the Steelers’ 27-6 win over the Cleveland Browns
summary: In a Week 8 battle for the AFC North lead, the Steelers let their play do the talking in a dominant win over the rival Cleveland Browns in Pittsburgh on Sunday. As always, there are plenty of takeaways to be had: 1. Some things never change It’s been a year of change in the AFC […]
full_text: Photo by Justin K. Aller/Getty Images | Getty Images In a Week 8 battle for the AFC North lead, the Steelers let their play do the talking in a dominant win over the rival Cleveland Browns in Pittsburgh on Sunday. As always, there are plenty of takeaways to be had: 1. Some things never change It’s been a year of change in the AFC North as three teams have new head coaches. Pittsburgh is no longer under the long-time leadership of Mike Tomlin, while the Browns, with Todd Monken replacing Kevin Stefanski, shocked the world by leading the division through seven weeks. But the Browns haven’t won a regular season game in Pittsburgh since 2003, and all that offseason turnover didn’t do anything to change that. History continued. Emphatically. The Steelers won 27-6 in their most lopsided victory yet this season. The Browns were repeatedly punched in the mouth in a game that never felt particularly close. Much in the way that it’s easy to dismiss what happens in a Steelers’ Thursday Night Football loss in Cleveland — in what feels more like an annually-scheduled night of disappointment rather than a football game with free will — I believe it’s a bit of an overreaction to suddenly declare the Steelers as Super Bowl contenders in a win as clearly telegraphed as this one was. But at the same time, the story of the game is less about the win and more about how the Steelers won. The pass rush was masterful. The run game was relentless. Pittsburgh’s roster seemed to relish every moment of punishing its rival. The team culture seems to be in a great place, and the Steelers have their most established identity of the season on both sides of the ball after the big win. When the Steelers hired Mike McCarthy, it was clearly in part a decision to try to keep a similar status quo from the Mike Tomlin era. Yes, plenty has changed in terms of scheme and other details, but the macro-level results: an above-average team, rebounding from brutal losses such as the Patriots in Week 2, and of course, routinely defeating the Browns at home, remains the same. 2. The Steelers dominate the trenches Eight sacks. Fourteen quarterback hits. Nonstop pressure. The Steelers’ pass rush was absurdly good Sunday afternoon, defeating the Browns’ offensive front with speed and power and making Cleveland quarterback Deshaun Watson distribute the ball from a war zone. What was even more impressive for Pittsburgh was how the production was spread across the board, with seven different defenders recording 0.5 sacks or more. The box score doesn’t do it justice, either. Outside linebacker Alex Highsmith was arguably the team’s MVP against Cleveland, logging just a 0.5 sack but generating six pressures against Browns left tackle Spencer Fano, including two quick pressures. He also drew three holding calls, per NFL Pro. I’ve been as critical as any in regards to the Steelers’ spending choices on defense in recent seasons, and even skeptical at times of the plan to extend (and properly use) all three of T.J. Watt, Alex Highsmith, and Nick Herbig. But Sunday’s game was an occurrence when all that star power clicked on at once. It’s one of the most dominant, fun-to-watch performances from a pass rush I’ve seen in recent memory, and although such gaudy numbers are an unrealistic expectation moving forward ( this wasn’t even the first time the Browns have given up eight sacks this season ), it’s still a promising sign for a group that has already been excellent for much of the year. Simply put, if the Steelers want to be any sort of contender come late-season, the pass rush, as the best position group on the team, is going to have to be the engine of that effort. Sunday was overwhelmingly a strong step in that direction. Equally as encouraging was the Steelers’ offensive line on Sunday, particularly in the run game. Pittsburgh averaged a strong 6.1 yards per rush, gaining 14 of the team’s 20 total first downs on the ground against Cleveland. One of the highlights of the game was Pittsburgh taking advantage of a pass-expecting Browns front on third and 13 to move the sticks on an interior run. Trap again! On 3rd-and-13 no less. Steelers dipping into the Wing-T playbook… pic.twitter.com/xP7GDZjZ0R — Kevin Smith (@KTSmithFootball) November 1, 2026 I feel like I’ve talked ad nauseam about how much Jaylen Warren has meant to this Steelers offense in the takeaways column this year, so there’s no reason to rehash those same points. But it’s also no secret that Warren’s star turn largely correlated with Brock Hoffman and Max Iheanachor joining the starting O-line on the right side earlier this season, and Pittsburgh continues to reap the benefits. In recent weeks, notably against the Saints and now the Browns, Pittsburgh has also turned to a higher dose of gap concepts in the run game along with more use of an extra offensive lineman jumbo package to further up its production on the ground. With that in mind, it’s probably not surprising to hear those two games have also resulted in Pittsburgh’s best two rushing performances of the year thus far (148 and 200 yards, respectively). Entering Week 8, the Steelers’ offense ranked 11th in yards before contact per carry and seventh in yards after contact per carry. That’s the sign of a true team effort between blockers and backs in the run game, and I’d only expect both statistics to improve after Next Gen Stats updates for Week 8. But moving back to the Browns game, it might be even more impressive that the Steelers ran for 200 given that the passing game (more on that later) only mustered 161 yards. Despite failing to achieving balance on offense, Pittsburgh still pulverized Cleveland on the ground and scored nearly 30 points. The Browns had every reason to sell out against the run and still couldn’t stop it. That’s the sign of a truly successful run game. 3. Still some passing game concerns Here’s the point in the column where I do my usual “Well, the Steelers weren’t entirely as good/bad as they might’ve looked” bit and try not to come across as annoying. Yes, it was a great win! Yes, the pass rush and run game looked elite! But those two incredibly bright spots covered up a lot of issues. I’m still mildly confused with the “complete” game narrative ( Aaron Rodgers also pushed against this ) floating around given just how incomplete parts of the team still looked on Sunday. Namely, the passing game. As mentioned above, the Steelers managed just 161 yards on the air. They didn’t have to throw it much on Sunday, to be fair, but Aaron Rodgers still just completed barely over half of his passes (13/25), averaging an uninspired 6.2 yards per pass. While the passing game to the tight ends worked (Darnell Washington logged three grabs for 94 yards), the team’s wide receiver core only combined for 43, with WR1 D.K. Metcalf contributing a paltry four. Once again, the Steelers’ passing game was largely restrained to short throws and quick-game screens and dump-offs. And no, this is far from a critique of just Aaron Rodgers. When the deep ball finally was an option, this happened: Rodgers looks deep for DK Metcalf, who bobbles it and it's intercepted by Denzel Ward. Works out to be a long punt, but man, what a missed opportunity. pic.twitter.com/FP1CZFWjxf https://t.co/jNrlt8aLT7 — Alan Saunders (@ASaunders_PGH) November 1, 2026 The Steelers’ unreal running game success made their passing game struggles somewhat negligible, but that won’t always be the case. If the Steelers want to rise to Serious™ contender status, the passing offense is still several tiers away from looking the part. But to be fair, while neither have been game-breakers, even getting one of Michael Pittman Jr. and Roman Wilson back soon after the bye would be a boost for a team awfully short-handed on starting-caliber wide receivers. 4. A tale of two red zones The Steelers’ strong defensive performance last week was still met with the cautionary title of “bend don’t break” — and against the Browns,…

title: Winners and Losers from a troubling Seahawks display against the Bears
summary: Well that was a nice reality check. No, the Seattle Seahawks don’t have a “could’ve won if…” situation. They got their asses kicked by the Chicago Bears in a 34-17 game that was somehow both not as close and yet closer than the final score indicated. Seattle doesn’t get to play the “barely lost” game […]
full_text: Well that was a nice reality check. No, the Seattle Seahawks don’t have a “could’ve won if…” situation. They got their asses kicked by the Chicago Bears in a 34-17 game that was somehow both not as close and yet closer than the final score indicated. Seattle doesn’t get to play the “barely lost” game this time around. This was a thoroughly deserved win for the Bears and a humbling defeat for the Super Bowl champs. It’s late at night and instead of prepping for Enemy Reaction, I’m here writing another disappointing Winners and Losers column on the cusp of midnight. Seattle Seahawks Winners Jaxon Smith-Njigba is the Seahawks offense I repeat, Jaxon Smith-Njigba is the Seahawks offense. He has almost 1,000 yards receiving through eight games, and he was honestly cheated out of that because of a couple of “run plays” that were narrowly backward. There isn’t a better receiver in the NFL and Seattle is blessed to have him in the now and long-term. Irv Charles balled out on special teams Minus the one asinine penalty, which at that point likely didn’t swing the game, I see the vision for Irv as a special teams superstar. He downed a Michael Dickson punt inside the 10 (doing what Rodney Thomas botched), was in on tackles on kick return duties, balling out as a gunner, and he had a deflected punt which unluckily went for 45 yards. He’s worth a conditional 7th in 2028. Zach Charbonnet being back is a personal win for him Charbonnet had just 23 yards on six carries and it wasn’t like the offensive line was opening up too many holes. I think for him, it’s an accomplishment to be back on the field inside of 10 months after an ACL tear. That’s a lot of rehab and effort to go through to be available when a January injury of that severity can cost you all of next year. I want to highlight that for Charbs. DeMarcus Lawrence kept Seattle in the game For the first time all season (unless you count Deebo Samuel dropping the ball because he blew out his hamstring), a Seahawks defender forced a fumble on a non-quarterback. Tank got the FF and the FR. I wish this swan song was going better. Seattle Seahawks Losers Sam Darnold was horrendous Outside of one deep shot to Jaxon Smith-Njigba for a touchdown, what did Darnold do well? Avoid sacks? No. Throw on time? Not really. Throw accurately on a consistent basis? Nope. The offensive line was bad and certainly Brian Fleury’s shelf life as an OC is now under question, but Darnold’s statistical downturn can be traced back to the four-interception meltdown against the Los Angeles Rams. With few exceptions (most notably and thankfully the NFC Championship Game), Darnold has leaned toward being an average quarterback at best for about an 18-game stretch. And if you think I’m being unfair lumping the Kubiak season with the Fleury games, he did not end the regular season well in 2025 . The run game just got hot at the right time to replace some of the explosives lost in the passing game. Sam Darnold from last year's Rams loss until now: 334/551 for 3,936 yards, 23 TDs, 17 INTs, and a sub-6.0 ANY/A. His ANY/A plummeted toward the back-end of last season. Darnold's downturn didn't start with Fleury. There's a clear inflection point. No run game crutch this time. — Mookie Alexander (@mookiealexander) November 3, 2026 He touched the wrong quadrant in the back-end of 2025 but salvaged things with a great playoff run. He’s back to being in the wrong quadrant in 2026. That was a showing worse than either of the Denver Broncos or San Francisco 49ers losses. We can likely shelve “start Drew Lock” while Lock is nursing his own injury, but at the very least he is not in any contract extension territory. He can play out his contract in 2027 or leave sooner than that if things don’t turn positively. Brian Fleury is in trouble That one-week reprieve where it looked like he found the magical potion sure wore off quickly. Why were the Seahawks taking an age and huddling up down by 10 in the 4th quarter? Why did they call so many run plays to the right side of the line? No urgency, no easy offense, no cohesiveness, no sensible gameplan. Once again they stalled out in the red zone because they burned first down on a doomed running play and took no end zone shot. I’m sure he interviewed well and knows ball extremely well, but there are a lot of great mathematicians who make terrible teachers. Fleury is not a great OC right now and the repeated dysfunction in situational football and in the general flow of the game is reaching untenable status. Mike Macdonald moved on from Ryan Grubb after one season and he probably would’ve moved on sooner if he was not a rookie head coach. Fleury may not be here past the bye week with how ruinous the offense is. I can’t blame Fleury when guys fumble or when Sam Darnold goes into self-destruct mode unforced, but I can blame him to some degree when the offense as a whole doesn’t look well coached. The offensive line was a mess It’s not wholly unexpected when you have a backup left tackle and a left guard who’s now a right guard because the new left guard is Quenton Nelson. There was going to be a problem getting everyone organized. This is not a well-functioning unit even when healthy. Abe Lucas continues to struggle and it’s more of a concern about his physical health than anything else. Zabel got owned by Jeffery Simmons off the jump, and the Bears regularly got pressure with four. Forget about the run game woes. This was supposed to be a strength and may yet be a strength when Charles Cross is back and we figure out Jalen Sundell’s injury, but right now they’re accomplices in the first-degree felony that is this offense. Nick Emmanwori got picked on all night A week after one of the best games of his career, it was a tough night for Emmanwori in terms of run defense and tackling. Between missed tackles, getting beaten on the touchdown to Luther Burden, and some difficult reps against Colston Loveland, this was easily one of his more disappointing outings. The screen to Kalif Raymond was the dagger and he was blocked out of the play. Ben Johnson made it a point to pick on him and he lacked any positive impact. And the roughness penalty (again!) he picked up when the game was still reasonably in doubt was selfish and he needs as much criticism for that as we regularly gave Riq Woolen. He’s done that twice in less than a month and it’s led to points both times. Rylie Mills’ training camp has not translated into positive regular season play It wasn’t like the Seahawks run defense struggled or anything, but Mills entering the game is a signal to the opposition to run at him. He’s driven back by double teams too easily, struggles with his anchor, and isn’t offering enough as a pass rusher. This leaves Seattle essentially three-deep on the interior with Leonard Williams, Byron Murphy II, and Jarran Reed. I can’t imagine justifying more snaps for Mills if Williams has to miss time. Special teams outside of Irv Charles was not good In fact, they were mostly bad. Rodney Thomas inexplicably took a punt downed at the 2 and slid himself and the ball into the end zone. The trajectory of that ball was going away from the end zone and the Bears gained 18 yards of field position before scoring a touchdown. Jason Myers shanked a PAT and later had a short field goal blocked. Mike Morris committed a really silly late hit on a kick return that gifted the Bears terrific field position. Even Irv Charles, who had a great night, sullied it with his own silly roughness penalty. Mike Macdonald has to own this complete unpreparedness Coach Macdonald has won a Super Bowl and Seattle has won far more than they’ve lost in two-and-a-half seasons with him at the helm. This is as bad a three-phase effort as this team has put out. Maybe not since the Buffalo Bills blowout two years ago, or the Green Bay Packers blowout in primetime. The defense gave up an opening drive touchdown, didn’t have a lot of answers for the intermediate play-action game,…

title: Seahawks vs. Bears post-game reaction: What we learned from a damaging Monday night defeat
summary: The Seattle Seahawks are in trouble. By no means is the season over at 4-4, but the NFC is deep enough just through the North alone that Seattle has to worry about making the playoffs, forget about making it back to the top of the NFC West. Their 34-17 loss to the Chicago Bears was […]
full_text: The Seattle Seahawks are in trouble. By no means is the season over at 4-4, but the NFC is deep enough just through the North alone that Seattle has to worry about making the playoffs, forget about making it back to the top of the NFC West. Their 34-17 loss to the Chicago Bears was their heaviest under Mike Macdonald since 2024, and the defense finally broke down after the offense spent the whole night spamming three-and-outs. Myself and Bryce Coutts are here for post-game immediate reaction podcast, which will start at around 8:40 pm PT. You can catch it live or just watch it afterward when you’re in a mood to listen to a lot of ranting. Quick takeaways from Bears 34, Seahawks 17 Brian Fleury’s magic lasted a week, he’s back on the hot seat . Where was the sense of urgency in this offense? Why are they constantly burning early downs with runs to the weaker side of the offensive line? Why does the offense look so consistently labored? How is the offense this broken when the ball isn’t being thrown to JSN? Fleury looks like he’s not in a good position to lead this offense. Sam Darnold was terrible and worse than the stats suggested. The one pick was kind to Darnold. The sack number could’ve been much higher if not for repeated undisciplined penalties by the Bears secondary. He had happy feet, inaccurate throws, basically everything we weren’t seeing last week against the Kansas City Chiefs. This is not a quarterback playing with confidence or trusting what he sees, and the combo of his struggles and Fleury’s struggles could be tied together. It turns out the running game just isn’t magically fixed overnight . Quenton Nelson is here, which is cool. Zach Charbonnet and Jadarian Price are back. That’s super cool. The run game stinks. That’s not cool. Only 61 yards on 17 carries from running backs. Even “The Dark Side” is fallible . Caleb Williams made some magnificent plays, but the Seahawks defense was not at their sharpest. They gave up a few preventable pass game explosives, and that screen to Kalif Raymond at 20-17 was a killer to concede. With Leonard Williams out with a stinger, the hope is it’s not a major issue because the d-line gets much thinner when he’s not in the lineup, and the defense is worse off. Nick Emmanwori was last week’s darling and one of this week’s worst performers. The Seahawks special teams was horrendous . Penalties, missed kicks, blocked field goals, and poor kick returns galore. This was an unacceptable performance by a unit that was magnificent last year and has been way too inconsistent this year. Seattle’s postseason hopes are in jeopardy . While Seattle doesn’t have another daunting stretch on the schedule, this team isn’t playing well enough to trust that they’re capable of comfortably winning against anyone right now. A lot of things need fixing and I’m not sure how much can be fixed this year. Video

title: NFC Playoff Picture: Seahawks can’t move into Wild Card spot after loss to Bears
summary: A win by the Seattle Seahawks on Monday night would have moved them into the final playoff spot in the NFC. Instead, they were outclassed on their home turf by the Chicago Bears. Seattle still sits in eighth place in the conference and just one game out of a playoff spot, but that tiebreaker could […]
full_text: SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - NOVEMBER 02: Montez Sweat #98 of the Chicago Bears sacks Sam Darnold #14 of the Seattle Seahawks during the third quarter of the game at Lumen Field on November 02, 2026 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Olivia Vanni/Getty Images) | Getty Images A win by the Seattle Seahawks on Monday night would have moved them into the final playoff spot in the NFC. Instead, they were outclassed on their home turf by the Chicago Bears. Seattle still sits in eighth place in the conference and just one game out of a playoff spot, but that tiebreaker could come back to haunt them. All four NFC North teams are in playoff spots right now and at least two games over .500 while the Seahawks are even at 4-4, a game back. In the NFC West, the San Francisco 49ers were on a bye and moved into the one seed in the NFC anyway after the Minnesota Vikings lost. The Los Angeles Rams won to tie Seattle at 4-4, but the Seahawks have the tiebreaker on division record. The Arizona Cardinals won a wild game over the Dallas Cowboys and are just ag ame back of Seattle and L.A. NFC playoff standings after Week 8 1. San Francisco 49ers (6-1, strength of victory .456) 2. Minnesota Vikings (6-1, strength of victory .400) 3. New York Giants (4-2-1) 4. Carolina Panthers (3-4) 5. Chicago Bears (6-2) 6. Detroit Lions (5-2) 7. Green Bay Packers (5-3) 8. Seattle Seahawks (4-4, 1-1 NFCW) 9. Los Angeles Rams (4-4, 0-2 NFCW) 10. Tampa Bay Buccaneers (3-5, win over ATL, 1-0 vs DAL+ARZ, 3-2 NFC) 11. Atlanta Falcons (3-5, loss to TB, 3-3 NFC record) 12. Arizona Cardinals (3-5, 1-0 vs DAL+ARZ, 2-4 NFC) 13. Dallas Cowboys (3-5, 0-2 vs TB+ARZ, loss to ARZ) 14. Washington Commanders (2-4-1) 15. New Orleans Saints (2-5, 1-3 NFC) 16. Philadelphia Eagles (2-6) Explaining the 3-5 tiebreaker in the NFC First, you get to one team per division so the Falcons and Buccaneers are against each other. Tampa has a win over Atlanta, so they have the tiebreaker. Tampa vs Arizona vs Dallas is a head-to-head tiebreaker where Atlanta and Arizona move on since they both have wins over Dallas. The Bucs are 3-2 in the NFC vs the Cardinals at 2-4, so Tampa is the 10 seed. Then the Falcons go into a three-way tiebreaker with the Cardinals and Cowboys. It goes straight to NFC record where the Falcons are 3-3 and the Cardinals and Cowboys are 2-4. Atlanta is the 11 seed. The Arizona Cardinals beat the Cowboys so they win the head-to-head tiebreaker in the two-way decision. Arizona is 12th and the Cowboys are 13th.

title: Seahawks-Bears score: Seahawks blown out in Monday night horror show
summary: All the good feelings the Seattle Seahawks (4-4) brought back after dominating the Kansas City Chiefs were immediately canceled out and then some after a disappointing 34-17 home loss against the Chicago Bears (6-2). Caleb Williams was as brilliant as Sam Darnold was worryingly atrocious. This offense is Jaxon Smith-Njigba or nothing. The run game […]
full_text: All the good feelings the Seattle Seahawks (4-4) brought back after dominating the Kansas City Chiefs were immediately canceled out and then some after a disappointing 34-17 home loss against the Chicago Bears (6-2). Caleb Williams was as brilliant as Sam Darnold was worryingly atrocious. This offense is Jaxon Smith-Njigba or nothing. The run game struggled even with the return of Zach Charbonnet and Jadarian Price. Seattle’s vaunted defense had some wins and some devastating losses against the high-flying Bears offense, which looks like a Super Bowl caliber unit. Chicago had 363 yards of total offense, the most by any Seahawks opponent this season, while Seattle had a meager 252. As usual, JSN had 118 of those 252 yards. Seattle won the Super Bowl last season and it should be cherished forever. This year’s team is not a lock for the playoffs. It is not playing complementary football and the sloppiness is too hard to gloss over. It’s a disappointing first half of the season and the longer term outlook on this team is significantly altered by the continued struggles of Sam Darnold. How can you have a contender when the quarterback play is this shaky? Whether Brian Fleury is good or not, Darnold is a problem. A big problem. The Seahawks offense has threatened a blowout loss all season with their erratic play. It finally happened. The defense cannot bail you out forever. Seahawks vs. Bears 1st half recap The Seahawks started on offense, giving Zach Charbonnet the ball in his first touch since January 2026. Sam Darnold was rocked for a hurried incomplete pass on 2nd and 5, then Tory Horton was leveled by Cam Lewis on 3rd and 5 in a very legal and physical collision. Seattle had Chicago pinned at the 2-yard line, if not for Rodney Thomas ridiculously sliding for no reasons and driving the ball into the end zone. Poor decision and costly for field position reasons. Chicago’s opening drive against the league’s top-rated defense was a thing of beauty. Caleb Williams led a 17-play, 80-yard drive that included three conversions on 3rd down, as well as a D’Andre Swift 4th and 1 conversion to keep the series going. Luther Burden capped off an 8:32 drive with a touchdown grab on a rollout throw by Williams. That was impressive. 7-0 Bears. @CALEBcsw with a strike to @lutherburden3 for 6 😮‍💨 📺: ESPN pic.twitter.com/69vDVHE8mX — Chicago Bears (@ChicagoBears) November 3, 2026 Jeffery Simmons made an immediate impact in his Bears debut, sacking Sam Darnold on the first play of Seattle’s second series. However, Grady Jarrett’s silly face mask grab of Jalen Sundell resulted in a free 15 and a new set of downs. Seattle still didn’t get a first down on its own, with Darnold sliding and getting jarred by former Seahawks linebacker Devin Bush. Somehow, this wasn’t deemed a penalty, and Seattle punted. Dude's trying to literally tackle somebody using his back. If you showed that to a rugby defense/ defence coach they'd have a heart attack. pic.twitter.com/YyyJrAwBKM — Sam Monson (@SamMonsonNFL) November 3, 2026 Luckily, Irv Charles showed everyone how its done and downed a Dickson punt inside the 5. The Bears went three-and-out after Caleb Williams was pressured into an overthrow of Kalif Raymond. Tory Taylor’s short punt had a short return by Tory Horton, but Seattle was near midfield nevertheless. When in doubt, go to Jaxon Smith-Njigba. A couple of quick screens to JSN gained 35 yards and Seattle was in the red zone in next to no time. Jadarian Price’s first carry back from injury gained eight yards, a promising sign for his health and explosiveness. Unfortunately, the red zone series was ugly and featured nothing but Charbonnet touches that didn’t get Seattle particularly close to the end zone. Jason Myers put Seattle on the board with a 27-yard field goal. 7-3 Bears . The Bears went three-and-out again, then the Seahawks looked like they had a huge special teams play from Irv Charles. He deflected a Tory Taylor punt and somehow it took a friendly, untouched bounce for 45 yards. Seattle went three-and-out and punted it back to the Bears. never seen a punt get blocked and then go this far pic.twitter.com/ecrQBrE53J — NFL (@NFL) November 3, 2026 Chicago added to its lead thanks to a big play-action shot to Luther Burden for 23 yards. It took only three plays for Seattle to get into field goal range, where the drive stalled. Cairo Santos was true from 44 yards. 10-3 Bears . Another three-and-out resulted in nervous energy from the Lumen Field crowd. The Bears had a chance to double up with points before the half and then to start the second half. Williams again was on target with explosive plays, as Rome Odunze broke free for 24 yards after a long time for Caleb Williams in the pocket. Interestingly enough, Ben Johnson dialed up a D’Andre Swift run on 3rd and 6 on the other side of the two-minute warning. Swift gained four yards and set up 4th and 2. Johnson called for the hard count, which was unsuccessful, and then kicked another field goal. 13-3 Bears. A Jaylon Johnson PI penalty gifted Seattle some free yards in their one-minute drill. JSN broke Jaylon Johnson’s ankles two plays later to get into Chicago territory. On 3rd and 10, Darnold dialed up a deep shot to JSN for a wide open 43-yard touchdown. Tyrique Stevenson bit on the slant and there was no safety help, so you know the rest! The only bad thing was a horrific missed PAT by Jason Myers. 13-9 Bears at halftime. 43 YARDS TO THE HOUSE 🏠 @jaxon_smith1 📺: @ESPNNFL pic.twitter.com/qIKpU6RWlO — Seattle Seahawks (@Seahawks) November 3, 2026 Seahawks vs. Bears 2nd half recap The Bears and Seahawks traded punts out of halftime, but Chicago punished Seattle for yet another limp three-and-out. A 10-play, 69-yard drive took over six minutes off the clock. D’Andre Swift punched it in from a couple yards out to make it 20-9 Bears . Swift for 6️⃣ 📺: ESPN pic.twitter.com/9USEZuUO2J — Chicago Bears (@ChicagoBears) November 3, 2026 Seattle took a preposterous 6:29 to move slowly, barely effectively, and not score any points. A very iffy pass interference penalty on Jaxon Smith-Njigba, the first of his entire career, took away a completed ball to the Chicago 1. That put the Seahawks behind the sticks, and inevitably they settled for a field goal. Jason Myers’ 33-yard kick was blocked. Brutal. BLOCKED BY BOOKER 🚫 📺: ESPN pic.twitter.com/xrOxDjl4vP — Chicago Bears (@ChicagoBears) November 3, 2026 But wait! A twist on the next drive! Caleb Williams was almost picked off by Julian Love on an overthrow, then sacked by Mike Morris for the first of Mike’s career, and a give-up screen on 3rd and 20 was fumbled by Colston Loveland. DeMarcus Lawrence forced the fumble and recovered the ball all at once! DEMARCUS LAWRENCE FORCES A FUMBLE THIS GAME IS NOT OVER. CHIvsSEA on ESPN Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/LjmRJmoVjQ — NFL (@NFL) November 3, 2026 Seattle turned that turnover into points, but not without referee help. Darnold was picked off on a terrible double coverage throw, but Clark Phillips was called for a hold of Jaxon Smith-Njigba and that took away the turnover. Two plays later, Darnold hit an open Cooper Kupp for a touchdown. Tory Horton kept the feet down in the back of the end zone for two valuable points. 20-17 Bears with 11:46 to go . TWO FOR TORY ✌️ @toryhorton11 📺: @ESPNNFL pic.twitter.com/AOZzRZDsge — Seattle Seahawks (@Seahawks) November 3, 2026 TWO FOR TORY ✌️ @toryhorton11 📺: @ESPNNFL pic.twitter.com/AOZzRZDsge — Seattle Seahawks (@Seahawks) November 3, 2026 A really awful penalty committed by Mike Morris resulted in great field position for the Bears on the ensuing kick return. Seattle still had a chance to get the Bears off the field on third down in fringe field goal range. A delay of game actually saved the Bears from a failed 3rd and 4 conversion. On 3rd and 9, a screen to the speedy Kalif Raymond broke through for a 39-yard gain and it officially goes down as a run. D’Andre Swift scored on the next play.…

title: Seahawks vs. Bears, ‘Monday Night Football’ game chat and live discussion
summary: The toughest stretch of the Seattle Seahawks regular season schedule concludes on Monday Night Football against the Chicago Bears. They fell to the San Francisco 49ers and Denver Broncos, bounced back big time versus the Kansas City Chiefs, and now the reigning Super Bowl champions have a big showdown in prime-time against the high-flying Bears […]
full_text: The toughest stretch of the Seattle Seahawks regular season schedule concludes on Monday Night Football against the Chicago Bears. They fell to the San Francisco 49ers and Denver Broncos, bounced back big time versus the Kansas City Chiefs, and now the reigning Super Bowl champions have a big showdown in prime-time against the high-flying Bears offense. Seattle’s defense showed up in a big way to stymie the Kansas City offense. It’ll be a tougher task on Monday against a better set of receivers. and a terrific offensive mind in Ben Johnson. Caleb Williams’ last time playing a Mike Macdonald defense was the 6-3 “classic” at the end of the 2024 season. Ben Johnson wasn’t the coach at the time, the Bears have revamped their offensive line, and the Seahawks roster has undergone significant overhaul on offense and defense. For the Seahawks offense, we’ll get the return of Zach Charbonnet and Jadarian Price, which should help boost the run game. It’s also the debut of Quenton Nelson on the offensive line, although he won’t have Charles Cross alongside him due to injury. The Seahawks have been turnover prone in their losses (read: Sam Darnold has been turnover prone in Seattle’s losses), and when they max the turnovers out at one then they win. Let’s see if there’s a trend-breaker in this stat, or if the Seahawks turnover count will once again tell us the outcome of the game. Join us in our MNF game chat! full_text: Coming off a momentum altering victory over the Kansas City Chiefs in which the Seattle Seahawks’ ‘Dark Side’ defense allowed just three points, they’ll be missing a burst as star linebacker Uchenna Nwosu will be sidelined against the Chicago Bears tonight. title: Cardinals bench Jacoby Brissett, will start Gardner Minshew vs. Seahawks
summary: After backup quarterback Drew Lock led the Seattle Seahawks to a one-sided 31-7 win over the Arizona Cardinals in Week 2, it’s the red birds who will have a different signal caller in their final regular season matchup of the season. Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur announced Gardner Minshew II will take over as the […]
full_text: After backup quarterback Drew Lock led the Seattle Seahawks to a one-sided 31-7 win over the Arizona Cardinals in Week 2, it’s the red birds who will have a different signal caller in their final regular season matchup of the season. Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur announced Gardner Minshew II will take over as the team’s starting quarterback moving forward, with the decision coming just a day after he led Arizona to a heroic 33-30 overtime comeback victory over the Dallas Cowboys. Rookie Carson Beck will serve as the backup, with Jacoby Brissett reverting to the Emergency QB3. The #AZCardinals are naming QB Gardner Minshew as their starting QB, one day after his heroics led to a dramatic win over the #Cowboys . Jacoby Brissett heads to the bench. pic.twitter.com/aNeVUZlzIu — Ian Rapoport (@RapSheet) November 2, 2026 Minshew’s last start came in Week 16 of the 2025 season as a member of the Kansas City Chiefs, although he suffered a knee injury during it. Prior to a brief stint with Kansas City, the journeyman quarterback spent time with the Jacksonville Jaguars, Philadelphia Eagles, Indianapolis Colts and Las Vegas Raiders—where he was benched prior to Week 6 of the 2024 season after a brutal start to the year. However, Minshew’s coming off a career-best game against Dallas, in which he stepped in during the final two minutes of the third quarter with the Cardinals trailing 17-3 and threw for 188 yards as well as three touchdowns to help Arizona improve to 3-5. It was a glimmer of hope the team hadn’t seen under Brissett. Despite going 1-11 as the starter in 2025, Brissett threw for 3,366 yards to go alongside 23 touchdowns and just eight interceptions, which—after a brief offseason holdout, lead to him signing a one-year, $15.5 million extension (could reach up to $21 million) with the Cardinals. However, Arizona’s struggles persisted in 2026 and so did Brissett’s, which ultimately led to the quarterback change. Through eight starts, he recorded 1,719 yards and a 10/7 TD-INT ratio. The Cardinals went 2-5 in that span. Although they’re turning the ball over to Minshew, he won’t have an easy go in his first start of the year set to come on the road in Week 9 against the Seahawks—who Arizona hasn’t beat since 2021. As if playing at Lumen Field wasn’t difficult enough, he’ll face head coach Mike Macdonald’s defense, who’s allowing the fewest yards and third-fewest points per game.

title: Seahawks activate Jadarian Price from injured reserve ahead of ‘Monday Night Football’ vs. Bears
summary: Jadarian Price is back.  After the Seattle Seahawks opened the 21-day practice window for their first-round pick on Thursday, they activated him to the 53-man roster on Monday, ahead of the team’s prime-time clash with the Chicago Bears. Undrafted rookie Robert Henry Jr was waived to make room for Price. Price has been out with […]
full_text: SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - SEPTEMBER 09: Jadarian Price #8 of the Seattle Seahawks runs the ball against the New England Patriots during the first quarter in the game at Lumen Field on September 09, 2026 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Steph Chambers/Getty Images) | Getty Images Jadarian Price is back. After the Seattle Seahawks opened the 21-day practice window for their first-round pick on Thursday, they activated him to the 53-man roster on Monday, ahead of the team’s prime-time clash with the Chicago Bears. Undrafted rookie Robert Henry Jr was waived to make room for Price. Price has been out with a chest injury since Week 4 , after he initially suffered the injury during the team’s Week 2 win over the Arizona Cardinals. Prior to being placed on injured reserve, the rookie had rushed for 119 yards on 28 carries across three games, adding four catches for 21 yards through the air. He had struggled with ball security and found himself in a greatly reduced role during Seattle’s Week 3 loss to the Washington Commanders after fumbling for a second straight game. The former Notre Dame tailback returns to a different looking running back room — and running game. Zach Charbonnet, who was on the PUP list when Price last suited up, is back on the 53-man roster and primed to make a return of his own tonight after completing his recovery from a torn ACL. Up front, the Seahawks’ offensive line has received a boost in the form of the pre-trade deadline acquisition of six-time All-Pro Quenton Nelson. Now Price, along with Charbonnet, can try to provide a boost to a running game that has struggled in its time led by Emanuel Wilson and George Holani, as Seattle looks to rediscover balance on offense in its first season under new offensive coordinator Brian Fleury.

title: The potentially good O-linemen the Seahawks lost in pursuit of the great
summary: There’s a saying: “Sometimes you have to say no to the good to get the great.” Seattle has aggressively taken on that mindset to wash the offensive line with talent over the last few years. It was a glorious thing to watch Seattle subvert the storyline, flipping it on its head for the world to […]
full_text: There’s a saying: “Sometimes you have to say no to the good to get the great.” Seattle has aggressively taken on that mindset to wash the offensive line with talent over the last few years. It was a glorious thing to watch Seattle subvert the storyline, flipping it on its head for the world to see on SNF. All season it’s been: “The Seahawks are missing Kenneth Walker III, that’s why they haven’t looked the same!” A dash of: “they messed up by letting Ken walk.” Seattle shut down a prolific back, and themselves rushed for over 150 as a team in a bounce back performance at Lumen, slamming the door on all the narratives. Anthony Bradford came back from injury, and played well, contributing to that rushing performance. Even so, the 2026 Seattle Seahawks are not getting complacent, choosing, rather, to run it forward. Quenton Nelson is an undeniable game changer and talent. His reputation alone may make defensive squads feel the pressure to line up to respect the run a little more. Seattle got it done to their standard of a ground game against KC… but they didn’t want to take any more chances of the offense devolving again, especially with a rematch against SF, and a double feature on tap against a still dangerous Rams team. Angling to get better at all positions led to the loss of Bryce Cabeldue to the Raiders. #Raiders HC Klint Kubiak is "very excited" to add G Bryce Cabeldue: "Talented young player. He fits our scheme, and it's up to him to keep improving." (via @Raiders ) pic.twitter.com/uzhxEHhWII — SleeperRaiders (@SleeperRaiders) September 11, 2026 Christian Haynes is the latest victim of Seattle’s transformation of the blocking unit. Former Seahawks offensive lineman Ray Roberts appeared on the Wyman & Bob radio show, and said: “Someone had to go, and you still don’t know what you have in Beau Stephens. You may have a better idea of what you have in Christian Haynes. I don’t think that Christian ever fit the mold that they were looking for. I can remember earlier, like his rookie year, I think Coach Macdonald made the comment that like, he can get it done, but it doesn’t look the way you want it to look getting it done. So, he’s a little bit, kind of awkward in his approach and everything. Also, they kind of give the dudes about three years around here, to kind of figure out whether you have staying power, or you don’t. Having all that been said, it’s still weird to see him in Dolphins colors already. New Dolphins offensive guard Christian Haynes, who was claimed off waivers on Wednesday pic.twitter.com/NfzoynJc6T — Omar Kelly (@OmarKelly) October 29, 2026 Matt Hasselbeck also appeared on Wyman & Bob and fleshed out developmental advantages to having Nelson on the squad. He explained that “the young guys on this roster are going to be better for having been his teammate, for having seen his process, seen how he works, seen how he prepares and studies. The most famous #8 in Hawks history went on to drop a gem of a saying: “more is caught than taught.” Quenton Nelson, for his part, sounds ready to go to battle for Seattle : “It’s great to have all those memories and years spent in Indy, but, like I said: I’m excited for this.” The future gold jacket player went on to say, “I think I can do any kind of scheme.” Cooper Kupp said that Nelson has, “seen a lot of football.” This falls in line with the Seahawks’ farm system , or, what I saw Seaside Joe calling, “ the buddy system .” Both Jeff Saturday, as well as Nelson’s replacement in Indianapolis, 4th-Round rookie, Jalen Farmer have independently mentioned how Q. has promised to stay in the young gun’s ear, even despite now being on a new team. That may not hold for the whole year, but it shows his dedication and intention as a teammate. That’s what great players do. How should we feel about Anthony Bradford? He’s come a long way: from public enemy #1 on offense, at times, to possibly even moving into the realm of good. Seattle’s has sights set on being more than good. Coach Macdonald on the messaging to Bradford: “It’s not an easy situation. I thought Anthony played really good football for us, and he has. He’s earned a significant role in our team, a starting level role. It’s one of those through, not around type of things with A.B. that is not easy. There’s really no way to sugarcoat it.” Seahawks GM, John Schneider was catching heat for a while for calling offensive guards “overpaid and over-drafted”, even after the seeming mistakes of getting rid of Max Unger and letting Damien Lewis walk to become a premier OG in Carolina. Talking about offensive guards, John Schneider said there's a lack of depth and talent at the position, which causes guys at that spot to get overvalued. “Guys get overdrafted at that position and, in my opinion, they get overpaid.” — Dugar, Michael-Shawn (@MikeDugar) March 15, 2024 Since then, he has been aggressive in reshaping this offensive line. Q. Nelson may be the finishing touch on that agenda. The pain of watching Laken Tomlinson let pressure through may have directly led to Grey Zable being drafted. How high can this line climb? Will it be the best in recent Seattle memory? Can it get this run game on track and on a dominant pace? All possible, but time will tell.

title: Bears-Seahawks live discussion: Can Caleb Williams steal the show on the road?
summary: Week 8 comes to a conclusion as two of the best teams in the NFC clash. The Chicago Bears just traded for Jeffery Simmons. That came after the Seattle Seahawks acquired Quenton Nelson. full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - OCTOBER 22: Caleb Williams #18 of the Chicago Bears celebrates a touchdown against the New England Patriots during the third quarter of the game at Soldier Field on October 22, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images) | Getty Images Week 8 comes to a conclusion as two of the best teams in the NFC clash. The Chicago Bears just traded for Jeffery Simmons. That came after the Seattle Seahawks acquired Quenton Nelson. The All-Pro defensive tackle going against the All-Pro guard is the cherry on top of what was already set to be an exciting game. The Bears enter on a two-game winning streak at 5-2. The Seahawks are 4-3. These are the third- and fourth-best point-differential teams in the NFC—and you could make a case for Chicago being even better whenever Caleb Williams is under center. The Seahawks will have their full complement of running backs for the first time in a long time, as they activated Jadarian Price from injured reserve. That should make life easier on Sam Darnold, as will Grey Zabel moving back to his natural position at right guard. Unfortunately for the Bears, Simmons can’t cover Jaxon Smith-Njigba. Chicago is dead last in yards per reception to opposing wide receivers. They allow the second-highest average depth of target. Perhaps Simmons, in an aggressive defense, will slow Seattle down, but expecting it to happen on such a quick turnaround feels like wishful thinking. Williams has always been the aggressor. He’ll need to make plays off schedule against what’s been the NFL’s best defense for two years running. The Bears have the weapons, but Seattle makes you one-dimensional. There’s also the voodoo element that Williams needs to deal with at Lumen Field. The ball has a funny way of bouncing. Seahawks 26, Bears 20.
