title: Cleats, controversy and the choice of Bears QB Caleb Williams
summary: Williams wore Caddix cleats Monday night in Seattle, but the logo was not visible as he tries to 'calm things down.'
full_text:
It was a letter Jack Rasmussen had been anticipating. The founder of Caddix, a cleats start-up that has squeezed its way into NFL locker rooms, knew that at some point the league would fine a player for wearing his shoes.

 Then, on Oct. 20, it arrived.

 The recipient was Chicago Bears quarterback Caleb Williams , who was fined $11,941 for wearing an "unauthorized logo" on his cleats in Week 6 against the Atlanta Falcons . On Thursday, the league fined Williams again , this time for $23,882, for wearing the Caddix footwear in Week 7 against the New England Patriots .

 All Williams had to do to avoid the fines -- which Caddix and company investor Joe Flacco said they were willing to pay -- is cover up the logo. Williams told ESPN last week that wasn't in his plans for Monday night's game against the  Seattle Seahawks , but he changed his mind , saying he wanted to "calm things down" for his team. He wore matte black cleats that did not show the Caddix logo. Williams had another strong game in a 34-17 victory.

 This season has been Caddix's breakthrough. After passing NFL testing in May 2025, Caddix was approved earlier this year as a non-licensed footwear company, allowing the cleats to be worn during games. But non-licensed footwear brands can't have their logos visible on the field.

 

 Companies pay the NFL millions of dollars to be allowed to show their logo and, as of now, that list includes just three brands: Nike, Adidas and Under Armour.

 Williams, who does not have an endorsement deal with Caddix, said there were times when his feet, ankles and knees would hurt when wearing footwear in the past. And after pitches from multiple footwear companies, he chose not to sign a deal with any of them. That led Caleb's dad, Carl, to ask Williams' longtime quarterbacks coach Tom Gormely if there were any other cleat companies to consider.

 He knew of one, a small start-up whose moveable cleats were designed to help prevent injury. Rasmussen said prototypes were developed about 12 years ago, and the company was incorporated in 2023. Flacco was the first NFL player to wear them on the field in 2024 while he was with the Indianapolis Colts .

 In August 2025, Gormely called Rasmussen with a vague message: He had an NFL quarterback as a client who was looking for new cleats.

 About a month later, after Gormely vetted the technology and the cleats, he told Rasmussen who they were for. As a small brand fighting for a sliver of the NFL cleat market, Rasmussen knew what having a player the caliber of Williams wearing his cleats could do for his brand. However, Gormely didn't want Williams to switch over to Caddix at the start of the 2025 season.

 Williams started working out in Caddix this offseason. He sprinted, cut and pivoted in them, and trained inside and outside. Throughout their sessions, Williams would provide feedback to Gormely, who would then share it with Caddix.

 "We got to a point where he really liked them," Gormely said. "He was like, 'Dude, these things feel good. I like them.'"

 In June, with training camp about a month away, Rasmussen needed to sit down with the Bears quarterback. He hopped a flight from his home in Baltimore to where Williams was training in Jacksonville, Florida, to get final measurements and any other last-second changes Williams wanted to make. Rasmussen was in Florida for about 24 hours and left with the final edits to Williams' version of the Caddix O.G. cleat.

 

 "Caleb is smart and decisive about what he wants, which makes the whole process easy," Rasmussen said. "I've only met him once, but I got the feeling right away that his mind works differently than most players his age.

 "We went through two or three interactions until landing on a final design. The differences between them were incremental, which impressed me because it speaks to how in tune he is with what he wears."

 Now Williams won't take them off. He said he's been wearing Caddix since the preseason but was not the first two weeks because he wore an all-white version that did not clearly show the logo.

 Williams has appealed the first fine and will have a hearing on Nov. 10. It's anticipated that Williams will appeal the second fine as well, a source told ESPN.

 "I think my joints, my ankles and my knees and my feet haven't bothered me as much [compared to] the other cleats that I've worn ... where you're consistently playing and you get up one day and your knees hurt or your ankles are hurt and your feet hurt or anything like that," Williams said. "Like I said, they've worked for me and I feel that I feel a difference.

 "That's my opinion, and somebody else can have another."

 

 Whatever fine Caddix might pay would likely pale in comparison to the massive publicity associated with Williams and the fines. Caddix even rented billboards around Chicago with the message it will pay Williams' fines.

 Caddix has 14 investors, according to Rasmussen, including five current and former NFL players. Among them are former tight ends Todd Heap and Dennis Pita, and current players  Ja'Kobi Lane  of the Baltimore Ravens and Joey Blount of the Arizona Cardinals . NWSL star Kayla Sharples also is an athlete investor.

 Word about Caddix has slowly spread through the NFL, mainly from word of mouth, players seeing other players wearing them and players seeing them on Instagram. Rasmussen's SmartStuds technology are promoted as allowing the tips of the cleat to move as players move. That is intended to reduce the rotational torque that's transmitted through the foot and into the knees and ankle, a force associated with non-contact ACL tears and other knee and ankle injuries.

 As an NFL-approved cleat, Caddix can now be purchased by equipment managers and handed out in locker rooms. Rasmussen said all 32 teams have bought at least one run of the cleats. Some are on their second or third purchase, he said.

 "I try to be healthy," Williams said. "They're smart cleats. They're science cleats, and they've been working for me."

 Courtney Cronin contributed to this story.

title: Seven things Solak thinks for NFL Week 9: Bucs atop NFC South? RB trades coming?
summary: Get ready for Week 9 with takes on the Bucs' division chances, why RBs could dominate the trade deadline and which teams should at least ask about Justin Herbert.
full_text:
Are you excited for NFL Week 9 ? It's the last week before the trade deadline next Tuesday at 4 p.m. ET. It's also the official midway point of the season. Feel that little bite in the air? Playoff football will soon cometh.

 Every Tuesday of the NFL season , I'll turn the page from the previous week to the upcoming one with seven things I think. These aren't full-scale predictions. They aren't concrete takeaways from the past week of NFL action, either; those are fired off Sunday or Monday. Instead, these are the uncertain topics. They are things that might be true, but it'll probably take the next few games to find out. And at the bottom, you'll find a few extra half-thoughts ... just those little inklings I'm unable to shake.

 
 Subscribe: 'ESPN's Leaguewide' 

 
 This week, I'll start with my headliner expectation for the 2026 trade deadline, irresponsibly put my faith in a 3-5 Buccaneers team and wonder just how much the Chargers would get if they traded  Justin Herbert .

 

 
 Jump to: 
 RB trades are coming before the deadline 
 Cowboys should trade Pickens 
 Irving will lead the Bucs to NFC South title 
 Steelers are going to win the AFC North 
 Three teams should try to trade for Herbert 
 Campanile will be a head coach candidate 
 Bears could be dangerous with Simmons 
 Some extra trade inklings 

 
 

 

 I think ... the running back movement will be the story of the trade deadline  
 The splashiest name included in the 2026 NFL trade deadline rumor mill is Colts running back  Jonathan Taylor .

 He is a special player who can have the same impact on a healthy offense that Saquon Barkley had for the Eagles in 2024 and Derrick Henry for the Ravens in the same year. Barkley and Henry had rushing success rates of 35.4% and 37.8%, respectively, and averaged 4.2 and 4.3 yards per carry, respectively, in the two seasons before they joined their new squads. Over the past two seasons, Taylor has a 41.2% success rate and is averaging 4.7 yards per pop. His recent body of work, along with the glimmer of elite play we saw in the early parts of the 2025 season, indicates that he can be a transformative addition.

  

 As such, the Colts are -- unsurprisingly -- demanding a big return for Taylor. NFL Network's Ian Rapoport and ESPN's Adam Schefter reported that the Colts' asking price is something in line with the Christian McCaffrey trade package from 2023 -- a second-round pick, a third-round pick and some more capital.

 If Taylor gets dealt for that much compensation to a team such as the Vikings, Giants, Broncos or Bengals (or a surprise team such as the Packers and Seahawks), it's possible the running back trade market will freeze up. If the Colts get that much in return for Taylor, what could the Titans get for Tony Pollard or the Jets for  Breece Hall ?

 Jets head coach Aaron Glenn shut down trade speculation involving Hall after the 2-6 Jets' loss to the Raiders this past week, saying, "We're in the business of keeping good players, and he's one of our better players. So, Breece will still be here."

 I'm inclined to believe Glenn. Then again, Glenn could be on his way out, and I don't think general manager Darren Mougey would lament making Glenn look silly by trading Hall should he receive a big offer from a team that misses out on Taylor.

 Similarly, I find the reports that the Eagles would never trade Barkley reasonable, but not absolute. Barkley was asked if the front office told him he'd be an Eagle beyond the deadline , and he responded, "It was mentioned to me." Of course, that's before the Eagles lost another game -- to the 1-4-1 Commanders. I would put the chances of Barkley not getting traded somewhere between 95-99%, but Roseman is the sort of GM to never say never.

 The more I look at the landscape, the more I see an environment ripe for running back trades. The need is great.

 Denver is entrusting a lot of backfield snaps to a fourth-round rookie in Jonah Coleman ( whom I like quite a bit) , but the Broncos need their running game to be more dangerous given the limitations on the Bo Nix -led passing attack. Quarterback  Kyler Murray  was Minnesota's leading rusher against the Lions, as the Vikings struggle to get their running game going to open their play-action pass attack. Josh Jacobs  returned for the Packers from the commissioner exempt list, but he still might be suspended and hasn't been the same since coming back. The Bengals are looking for an upgrade over Chase Brown , as are the Giants with  Cam Skattebo , whom they don't seem to trust to be a three-down player.

 

 But the market is paralyzed by Taylor, as all these teams stare down the Colts and their towering demands. Someone will soon break from the ranks and trade for Pollard, a steady, three-down back who has reminded the league of his characteristic energy after consecutive games of 100-plus rushing yards. (I vote for the Giants, as assistant coach Brian Callahan has familiarity with Pollard.) The Cardinals should trade someone off their roster, as Bam Knight , Tyler Allgeier and the soon-to-be-healthy James Conner  all don't need to split time while rookie Jeremiyah Love gets healthy . Jaguars running back  Chris Rodriguez Jr . has lost the timeshare to Bhayshul Tuten , but Rodriguez is still a solid player who would pair well with a twitchy counterpart (looking at you, Cincinnati).

 If I were general manager of the Vikings or the Packers -- both looking to make a deep NFC playoff run but terrified of handing the ball off more than 10 times a game -- I'd be making calls beyond the obvious options from the Colts and Titans.

 Raiders second-year running back Ashton Jeanty was all but benched in Week 8 -- rookie Mike Washington Jr. outcarried him 25-2 -- and Jeanty hasn't looked particularly healthy this season. Can a playoff contender acquire the former first-rounder for a Day 2 pick, rest him up and get him healthy for the postseason?

 The Rams are funneling carries to Blake Corum more boldly than ever; he has 29 touches to Kyren Williams ' 35 over the past two weeks, which are notably the two weeks after Williams said the Rams' energy was fluctuating drive over drive " probably because I'm not out there. " I think the Rams like their 1-2 punch, but I'd definitely call to make sure.

 The Chargers have three playable backs ( Omarion Hampton , Kimani Vidal and Keaton Mitchell ), and that is three more than their win total. The Seahawks also have three playable backs ( Zach Charbonnet , Jadarian Price and Emanuel Wilson ) on top of third-down pass protector George Holani . Travis Etienne Jr . will soon return from injured reserve to rejoin Alvin Kamara and Kendre Miller in the Saints' three-player backfield. Does Chuba Hubbard move if the Panthers fall to 3-5 next Sunday?

 

 There seems to be way more backs possibly available than during previous deadlines. The trade deadline frequently features running back movement. In four of the past nine seasons, at least two running backs were traded in October and November. In 2022, a whopping six running backs exchanged teams. This position has contracts that are fairly fungible and roles that can be easily catered to skill sets; it's easy to move them midseason.

 

 What I think is rare(r) this season is the need . Four clear contenders (Broncos, Bengals, Packers and Vikings) have serious run-game concerns, and there are running back depth charts that can be substantially improved. Taylor can go to only one of those teams, and the other three will be left scrambling for Pollard. Once that dust settles, the desperation could jack up the cost and muster a surprise, big-ticket trade.

 Or Taylor won't be dealt because the Colts hold firm on their demands and find no trade partner. And then, nothing else happens. But that wouldn't be an interesting column and sure would be a disappointment come Nov. 10 at 4 p.m. ET. So we won't think about that, will we?

 
 

 I think ... George Pickens forces his way out of…

title: Jeffery Simmons, Bears' defense handle Seahawks
summary: Caleb Williams and Jeffery Simmons had the Bears controlling both sides of the ball on MNF.
full_text:
SEATTLE -- From the moment Jeffery Simmons stepped onto the field Monday night, his impact provided the Chicago Bears an immediate return on their investment after trading two first-round picks and a fourth-rounder for the All-Pro defensive tackle last week.

 The move signaled the Bears are all-in on contending for a Super Bowl, and it paid off quickly as they took down the reigning Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks 34-17. It was their third straight win and fifth in their past six games.

 Simmons elevated everyone around him on defense, and his impact was felt throughout. Seahawks QB Sam Darnold completed less than 50% of his passes with Simmons on the field and was a perfect 5-of-5 with a TD when he was off.

 In consecutive games separated by 11 days, the Bears pulled off a franchise first, defeating the Super Bowl runner-up New England Patriots and then the defending champs in Seattle.

 The Seahawks have lost three of their past four games.

 

 

 

 Chicago Bears (6-2) 

 What to make of the quarterback performance: Right off the bat, Caleb Williams led the Bears on a 17-play, 80-yard touchdown drive, which was Chicago's longest opening drive since 2007 against the Packers. Williams used play-action passes, going 10-for-15 for 109 yards and a touchdown, the most completions and yards allowed by the Seahawks on play-action passes in a game this season. Seattle's defense entered Week 8 with the No. 1 pass defense in the NFL (144 yards allowed per game). Williams surpassed that mark by the two-minute warning in the first half and finished the game by completing 70.6% of his passes for 247 yards.

 

 Most surprising performance: Credit the Simmons effect for injecting life into the Bears' ability to generate pressure with their defensive line in ways they couldn't the past two seasons, when they had a 25% pressure rate with a standard pass rush (four or fewer pass rushers). Defensive coordinator Dennis Allen didn't have to blitz as much as in previous games, and much of that can be credited to Simmons' presence. In 48 plays with Simmons on the field, the Seahawks' offense generated 146 yards (3.0 yards per play) and one touchdown to go along with three sacks and an interception. In eight plays with the All-Pro defensive tackle off the field, Seattle's offense had 106 yards and a touchdown and averaged 13.3 yards per play.

 Stat to know: D'Andre Swift rushed 24 times for just 57 yards for a 2.4-yard average, but he ran for three touchdowns to boost his league-leading total to 10 (Buffalo's Josh Allen has nine). Swift is the first Bears player with 10 rushing TDs in a season since Raymont Harris had 10 in 1997. He is the first Bears player with 10 in the Bears' first eight games since Rick Casares had 11 in 1956. 

 Trend to watch: In back-to-back games, head-scratching blitzes at the end of the first half resulted in Chicago's defense giving up explosive, consequential gains. In Week 7 against the Patriots, the Bears rushed six instead of protecting the goal line with a 13-point lead and three seconds remaining, which led to a 48-yard TD. Up by 10 with 37 seconds left in the second quarter at Seattle, Chicago blitzed out of its dime defense on third-and-long and left cornerback Tyrique Stevenson isolated against Jaxon Smith-Njigba . Without any safety help, Stevenson gave up a 43-yard touchdown as the Bears clung to a 13-9 lead at halftime. -- Courtney Cronin 

 Next game: vs. Tampa Bay Buccaneers (8:20 p.m. ET, Nov. 8)

 
 

 

 Seattle Seahawks (4-3) 

 The Seahawks made a massive addition to their offensive line last week by acquiring All-Pro left guard Quenton Nelson in a trade. They got running backs Zach Charbonnet and Jadarian Price back from injury. But then they laid an egg offensively in their worst loss since December of 2024.

 Much of it was due to quarterback Sam Darnold being under constant duress, likely a product of a reshuffled offensive line that was also missing left tackle Charles Cross (ankle). The offensive struggles gave the Seahawks no chance on a night when their vaunted defense looked as vulnerable as it has in a while, allowing season highs in points (34) and yards (363).

 

 What to make of the QB performance: Make it six straight games with an interception for Darnold and nine total picks in that span. In his defense, his fourth-quarter interception was tipped right to a Bears defender. But he was far from sharp all night. Darnold was off target on 33% of his attempts in the first half, clearly affected by Chicago's pass rush. The Bears sacked him three times and registered six QB hits. Darnold finished 17-of-34 for 188 yards, two TDs and the interception. He had another would-be interception wiped out by a defensive holding penalty.

 Stat to know: Before the Bears went 80 yards on 17 plays for a touchdown on their first possession, the Seahawks had not allowed an opening-drive TD since the 2025 opener. They didn't allow a score of any kind on the opening drive over the first seven games of this season. Seattle's defense -- which entered Week 8 allowing the second-fewest points in the NFL -- responded with a pair of three-and-outs against Chicago and forced a turnover in the fourth quarter that briefly gave the Seahawks life. But Mike Macdonald's unit -- which played without outside linebacker Uchenna Nwosu (ankle) and lost defensive tackle Leonard Williams in the second half -- ultimately allowed too many chunk plays in the passing game.

 Most surprising performance: The Seahawks entered Week 8 ranked third in ESPN Analytics' special teams rankings after finishing first in 2025. Yet that unit committed five costly errors. Rodney Thomas II botched an attempt to down a punt inside the 5-yard line, resulting in a touchback before the Bears' 80-yard touchdown drive to begin the game. Jason Myers missed a PAT and had a 33-yard field goal try blocked. Mike Morris was flagged for unnecessary roughness on a kickoff, giving Chicago an extra 15 yards on what would be a touchdown drive. Irv Charles was flagged for unnecessary roughness after a kickoff return, backing Seattle up before Darnold's interception. Even a good play by Jay Harbaugh's unit went for naught when Charles blocked a punt, only for the ball to bounce so far forward that it was as though it was never touched. -- Brady Henderson 

 Next game: vs. Arizona Cardinals (4:25 p.m. ET, Nov. 8)

title: Trio brought in to replace All-Pro DE has shined for Bengals
summary: Hendrickson has two sacks in Baltimore; Lawrence, Allen and Mafe have produced 13.5 in Cincinnati.
full_text:
CINCINNATI -- The Cincinnati Bengals were staring at yet another improbable loss against a struggling team before a 350-pound wall of muscle intervened.

 With the Tennessee Titans perilously close to field goal range, defensive tackle  Dexter Lawrence II  made a play that could be a turning point in the team's season. Lawrence plowed past two offensive linemen and sacked Titans quarterback Cam Ward for a 13-yard loss that not only took the Titans out of scoring range but also kept the Bengals alive.

 Cincinnati didn't squander the chance in a 43-36 overtime victory. As many pointed out afterward, it was the type of game that Cincinnati squandered in previous seasons.

 One could easily argue that game was won in the offseason. Instead of re-signing Trey Hendrickson , a forme All-Pro selection, Cincinnati opted to beef up the interior of the line and supplement the edges with versatile edge rushers.

 

 And through nearly half the season, the plan has paid off.

 "That's why you trade for a guy like that," Bengals coach Zac Taylor said. "He stepped up and has been the impact player we hoped he would be."

 It's not just Lawrence, whom the team acquired by trading the No. 10 draft pick to the New York Giants in exchange for the three-time Pro Bowl player. Cincinnati also signed defensive tackle Jonathan Allen and edge rusher Boye Mafe in free agency.

 And how the Bengals (5-2) decided to build their defensive line could dictate the AFC North.

 Hendrickson, who signed with the Bengals in 2021, will go down as one of the best acquisitions and edge rushers in franchise history. In five seasons, he was a four-time Pro Bowl player and an All-Pro selection in 2024 after leading the NFL with 17.5 sacks. But after the Bengals were steadfast in their refusal to commit to him long term, the 31-year-old hit free agency and landed with the rival Baltimore Ravens on a four-year contract worth $112 million.

 The Bengals chose to spend a little bit differently. Between trading for Lawrence and giving him a one-year extension and signing Allen (two years, $25 million) and Mafe (three years, $60 million), the Bengals signed contracts worth $155 million. Including the offsetting costs of trading the No. 10 pick, Cincinnati inked a net difference of $10.2 million to add three players versus how much Baltimore pledged to Hendrickson.

 And that paradigm shift was intentional. Being able to shrink the pocket from the middle of the field and making the defensive line a true position of strength was a focal point this offseason.

 Doing that required getting more than just Lawrence. So at the start of free agency, Cincinnati assistant general manager Steve Radecivic and the front office zeroed in on Allen, a 10-year veteran and a onetime first-round pick.

 Allen cited a few key names -- quarterback Joe Burrow , defensive coordinator Al Golden and assistant coach Jerry Montgomery -- among the people who made the move enticing. But the Bengals weren't shy about showing just how much they wanted the former Alabama standout.

 In the end, the Bengals ultimately won out over Allen's other suitors, a mix that he said just happened to include the Ravens.

 "Honestly, other teams were trying to lowball me and see what kind of deal they could work out," Allen told ESPN. "Cincinnati was straightforward and to the point: 'We want you to be a part of this.' So honestly, it was a pretty easy decision."

 

 The fit couldn't work out any better. Lawrence has five sacks and Allen has three. Both have been big in helping the Bengals in the run and pass game.

 And then there's Mafe, who leads the team with 5.5 sacks and is 10th in the NFL in pass rush win rate as an edge rusher, according to ESPN/Next Gen Stats.

 Against the Titans, Taylor praised the way Mafe tracked down Tennessee's Ward on the overtime drive that led to the winning stop. Mafe also worked together with Lawrence for the sack at the end of regulation.

 In Baltimore, Hendrickson has still been productive. Despite dealing with a finger injury, he still has two sacks and is fifth among edge rushers in pass rush win rate.

 But through eight games, the trio Cincinnati invested in has given the Bengals a great return on investment. This season, the Bengals are fourth in the NFL with 23 sacks, 12 shy of their season total in 2025.

 Lawrence, Mafe and Allen have seamlessly integrated themselves into Cincinnati's defense. After any given practice, the voices and conversation from that section can be heard in every corner of the locker room.

 And with the Bengals nearly at the midway point of the season, it's easy to see why the newcomers have integrated so well.

 "I feel like the [defense] came into this year with something to prove," Mafe told ESPN. "And for me, that's an easy thing to buy into. I love to see an underdog story. I love to see people count somebody out and for them to show up as much as they can."

title: Kansas City Chiefs' late collapse vs. Denver Broncos opens up AFC West race
summary: Prior to Sunday's game, the Chiefs were 80-2 when leading by 10 or more in the fourth quarter under Patrick Mahomes.
full_text:
DENVER -- While the Denver Broncos celebrated Sunday, Kansas City Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes walked away with the disappointment, frustration and regret showing on his face.

 Instead of leading his teammates to a pivotal win in dramatic, comeback fashion, Mahomes had just finished the game, a 28-24 collapse of a loss , on his backside. The Broncos sacking Mahomes on the game's final play was a perfect punctuation to one of the Chiefs' most embarrassing losses under coach Andy Reid. After going up 11 points deep into the second half, the Chiefs lost the lead -- and their lead in the AFC West -- to the Broncos with an error-filled performance in the fourth quarter.

 

 "The execution just wasn't at a high enough level," Mahomes said. "We made big plays, and we made plays happen against a really good defense, but you've got to execute for the full 60 minutes. We weren't able to do it."

 Prior to Sunday's game, the Chiefs were 80-2, including the playoffs, when they led by 10 or more points in the fourth quarter with Mahomes as their starter.

 "You can't dwell on it," tight end Travis Kelce said. "Obviously in our hearts we felt we should've come out with a victory, but that's not the reality of things. We've got to fix a lot. We just didn't finish the way we should've."

 The Chiefs (5-2) went scoreless in the final 15 minutes. Meanwhile, the Broncos (6-2) scored 15 points on their final two drives. Sunday's game was the Chiefs' largest fourth-quarter point differential in a loss under Reid, who became their coach in 2013.

 Just about everything that could go wrong for the Chiefs did in their collapse. Reid made several conservative decisions, including punting early in the fourth quarter on a fourth-and-inches near midfield. The Broncos then marched 80 yards on nine plays to cut the lead to three points.

 The Chiefs' next possession ended in an even worse outcome. Facing a third-and-2 from the Broncos' 30-yard line, Mahomes made his biggest mistake of the game. Instead of throwing the ball away when his three pass-catching options were covered, he was sacked by linebacker Alex Singleton for a 6-yard loss. The play set up a 54-yard field goal attempt for kicker Harrison Butker , who missed it wide right.

 "I can't put [Butker] in that position," Mahomes said. "Obviously, we're in field goal range, in a big moment, and I'm trying to make a play. Their defense played well. They passed off [their zone] coverage really well. I've got to throw the ball away or get vertical. Whenever you're on the edge of field goal range, you don't want to move backward because it puts [Butker] in a tough spot."

 

 Reid did have another option, especially with Butker's struggles this season when kicking long field goals. According to NFL Next Gen Stats, a punt would have given the Chiefs the highest win probability ahead of going for it (74.3% vs. 72.5%). A field goal attempt, however, ranked last (71.5%). ESPN Analytics metrics also disagreed with Reid's decision to have Butker attempt the 54-yard kick (73.4% win probability) instead of punting (76.8%).

 "It's within Harrison's range," Reid said of his decision.

 Butker's miss continued his ongoing woes. Since the start of last season, Butker has missed 16 kicks -- 11 field goal attempts and five extra point attempts -- the most by any kicker in the NFL during that span.

 "It was just a really bad miss," Butker said. "I just completely missed the ball and didn't even give it a chance. It didn't feel good off the foot."

 Two plays later, the Broncos scored the go-ahead touchdown, a 5-yard touchdown run by  Jonah Coleman , who set up the score with a 51-yard catch-and-run the play before.

 

 In all, the Broncos needed less than five minutes to score the decisive touchdowns Sunday, highlighting the part Kansas City's defense played in the collapse. The unit pressured Broncos quarterback Bo Nix on only two of his 34 dropbacks (6%), the lowest pressure rate by any team in a game this season.

 "It's only one thing, rush the passer, get the quarterback down," pass rusher Chris Jones said. "We blocked a couple of balls, but I don't think we got [Nix] down. I put that on the D-line. We've got to win our one-on-ones. We've got to take advantage of that. We got a one-on-one, we got to win it."

 Speaking after the game, Reid identified a different area of concern: penalties. The Chiefs finished Sunday with a season-high 11 penalties for 105 yards, including a 15-yard roughing penalty by Alohi Gilman on Denver's first touchdown drive of the fourth quarter. On the season, the Chiefs have been penalized for 164 more yards than their opponents, the largest margin in the league. So of course it was a penalty that nullified their would-be game-winning touchdown on fourth-and-goal from the 1-yard line with four seconds left. On the play, Mahomes found Rashee Rice in the middle of the end zone, but right tackle Jaylon Moore was flagged for a false start penalty. On the next play, Mahomes was sacked by defensive end Malcolm Roach to end the game.

 "We ran a really good play that we liked a lot," Mahomes said of his pass to Rice. "You kind of showcased that play. We talked about that play [in] the meeting the night before [the game]. It gets a lot of attention on Travis and then you hit Rashee underneath.

 "We had to go to a different play [for] that last one, and they covered it well. Whenever you get that close, and you don't capitalize, you take that on yourself and you learn from it. I wish I'd done a better job of getting the ball out, just giving somebody a chance. It's fourth down."

 If the Chiefs had beaten the Broncos, they would've taken a commanding lead in the division. With a win, the Chiefs would've had an 86% chance to win the division crown, according to ESPN Analytics. Following Sunday's game, the Broncos now have a 52% chance to win it.

 "Now you're kind of in a dogfight for the division," Mahomes said. "You just try to get better and better, so that at the end of the year you're playing your best football."

title: C.J. Stroud turned down a big contract. A bigger one awaits
summary: Sources say C.J. Stroud turned down a deal similar to Trevor Lawrence's. He's in line for a bigger one.
full_text:
HOUSTON -- The Houston Texans had reached a tipping point.

 Teams tend to attempt to sign key players to long-term deals between the start of training camp and Week 1 of the regular season. The Texans had been trying to do so with their star quarterback, C.J. Stroud , who has shown major promise but was coming off a career lowlight -- a four-interception first half in a playoff loss in New England.

 Before camp, Houston made an initial offer to Stroud that reached what sources called a "respectable" range -- not at the top of the quarterback market but well within the $50 million-per-year club that 13 quarterbacks now occupy. Two sources familiar with the negotiation recalled Houston's offer was similar to the deal Trevor Lawrence signed with Jacksonville two years ago, placing Stroud in the second tier of around $55 million per year.

 "They made a pretty good effort," a source said, noting Houston's Nick Caserio is one of the league's most aggressive general managers. The Texans made Will Anderson Jr . the NFL's highest-paid non-quarterback and Derek Stingley Jr . the league's highest-paid defensive back while also signing Danielle Hunter , Nico Collins and  Azeez Al-Shaair  to significant contract extensions.

 The way Stroud's 2025 campaign ended had fueled a firestorm of offseason chatter and a ping-pong game of different scenarios for Houston: pay him, trade him, let him play out his fourth year.

 A trade was not happening, something about which Caserio was publicly adamant.

 It turns out Stroud made a choice of his own in the weeks leading up to the regular season.

 Stroud and his agent, David Mulugheta, made a counteroffer. They did not demand that Stroud be the league's highest-paid quarterback, per a source. Stroud understands the business side of being an NFL player, from market pay for players at multiple positions, to team construction. He knows if he takes every penny possible, paying the players around him becomes harder.

 But despite the back-and-forth, a deal was not imminent. Meanwhile, Stroud had made clear he was comfortable playing without a new deal, per sources. "Unless there's a better offer, we're good," is how one source recalled the messaging from Stroud.

 Once Houston chose not to put together a deal Stroud couldn't refuse, he opened the year against the Buffalo Bills with one mindset: Time to bet on myself. 

 

 This was not viewed as a contentious negotiation, and both sides seemed at peace. This leaves Caserio with the task of projecting Stroud's upward trajectory after his 2027 fifth-year option, which is worth $25.9 million.

 "Nobody was reluctant on anything," Caserio said. "We had discussions. We made an offer. All right, couldn't quite come to a final resolution or agreement. That happens. It's not the first time, it's not the last time. Not going to be the first time. Again, nobody's discouraged. I have a lot of respect for C.J. and David Mulugheta and their group."

 Stroud's well-timed breakout -- and his competition next offseason 

 Two months later, Stroud's seasonlong parlay has been a winning ticket so far. And the 2023 No. 2 pick hasn't allowed the contract situation to affect his play.

 "Something I was taught when I first went to Ohio State was just keep the main thing the main thing," Stroud said. "Football has always been there and it's not going nowhere. I hope not. I'm very blessed to play this game every single week. Practice, walk-throughs, meetings, I don't take anything for granted. If you chase the deal or the contract, I think that's when you kind of lose yourself."

 He's fourth in passing yards (1,867), 10th in passer rating (100.7) and 13th in touchdowns (11) with only one interception. Advanced metrics are even rosier; he's second in expected points added and seventh in ESPN's Total QBR.

 

 "He looks like he was expected to look after his rookie year," an NFL coordinator said of Stroud's recent play.

 Houston sits at 2-5 because a once-elite defense has regressed drastically to 19th in points allowed (24.3) after finishing second (17.4) in 2025. The preseason narrative surrounding the Texans' Super Bowl hopes centered on Stroud reaching his potential paired with a dominant defense. But while Stroud is doing his part, the defense has allowed four late game-winning drives.

 Despite that faith in Stroud, Houston's failure to reach a deal with him puts the team at the mercy of rising quarterback costs.

 "I don't think anybody's really too worried about it," Caserio said. "He's played really good football, which isn't a surprise to anybody. I think there are very few people, maybe [coach DeMeco Ryans], myself, who supported him all offseason when he was essentially bad-mouthed for like four months about one bad half of football."

 

 Part of Stroud's conviction in playing out his rookie deal came from a forecast of an exploding market in 2027, multiple league sources said. Quarterbacks from the 2024 draft class -- the Chicago Bears' Caleb Williams , Washington Commanders' Jayden Daniels and Patriots' Drake Maye -- are among those eligible for new deals this offseason. Maye reached the Super Bowl in Year 2 and Daniels appeared in a conference championship as a rookie. Daniels' career has been similar to Stroud's, as he had a meteoric start followed by turbulence.

 Baltimore Ravens quarterback  Lamar Jackson will also enter the last year of his contract with an albatross cap hit of $84 million. Stroud, to his credit, has three playoff wins, all in the wild-card round. The more Stroud delivers, the higher his price climbs. One industry source projects that the quarterbacks named above could push the $70 million-per-year threshold. Stroud's place in that tier is looking promising.

 "He's making himself a lot of money," an AFC executive said. "New tax bracket. If he keeps playing like this and they somehow get in the playoffs and make a run, there's no reason why he can't be somewhere close to the highest paid." After all, Stroud's rookie year, when he set multiple records during a historic debut season, sparked assumptions that he would reset the market when contract-eligible. After up-and-down production the past two seasons, the tenor around Stroud's perception changed a bit. But this season, Stroud has held up his end of the bargain.

 The Texans' aggressive move to get Stroud help last month -- trading a second-round pick to Arizona for Marvin Harrison Jr ., Stroud's teammate at Ohio State -- signals faith in Stroud's long-term impact.

 Caserio has no concerns about the contract situation becoming tumultuous when the two sides revisit it in the offseason. In fact, the expectation is the Texans and Stroud will agree to a contract extension in the offseason, barring a massive unforeseen downturn in his play, according to a team source. The Texans' owners, Cal and Hannah McNair, love Stroud and don't mind paying the potential new market value, according to a team source.

 "Chasing the game, not chasing what people would think is like the bag or whatever," Stroud said. "I'm grateful that I have a lot of people who keep me focused on what's important in life."

 No reason for panic, but challenges near for Texans 
 
 
 An offseason impasse on a contract negotiation could create a ripple effect despite the presence of that fifth-year option. The fifth-year option is well below market -- especially for a player currently taking on multiple risks: of injury, of a potential slump like he sustained last winter, and of declining players around him. It's no secret that Houston has struggled to configure a strong offensive line. The Texans have used 25 different offensive combinations to start a game, which is the ninth most in the span since Stroud entered the league in 2023. Houston acquired running back  David Montgomery  in March via trade from Detroit and changed two starting spots on the line. The result: The Texans are rushing for 3.6 yards a carry and only 84.7 yards per game…

title: Why Colts are right to consider trading Jonathan Taylor
summary: As the Colts begin their rebuild, they need draft picks, and Taylor is their most valuable asset.
full_text:
INDIANAPOLIS -- The  Indianapolis Colts  had been eyeing Jonathan Taylor closely for months before the 2020 draft.

 The running back was well-regarded among scouts after his prolific career at Wisconsin, where he registered back-to-back 2,000-yard rushing seasons in 2018 and 2019. But at a time when running backs had been treated dismissively by the NFL, how would he be viewed in the draft?

 For the Colts, that answer was clear.

 Taylor was among their top targets. So, when the Colts saw Taylor sliding in the second round, they pounced. At the time, owner Jim Irsay implored general manager Chris Ballard to trade up for the player he'd been talking about endlessly in draft meetings.

 Just like that, the Colts made Taylor the No. 41 pick.

 Now, years later, the Colts are contemplating a much different sort of decision about Taylor. The organization is weighing offers to trade one of the best players in franchise history.

 Taylor has run into the Indianapolis record books with a franchise-record 77 rushing touchdowns. Only Baltimore's Derrick Henry has more explosive runs (10-plus yards) since Taylor entered the league. Every indicator says Taylor is a game-changing player. But is it time the Colts consider a deal that would result in Taylor changing teams before the Nov. 10 trade deadline?

 An honest assessment of the situation strongly suggests the time is now.

 We do not know who will be calling the shots for the Colts next season or who will be coaching the team. Ballard has already been fired and coach Shane Steichen could be next.

 

 But there is no mystery about ownership's position on the direction this team is headed. This is an obvious rebuild.

 Taylor might have been somewhat oblivious to this when, during an interview with local reporters Thursday, he seemed surprised at the line of questioning.

 "You think we're rebuilding?" he asked.

 All Taylor had to do was look at how the team's decisions have been trending. The Colts have in the past nine months parted ways with key players Zaire Franklin , Michael Pittman Jr ., Kenny Moore II , Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner . They had kept a large core of players together for years, hoping to see the group take a step toward competing for something meaningful.

 It never happened.

 The moves of the past week -- the trades of Nelson and Buckner -- are potentially a preview of what is to come. The Colts were taking one more shot with the remaining cast, pairing them with Alec Pierce and quarterback Daniel Jones , who were re-signed during the offseason. Now, Pierce is on injured reserve, Jones' starting job is jeopardy and the Colts are 2-6.

 But there's more. The Colts are fielding one of their worst defenses in years. The unit is ranked 30th in points allowed per game (27.8), yards per play (5.9) and yards per rush (4.9). Look for things to only get worse with the departure of Buckner, who looked revitalized after offseason neck surgery.

 If this isn't a rebuild, then what's the alternative label?

 If this winds up being a Miami Dolphins -style teardown, the Colts are looking at an uncompetitive season in 2027. That means, optimistically, 2028 is their target year to rebound. By that time, Taylor will be 29½ years old with a significant amount of wear and tear on his body.

 Relatedly, there's the reality that every rebuild requires one important component: draft picks.

 The Colts' decision to trade two first-round choices to the New York Jets for cornerback Sauce Gardner last year continues to reverberate in Indy. And the team's best remaining asset is Taylor. Already, the Colts have been offered a package that included a second-round pick and a later-round pick for Taylor, according to a source.

 

 If Taylor could generate that kind of offer nearly two weeks before the trade deadline, is it preposterous to wonder if the Colts might possibly acquire a late-first round choice for a game-altering player? Maybe so, but they should do themselves a favor and find out for certain.

 The picks the Colts landed for Nelson and Buckner, ranging from the third to fifth rounds, are helpful. But the Colts, who lack a long-term starting quarterback, have numerous holes to fill. It's going to take a lot more than a few extra midround picks to pull that off.

 There has been an internal shift in the past week at Colts headquarters. Team personnel and players have gone from scoffing at the idea of a Taylor trade to accepting the possibility. That includes Taylor, who last week finally seemed resigned to the fact that it might happen.

 "At the end of the day, the business side is going to move with or without you, with or without your permission," he said. He later added, "You know that the day comes for many players, whether you like it or not."

 The Colts' unenviable situation might mean that Taylor's day is near.

title: Foyesade Oluokun continues to quietly excel as Jaguars return to winning ways
summary: Foyesade Oluokun may not be one of the most talked about defensive players in the NFL, but his performances this season have been up there with the most consistent.
full_text:
Foyesade Oluokun may not be one of the most talked about defensive players in the NFL, but his performances this season have been up there with the most consistent and he delivered again in the Jacksonville Jaguars' Week 8 win over the Indianapolis Colts.

 Oluokun made nine tackles, including two for a loss, and picked up a sack as the Jags beat the Colts 42-7. This performance earned the linebacker of Nigerian family lineage his second Africa Player of the Week gong of the season.

 On offense, Emmett Johnson - who is of Liberian descent - was a standout performer, with Jaxon Smith-Njigba (Sierra Leonean heritage) tallying over 100 receiving yards for a fourth straight game.

 African Player of the Week: Foyesade Oluokun (Jacksonville Jaguars) 

 

 Oluokun - a first-generation Nigerian-American linebacker - made several big hits in the Jags' win over the Colts, but the ones early in the first and second quarters were arguably the most consequential in terms of setting the tone.

 He brought down Jonathan Taylor for a seven-yard loss on third down on the first drive of the game. The next play was a punt, and then the Jaguars scored the game's first touchdown over 12 plays on the next drive.

 That was the only touchdown of the first quarter, which ended with the Jags 7-0 to the good. On the first drive of the second quarter, Oluokun sacked Dan Jones. That set the tone for a quarter which they would utterly dominate, effectively putting the game to bed by half-time at 28-0.

 

 Oluokun and the Jaguars showed little sign of letting up in the second half and saw out a comfortable win to go 5-2 for the season - the perfect response after a narrow 34-31 loss to the Houston Texans two weeks ago.

 African Moment of the Week: Emmett Johnson (Kansas City Chiefs) 

 The Kansas City Chiefs lost 28-24 to the Denver Broncos, but Emmett Johnson - the son of parents who moved from Liberia - capped an impressive performance for the Chiefs with a 73-yard touchdown.

 Johnson had Taylor Rapp to beat on his way to the end zone, so he cut inside, but stumbled. However, Johnson managed to regain his footing and then beat Rapp round the outside.

 That touchdown was far from the only highlight for Johnson - who tallied 128 yards across five receptions, as well as 15 rushing yards and 44 yards on a kickoff return.

 Honorable mentions 

 Boye Mafe recorded a sack for the fourth successive game as the Cincinnati Bengals beat the Tennessee Titans 43-36 in overtime despite fellow Nigerian-American player Chimere Dike's touchdown for the losing side.

 Jaxon Smith-Njigba, who has ties to Sierra Leone through his grandparents, tallied 118 receiving yards across six catches for the Seattle Seahawks and scored a touchdown in their 34-17 loss to the Chicago Bears.

 Chuba Hubbard and Bobby Okereke - both with family ties to Nigeria - also lost despite major Week 8 contributions for the Carolina Panthers, who went down 27-19 to the Green Bay Packers. Hubbard scored a rushing touchdown, while Okereke picked up a fumble reception.

 Davison Igbinosun - of Nigerian descent - got his first NFL career interception in the Buffalo Bills' 36-10 win over the Baltimore Ravens.

 One match which saw major contributions from players of African heritage on both the winning and losing sides was the Washington Commanders' 27-10 win over the Philadelphia Eagles.

 Charles Omenihu and Odafe Oweh (both of Nigerian descent) both picked up sacks for the Commanders, while Zimbabwe's Andrew Mukuba had an impressive outing even in defeat for the Eagles with nine tackles, a pass defended and a forced fumble.

 Nigerian-American duo Josh Uche (Miami Dolphins, lost 24-19 to New England Patriots) and Donovan Ezeiruaku (Dallas Cowboys, lost 33-30 to Arizona Cardinals) both picked up sacks in defeats. Another Nigerian-American NFL star, Nnamdi Madubuike, picked up half a sack for the Baltimore Ravens in their loss to the Bills.

 Africa-born Player Watch 

 Mukuba - born in Harare to a Congolese family - had an outstanding week for the Eagles even in defeat.

 His compatriot, Nate Landman - born in the very same city - made eight tackles for the LA Rams in their 24-9 win over city rivals the LA Chargers. Seven of those tackles were solo and his contribution was vital in the win.

 The Rams will face the Commanders next on Sunday in a clash which is likely to feature many of the top African talents - whether through birth or family lineage - in the NFL.

title: Sizing up wild NFL Week 8: Lamar Jackson's injury, Bucs' win, Cowboys' collapse
summary: Lamar Jackson's return lasted one snap, the Cardinals upset the Cowboys with their QB2 and RB2, and the Buccaneers won by 16 despite 0 passing yards.
full_text:
What looked like a relatively quiet set of Sunday games in NFL Week 8 turned into something much more unexpectedly dramatic and substantial. The day started with a franchise- and season-altering injury, as Lamar Jackson suffered a thumb injury on his first snap of the game against the Bills , turning the most anticipated matchup of the afternoon into a one-sided blowout.

 By the end of the early slate, eight teams had scored 30 or more points, two games had gone to overtime and one team won in a way we haven't seen since the early 1970s. Throw in a dramatic comeback win for the Broncos in the afternoon and Week 8 was truly wild.

 
 Subscribe: 'The Bill Barnwell Show' 

 
 Let's break down six events from an unexpectedly wild Sunday afternoon. I have big plays, bad decisions and quarterback benchings to discuss. It seems natural, though, to begin with the scene in Buffalo, where a Bills blowout was overshadowed by the return and immediate departure of a two-time MVP.

 

 
 Jump to: 
 Jackson's short return 
 Cardinals beat Cowboys 
 Bucs go 0-for-3 and win 
 Chiefs blow double-digit lead 
 Titans push Bengals to brink 
 Jeanty, Taylor see surprising work 

 
 

 

 Lamar Jackson 's return from injury lasts one snap 
 Baltimore's day started with Jackson making his return from a left ankle injury and ended with emergency quarterback Joe Fagnano fumbling away a snap for the Ravens' third and final turnover of the day. What happened in between could drastically change the present and future outlook of the organization. After missing 3½ games with a high ankle sprain, Jackson injured his thumb on his first snap of the game against the host Bills and did not return.

 ESPN's Adam Schefter reported that Jackson will require thumb surgery and hit injured reserve, with Baltimore coach Jesse Minter unsure whether the injury will end Jackson's season. For good measure, backup Tyler Huntley suffered a toe injury and was unable to return, leaving Fagnano to take the final 38 snaps of the contest. Unsurprisingly, the rookie free agent wasn't able to do much in what would be a 36-10 Bills victory.

 Minter, general manager Eric DeCosta and the Ravens organization now find themselves at both short- and long-term crossroads. Let's start with the 2026 season. Even if we assume Jackson can make it back later in the season, the Ravens are clearly in a compromised situation. At 4-4, they sit in last place in a very competitive AFC North. They've already traded a future second-round pick for Cam Jurgens  in October and attempted to trade two first-round picks  for Maxx Crosby in the offseason before rescinding the deal after Crosby's physical. Trey Hendrickson , their de facto replacement for Crosby, has two sacks in six games.

 

 With just over a week to go before the trade deadline and his top two quarterbacks both out injured, DeCosta can go in one of two directions. If the Ravens think they have a team that can potentially stay afloat and survive in the playoff picture long enough for Jackson to return, DeCosta could try to swing a trade for another option at quarterback. Jacoby Brissett was  just benched in Arizona. Daniel Jones might be next in Indianapolis, where the Colts could save $13.8 million in cash over the next two years by trading away their embattled starter. Baltimore could also re-sign Cooper Rush , who was in the building last year, albeit in a different offensive scheme. None of those options are going to be very exciting to Ravens fans, but there aren't many high-end quarterbacks available in November.

 Does the rest of this team support making some sort of move? It's tough to believe that's the case. The Baltimore defense has put together good halves of football, but it's 20th in points allowed per possession and EPA per defensive snap. Derrick Henry has averaged 3.6 yards per carry with a 41.8% success rate since Week 2. The decision to re-sign Mark Andrews and let Isaiah Likely leave in free agency has looked disastrous, as Likely has excelled with the Giants while Andrews has been unable to generate any sort of explosion and has dropped four passes. Injuries have also created real problems for the Ravens on the interior, necessitating the trade for Jurgens, who hasn't been a major upgrade since returning from  a concussion he suffered with the Eagles.

 The more practical option might be heading in the opposite direction, writing off any chance of making a serious impact in 2026 and hoping that things will be better with a healthier Jackson in 2027. But outside of veterans like Henry and Calais Campbell , who might prefer not being dealt at this point of their careers, the Ravens don't really have many tradable options. DeCosta won't want to move young cornerstone pieces like Zay Flowers and Nate Wiggins , while the likes of Andrews and Marlon Humphrey aren't playing well enough to attract meaningful trade interest at their existing salaries.

 If he does miss the rest of the year, will Jackson even be part of the equation in 2027? As was  discussed this offseason , his future with Baltimore is tenuous. Jackson has a massive $84.8 million cap number in 2027 to go with no-trade and no-tag clauses. While the Ravens can restructure his contract to create cap room, all that would do is spray dead money on their cap in 2028 and 2029, years when Jackson might be part of another organization anyway.

 The two sides weren't able to come to terms on a contract extension before the season, leaving Jackson with more leverage as he gets closer to unrestricted free agency. Missing most of the season with injuries won't exactly put Jackson's best foot forward, but remember that Dak Prescott was able to parlay a 2020 season abbreviated by a serious ankle injury  into a record-setting contract with the Cowboys because the leverage of unrestricted free agency was more powerful and significant than the blow of the injury.

 

 At the same time, if Jackson did decide after the season that he wanted to leave and gave the Ravens a handful of potential landing spots, would DeCosta really be able to negotiate a significant trade haul? Jackson is a two-time MVP and a future Hall of Famer, but when teams had the ability to negotiate with Jackson on the franchise tag  in 2023, offenses with the likes of Desmond Ridder and Kyle Trask as their nominal starters at the time had no meaningful interest. Negotiating off the tag is different from negotiating a trade, but some of the arguments for  why teams didn't pursue Jackson at the time  were myths, too.

 Since then, Jackson has won a second MVP, come close to winning a third and put together the best passing performances of his career. He's also going to be 30 years old in the 2027 offseason and will have missed significant time in four of the past six seasons. I think Jackson is an absolutely incredible player, and what we saw from him before the ankle injury hinted toward a potentially special season in 2026.

 Getting another team to agree, hand Jackson a record-setting contract and send the Ravens the sort of draft pick haul they would want to justify trading Jackson might not be realistic or possible for DeCosta, though. It would be difficult for Baltimore to accept anything less than what the Broncos sent the Seahawks for Russell Wilson , which included two first-round picks, two second-round picks and three players. Losing Jackson for nothing in 2028 would be disastrous, but trading him for something less than market value in 2027 wouldn't be great business, either.

 Even if Jackson is back next year, the guys lining up around the star quarterback will be different. Henry, Humphrey, Andrews and others could be cap casualties. Offensive coordinator Declan Doyle could earn a head coaching job somewhere, even if the offense struggles without Jackson under center. The Ravens were already facing a potential transition in 2027. That transition might have begun unexpectedly early in western New York on Sunday.

…

title: Dolphins' blown lead another lesson in a season full of them
summary: The Dolphins are hoping to learn another lesson from the Patiots: It takes from kickoff until the final whistle.
full_text:
MIAMI GARDENS, Fla. -- Chris Johnson couldn't have played the down much better.

 The Miami Dolphins rookie cornerback fought through two sets of blocks on fourth-and-two during Sunday's game against the New England Patriots and tackled wide receiver DeMario Douglas short of the sticks.

 The Dolphins' offense took the field, clinging to a three-point lead with the momentum of a critical stop behind them -- but it didn't last long.

 Officials overturned the play, awarding New England the first down; it scored six plays later to take the lead for good.

 Miami saw a ten-point halftime lead turn to a 24-19 loss to the Patriots, marking another chapter in this team's education. Last week, coach Jeff Hafley's team learned how to win; this week, it learned how quickly a win can slip from its grasp.

 "I thought it was probably the best half that we played all year in the first half in some phases," Hafley said. "We came out and I believe we held them to a three and out. And then those are the opportunities where you got to learn to put people away. And when you let really good teams that have experience and have been through big games, when you let them hang around, that's what happens.

 "It's the first time we've been in that situation. So I think you do a really good job of using this as a teaching moment, as hard as it feels and as much as it hurts, you got to learn from wins and you got to learn from losses and we have to grow from that."

 As the youngest team in the NFL, the Dolphins have struggled overcoming momentum swings like the one they experienced Sunday. In Week 1, a taunting penalty negated a third-down stop on a drive that ultimately led to points for the Raiders. In Week 3, an illegal shift penalty wiped out a touchdown, and the Dolphins had to settle for a field goal.

 Even Sunday, the reversed turnover on downs was preceded by a Patriots touchdown that was initially ruled an incomplete pass, followed by an unsportsmanlike conduct penalty that effectively ended the Dolphins' ensuing drive.

 "We had such momentum after that one fourth-down stop. Those are the swings of the game and I think you have to learn and we all have to learn that that's football," Hafley said. "There's going to be huge momentum shifts in the game ... you've got to learn to just play the next play and you can't get too high, you can't get too low throughout a game."

 Last week, the Dolphins opened a two-score lead at halftime but found themselves ahead by just three points with three minutes remaining. They were able to stave off the Jets' comeback and hold on for their first win of the season.

 Safety Dante Trader Jr . said the energy from that win carried over into the first half Sunday, and linebacker Jacob Rodriguez said it fueled their best week of practice to date.

 The Dolphins fell behind by a field goal in the first half Sunday but responded with 13 unanswered points, including an 11-play, 70-yard touchdown drive to end the first half. Linebacker Jordyn Brooks said the eventual loss will serve as a lesson to remain composed, especially against teams like the defending AFC champion Patriots.

 "We looked fired up in the locker room at halftime, man, everybody was excited," he said. "After playing a great first half, I think we were a little too fired up. An experienced team like the Patriots, who's been there, done that, they just remained calm through the whole thing and just made crucial plays when they needed it, and it was enough for them to win."

 Even after their lead dissipated, the Dolphins gave themselves a chance Sunday. After allowing three straight touchdown drives in the third and fourth quarters, they forced a punt with four minutes remaining and answered with a 35-yard touchdown pass from Malik Willis to Kevin Coleman Jr .

 Miami couldn't recover an onside kick attempt and failed to get a stop on third-and-5, allowing New England to kneel out the clock.

 Hafley said he was proud of his team's resolve while acknowledging its need to learn how to fight for an entire game -- without the lulls it has experienced in the second half of its past two games.

 "It felt like they had us on the ropes," he said. "What I liked at the end of the game was despite everything that we just went through and all the momentum shifts that everybody talked about, for a young team, what was cool to see is we stopped them. We stopped them in four-minute mode and then we scored. So then we get a chance to have an onside kick.

 "So again, the team does show resiliency. It's just we got to learn how to do it for all four quarters."

title: Drake Maye digs the long ball: Patriots QB's success on deep passes keying surge
summary: After struggling on deep passes early, Maye has been one of the best in the league at producing chunk plays in the pass game over the past few weeks.
full_text:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. -- For those who dig the long ball, the New England Patriots ' upcoming home game against the Green Bay Packers on Sunday ( 4:25 p.m. ET, Gillette Stadium, Fox ) is the place to be.

 Patriots quarterback Drake Maye and Packers signal-caller Jordan Love have been on heaters with their down-the-field connections, with Love leading all quarterbacks with 14 completions of at least 20 yards since Week 4 and Maye second with 11. With Tom Brady in town for his first-ever television broadcast featuring the team for which he played 20 seasons and won six Super Bowl championships, the possibility of fireworks is tantalizing.

 And if not for Maye's deep-ball proficiency, the vibes around the 5-3 Patriots might be much different this week.

 New England was in a compromising position Sunday in rain-soaked South Florida against the underdog Dolphins, trailing 13-3 at halftime. But Maye's 43-yard touchdown strike to speedy receiver Kyle Williams , followed by his 48-yarder to receiver DeMario "Pop" Douglas , instantly changed things in a 24-19 win .

 The turnaround mirrors Maye's individual U-turn this season.

 

 Since Week 4, Maye has six touchdowns and no interceptions on passes at least 20 yards downfield. That leads the NFL in that stretch and is double the next-closest total of any quarterback -- Love and the Las Vegas Raiders ' Kirk Cousins are tied for second with three each.

 Through the first three weeks of the season, Maye had no touchdowns and three interceptions on passes at least 20 yards. He admitted he was struggling to strike the balance between the right decision (e.g. -- taking what's there) and the big play. Maye, who earned one of four game balls from coach Mike Vrabel on Sunday after playing a turnover-free game in challenging weather conditions, has decisively found it, leading the NFL in QBR while pressured (61.0) since Week 4 according to ESPN Research. For context, the league average in that span is 13.5.

 Facing more favorable defenses after seeing the Seattle Seahawks , Pittsburgh Steelers and Jacksonville Jaguars in the opening three weeks has aided Maye's revival. Four of the past five teams the Patriots have faced are ranked 21st or lower in defense according to ESPN's Football Power Index , with the Dolphins last at No. 32.

 Nonetheless, it's impressive that he has turned things around with several top pass catchers sidelined due to injury, a group that includes Mack Hollins ( calf ), Romeo Doubs ( shoulder ) and A.J. Brown ( knee ). And top tight end Hunter Henry was limited to eight snaps on Sunday due to a foot injury.

 "He'll be a great quarterback in the National Football League," Vrabel said of Maye. "There's not a whole lot of excuses. You go out there and you find ways to win for your football team. And I know that that's one who he is, and that's what he wants to continue to be.

 "So, he just throws to the open guy and controls our offense and gets guys in the right spot. That's being one of the best quarterbacks in the league; that's what the job description requires."

 

 Hollins is eligible to return from injured reserve this week, and his presence with the team on the past two road trips indicates he could be on the cusp of being activated. Doubs isn't eligible to return until late November, while Brown continues to receive treatment, according to Vrabel, and is being evaluated daily.

 Vrabel didn't have an update on Henry, with Maye saying after Sunday's game: "I saw when he got up from the catch, I was worried about him. I probably shouldn't be worried about him, but I'm worried about Hunt. I know he went back to the locker room, but he seems like he's walking around fine and he's got a smile on his face."

 Love is one of the few quarterbacks who can rival Maye in the deep passing game, and the 5-3 Packers have needed it because they average only 60.6 rushing yards per game, the fewest by any team through eight games since the 2019 Bengals (59.5). In the Packers' win over the Panthers on Thursday, Love threw two touchdown passes 10-plus yards down the field and was 7-of-14 for 154 passing yards on those throws.

 When it comes to success in the deep passing game, Vrabel said it starts with having receivers who can get downfield and make plays. Protection is obviously critical. And then it comes back to the quarterbacks.

 "Certainly touch is involved, right? And if you have to drive the ball -- arm strength," he said. "But I think probably just having a good feel of, 'Do I need a 35-yard pass that's in the air, or do I need a 50-yard ball?' and being able to judge that differently."

 Maye has been hot in that department, which Packers coach Matt LaFleur noted Monday.

 

 "He's really athletic, too, and so we got to do a good job of trying to contain him the best you can because a lot of their explosive plays are when he gets loose in the pocket and can get out," LaFleur said. "And he's got a big-time arm."

 Douglas, who has been the Patriots' most targeted receiver since Hollins went on IR after Week 4, has enjoyed the front-row view of Maye's turnaround.

 "That's a dawg," Douglas said. "His growth that I've seen is crazy -- from Year 1 to now. And then you see the beginning of this year and how he's rocking out now. That shows a champion in him."

 ESPN Packers reporter Rob Demovsky contributed to this story.

title: Five things Saints must fix entering Week 9 vs. Browns
summary: Protecting QB Tyler Shough, getting the run game going and igniting slow starts are among areas coach Kellen Moore is fixated on repairing.
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints have 10 games to turn their 2026 season around.

 The Saints are coming off their bye week after an embarrassing showing in Paris against the Pittsburgh Steelers . The Saints (2-5) lost 16-10, but they rushed for only 18 yards while allowing 148 rushing yards.

 Some of the Saints' problems in their Week 7 loss are problems that have persisted since the beginning of the season when New Orleans lost at Detroit in overtime.

 As New Orleans prepares to host the Cleveland Browns on Sunday ( 1 p.m. ET, CBS ), here are five areas of concern that need fixing after a week in which Saints coach Kellen Moore said Monday that he was devoted to "self scouting" and figuring out the root of their issues.

 

 Saints need to improve on running the ball 

 The most significant change the Saints made coming out of their bye week was firing run game coordinator T.J. Paganetti on Monday . Moore said moving on from the coach will improve "workflow" with offensive line coach Brendan Nugent, who will be preparing the run game plan moving forward.

 It's unclear how much this move will change things as Moore said both Paganetti and Nugent both had a hand in the run game plan before.

 "There's elements of what we do from a presentation standpoint. There's the back end of putting together the game plans," Moore said. "And so Nuge has done some of the installations as far as in front of the team. I think we'll keep that consistent and there'll be some other changes as we go, but again, this is just trying to maximize our workflow."

 Moore said "there's no exact science," when asked why Nugent was retained over Paganetti, but repeated that this would help the team's process.

 

 "These decisions are never easy. Again, we'll shuffle some other stuff within the staff just to help our workflow and I think it'll put us in a good position," Moore said.

 Moore said he made the decision to cut ties with Paganetti over the weekend after a week of evaluation regarding the team's performance to date.

 "Some of the adjustments that we'll do schematically and fundamentally," Moore said. "Some of the adjustments we'll do from our workflow standpoint. Just felt like this was the most beneficial thing we can do."

 The Saints' 29th-ranked run game has averaged only 86 rushing yards per game and has been one of the team's biggest disappointments after the signing of free agent guard David Edwards and running back Travis Etienne.

 "I know that TJ had a great impact on our room ... and has been in successful systems. And so I feel like he had a big impact on us and he's a great human being, a great coach." Edwards said. "You feel somewhat responsible because us as players, us as linemen, we're not having success and you feel directly responsible for a decision like this. That's what makes it hard."

 Etienne, currently on injured reserve with a hamstring injury, has played in three games this season. His best game prior to the injury was a 57-yard rushing game against the Las Vegas Raiders in Week 3. The Saints have not had a 100-yard rusher this season, although Kendre Miller came close with a 70-yard game against the New York Giants . The Raiders (31st in run defense) and Giants (26th in run defense) were the only teams the Saints were able to run the ball against.

 Miller said the Steelers in particular had an answer for anything they tried to do on the ground.

 "They definitely had us schemed-up every run we had, had an answer for it," Miller said. "So I feel like it's just kind of one of those deals. They get paid like we do. So it's kind of just tough, but we just got to go out and execute better if that happens."

 Moore said he felt good about the emphasis on the run game in the offseason, particularly in training camp and joint practices. But he said the lack of consistency has been the issue.

 "For us it's about defining how we can play more consistent football, what from a schematic standpoint can we focus in on and what from a fundamental standpoint," Moore said.

 
 

 Kicking decisions are still up in the air 

 Moore said he doesn't plan to bring in kickers this week despite the struggles of veteran kicker Daniel Carlson , who has made just 66.7% of his kicks this season -- tied with Kansas City Chiefs kicker Harrison Butker , among others, for the second-worst percentage in the league.

 The Saints signed Carlson after neither Charlie Smyth nor Tanner Brown (who is no longer on the team) showed enough in training camp to win the job.

 "Obviously we just got to continue to evaluate the field goal opportunities," Moore said. "And so that'd be something that we'll just have to work through and discuss and find the best solution for Sunday."

 Moore did not say whether this would be an open competition with Smyth, only that the team would "see how this goes" this week.

 Carlson has made 8-of-12 kicks and has also missed two of his 18 PAT attempts. Most of Carlson's misses have been at the 50- to 60-yard range, with a miss from 62 yards in Week 1.

 If the Saints cut Carlson, they'll either go back to Smyth, who is on the practice squad and briefly kicked last season, or they'll have to find a veteran kicker available in November.

 

 Slow starts and finding 'a way to score points' 

 The Saints have tried to fix their issues with slow starts by tweaking their practice schedule, but have made no progress.

 New Orleans is last in the league in first-quarter points and have only scored points in the first quarter one time this season (Week 3 against the Raiders). That presents a problem in a game like the one against the Steelers, when possessions were limited and the Saints only got the ball six times on offense.

 

 If the Saints can't fix the slow starts, then how do they fix the bigger issue that is leading to the team's losses?

 "Obviously I'm going to spend a lot of time focused on how we can find a way to score points," Moore said during the bye week. "We've been able to defer a number of times to start the game. We've had a few instances like this past game where we've had some success, we've moved the ball and then we've just got stalled out as the drive has progressed."

 The Saints had to punt on their first possession against the Steelers after driving from their own 15-yard line to the Steelers' 48-yard line, but they were able to kick a field goal on their next possession, which came in the second quarter.

 "We just got to find a way to get ourselves in position to get those points in the opening drive. Second drive is obviously a field goal and third drive is a touchdown. That was a six-possession game. So obviously those don't come out around very often in this league, but obviously you recognize how valuable each possession is in those types."

 

 Putting more effort into protecting QB Tyler Shough 

 Shough went into the Steelers game with an injury to his left hand, and he appeared to come out of it with an injury to his right hand after taking a sack early on.

 Moore said during the bye week that Shough's new hand injury wasn't going to be a lingering problem, but it clearly affected QB during the game. Shough averaged 10.4 air yards per pass attempt before the sack and only 2.7 yards after, according to ESPN Research.

 Shough has two broken bones in his left hand. While he has a week to heal both hand issues, the inability to protect him could turn out to be the reason the Saints lose games down the stretch. Shough has been sacked 15 times (tied for eighth most in the NFL), but he has also been hit on 42 of his dropbacks (tied for ninth most in the NFL). If the Saints can't figure out a way to elevate their offensive line and protect him, their season could be lost.

 One key aspect could be getting left tackle Kelvin Banks Jr . back after he went on IR because of ankle surgery. While Banks does not have a timetable to return beyond "later in the season," he has now been out since Week 2.
